"rrENTEI SOCIETY SIFTATE ": A Social Brochure. -By kLEXANDER WADDELL. _ . _ _

Excerpts from some of the many Press opinions:— " The writer urges the necessity and the pleasure of spiritual intercourse with GOD."—Liverpool Mercury, April 15, 1891. "Mr. Waddell writes iu a pleasant wad earnest style, sifting the experiences he has had in various kparts of the country with a '<view topresenting something to the reader which is well worth considering."—,Warrington Axaminer, June 27th, 1291.

"Tire {papers are written from a remarkable knowledge of Seriptune, and resommend themselves by-heir quiet earnest- ness of style."—Seotsman, March 23rd, 1891. "With this key to the character of the work, the pages which follow prove interesting reading, and reveal the author as a close and appreciative observer of nature, and one who sees sermons in stones, books in the running brooks, and good in everytiaing."—Preston Herald, April Cb, 1891. , "A deep ragious tone pervades the book, and as the writer has evidently travelled far and near, his anecdotes and description of places are both telling and interesting."—The rsle of Wight nines, May 7th, 1891. "'The Tenth Society Siftate' deserves, and shanld have, a wide circulation.**—Northampton Herald, May 2114, 1891. ' "There is the ring of sound common sense in all the writer says. He sets up before young men a high ideal of life. * * It Is bright and interesting and in many parts, especially the •first chapter, it is lnunorous."—Christiun Union, April/8, 1891. Extract from letter received by the author from his friend, the Rev. J. Lewellyn Roberts, M.A. vicar of Spratton, and Hon. Canon of Peterborough, March 22nd, 1891.—" There is something so chattyand cheerful, so kindly and friendly, that one takes up the book and lays It clown again, and dips in here and dips in there, and finds that one has learned a good I deal, or received many a happy suggestion, all by way of a ' pleasant talk." "It is uot,often that an unprofessional author writes with such tact and skill,, with such ease and grace, and yet with such masterly farce as the author of the Tenth Society Siftate. The treatise has isa it all the traits of that originality and piquancy that makes a social brochure popular and fascin- aung."—ne arisgian union (2nd Notice), Juno 20th. 1891.

AIICTIONEERS have a nod way of accepting bids. IT is seldom that a good bank teller will tell any. thing about his bank. WE hear of men sowing wild oats, but who ever heard of a woman sowing anything but tares? "THIS LS not what it's cracked up to to be," as the miner said who pulverized quartz for gold and

found only mica. WHAT man is it that, when you have any deal- ings with him, you always like to have "give you fits ?" Your tailor. "LIFE is full of golden opportunities," remarks a philosopher, "but they aren't worth their salt when you try to cash them.' A YOUNG- lady attending balls and parties should have a female chaperone until she is able to call

some other chap her own. • IT sounds the same, but it makes some difference to the criminal if the judge decides to suspend sen- tence instead of sentencing to suspend. THE young lady who had a poor partner in the waltz changed him for a skilful one, because, she said, she believed in a better whirled. A SAVANT has discovered that man descended from the bear. We have heard before that man ascended from the bear, and have been shown the
tree where it occurred. A LITERARY man who recently tried the power of the human eye on a ferocious bull, is recovering from his wounds and bruises, but has lost all faith
in such mesmerism. THE arithmetic says that forty rods make one rood, but one rod -will sometimes make one rude . . __

boy. 'civil. SERVANT (to head of tha head)—" The butcher boy, sir, is at the door with the bill. What shall I tell him, sir?"—Head of the house—" Tell him to send a ten-pound sirloin roast for dinner." "WHY do you publish so many records of crime ?" asked a , gentleman of the late Horace Greeley. "Because they are the sin news of the paper," was the reply. AN old bachelor, who is not at all posted as to the fashions, says he would "like to know what the difference is between a travelling dress and a walking suit." A SAILOR on the way to his ship, met a boy on his way to, a circus. "I am going to sea," said the sailor. "I am going to see, too," responded the boy. A POOR Irishman, seeing a crowd of people ap- proaching, asked what was the matter. He was answered, "A man going to be buried." "Oh," he remarked, "I'll stop to see that, for we carry them to be buried in our country."

TERRIBLE EXAMPLE.—" I know a victim to tobacco," said a lecturer, "who hasn't tasted food for nearly thirty years." How do you know ?" asked an auditor. "Because the tobacco killed him in 1856," was the reply. " IF."—I would box your ears," said a young , lady to her stupid and tiresome admirer, if—" "If what ?" he anxiously asked. "If," she re- peated, "I could get a box large enough ' for the purpose." PLENTY of milk in your cans this morning ?" a customer asked a milkman the other morning. And the milkman nodded gravely, as, without a wink of his eye, he made reply: " Chalkful." "You are such a strange girl," said Charlie. "Really, I don't know what to make of you." Well, then, I'll tell you, Charlie," replied Ara- minta • "make a wife of me." Charlie did so at the earliest opportunity. MARITAL CONFESSIONS.—" My dear," said a fond wife, "when we were engaged, I always slept with your last letter under my pillow." "And I," mur- mured her husband—" I often went to sleep over your letters." THEY were sailing in the little boat together, and she said: "Are we running before the wind now, George ?" "No, my darling," said he • "our boat is hugging the shore." " Ah," she exclaimed, "what a beautiful example you have here !" A YOUNG lady (hesitating for a word in describ- ing a rejected suitor)—" He is not a tyrant, not exactly domineering, but—"—" Dogmatic," sug- gested her friend. "No, he has not dignity enough for that. I think pupmatic would convey my mean- ing admirably." • A GOOD old lady, a widow, having been asked if she didn't think that her husband shortened his days by too much hard work, replied: "No, I don't think he did. As near as I can remember, every one of his days was just as long as other people's." SENSIBLE CREATURES.—Women somehow get over childish notions that men never outgrow. Some men celebrate the anniversary of every birthday as long as they live, while women abandon the childish custom almost as soon as they grow up. "Mn.COLDCASH, I have come to ask for t

hand of your daughter." "My daughter, sir ? " "Yes. I can't live without her." "Well, sir, finish your sentence." "Finish my sentence ? " "Yes, you were about to say you could not live without her income. Let us be frank, my dear sir."

As a young couple were on their bridal trip to Europe, the husband remarked to his bride, as the vessel stopped at her first port: "My dear, they have dropped their anchor." To which she naively replied: "Well, it serves them right, for it has been hanging over the side during the whole voyage." A FRENCH lady, on her arrival in this country, would eat only such dishes as she was acquainted with, and being on one occasion pressed to partake of a dish new to her, she politely replied, think- ing she was expressing herself in admirable English: "No, I thank you; I eat only my ac- - quaintances." A.GENTLEMAN, having occasion to praise a kind- hearted Irish woman for her good deeds, said to her: "Well, well, Kate, if there is heaven in the next world, you will get to it." As quick as lightning came the reply: "God bless ye Mr. P.; an' sure, If I do, I'll lave the gate open for you." A COUPLE of young men staying unconscionably late one night with their sweethearts, were sur- prised to see the "old man" looking about the hall, and finally the parlour, as though in search of something. What are you looking for, pa ? " at last asked ow of the girls. "The morning papers," growled the old man, and the young men took a hasty leave. TOUGH ENOUGH.—" What do you want to set such a tough chicken before me for ?" indignantly exclaimed a fair damsel in a restaurant the other day. "'Age before beauty' always, you know, ma'am," replied the polite attendant, who well "knew how to serve his employer and a tough .ohicken at the same time. "WHAT a very pretty girl your friend is, Miss Constantino. !" said Dumley. Such bright eyes and clear complexion one seldom sees. Hasn't she Irish blood in her veins ?" "Oh, yes," Miss Con- stantino, replied • "she is a true daughter of Erin Go Bragh." "Well, all I have to say is," added Dumley, "that Mr. and Mrs. Go Bragh ought to be proud of her." ME story is told that Whittier and Ticknor, his.publisher, were making a short pedestrian tour some years ago, when, to their stfrprise, an angry bull stood on the footpath, evidently determined to demolish both poet and publisher. I think," said Ticknor, "that it will be prudent to give this reviewer a wide margin." "Yes," replied tht poet; "it appears to be a disputed passage." SNOBSON (who, at the club, is discussing with young Bullock their respective pedigrees)—" It's all very well for you to tawk, my deals fellaw, but Bullock is a dooced vulgaw name, don't chew know ?" Bullock—" Vulgaw, saw I What do you mean, saw? Why, the Bullocks came from Yawkshire, saw, mow than five centuxies ago." Snobson—" Yaas, I know, of cawse. The Snob. sons ate them when they got to London, don't chew know ?" A MAN rather below the medium height says that he. cannot avoid being offended at any refer- ence to his size, and relates how he was once utterly crushed in an argument. He had the best of it, and was walking the room the more strongly to lay down and emphasize his points, when the other fellow calmly remarked: Sit down, Jones; you look taller sitting down." It made him so mad that he could not say another word. "A BACKWARD fall," said a member of the legis- lature recently, when his colleague suddenly sat down on the slippery walk leading from the capitol. "An early spring," answered the nimble law maker _jumping to his feet instanter.

div.head: " CAPITAL " CHAT.
div.p: " CAPITAL " CHAT.

Mr. Gladstone was prevented from attending the funeral service for the late Sir Charles Forster, M.P.,at St. Margaret's solely by the stormy weatker. The "Chester Chronicle" stetes that Mr. Gladstone is giving two sittings to Sir J. Everett Millais, who is making important alterations in the last(Jubilee) picture painted of him.
The following is "Punch's" epigram on the win- ner of the Queen's prize:
WELL DONE, DEAR. We've levelled farms, we've planted trees; And many mighty men of means Have shot at deer, and, if you please, A Dear has shot and won the Queen's.

The committee of the International Working Class Socialist Congress, which is to assemble in Brussels on the 16th of August has issued an ad- dress of invitation to the working-class organisa- tions of all countries. Eight days will be occupied in the debates, which will embrace a wide range of subjects relating to industrial organisation,political enfranchisement, legislation for the protection, and in the interests of the working-classes, internation- al action, and other kindred topics.
The following entry in the Journal of the House of Commons commemorates Mr. Atkinson's futile opposition to the third reading of the London and South Western Railway Rates and Charges Bill: . .

"The Speaker stated he-thought the Ayes— hail it; but on his decision being challenged, it appeared to Mr. Speaker that the division was frivolously claimed,and he directed the Noes to stand up in their places; whereupon, one member having stood up, Mr. Speaker declared that the Ayes had it."

The Prince of Naples, after visiting the House of I Lords on Tuesday, where he stayed five minutes, went on to the House of Commons, where he re- mained for ten. He was accompanied by the Italian Minister, and was conducted to the Diplomatic Gallery by Colonel Legge,the Assistant Sergeant-at- Arms. The appearance of the House must have been disappointing to his Royal Highness's precon- ceived views of the historic institution. Dr. Clarke was on his legs, addressing an audience of nineteen persons.

The "Daily Chronicle" says :—That "ridiculous piece of humbug," as Lord Grimthorpe styles the formal confirmation of an archbishop's election, was solemnly performed at St. George's Chapel, Hanover-square, on Wednesday. All the provin- cial and diocesan officials who bag enormous fees from the translated prelate were of course loudly in attendance, and the customary formalities ensued in Dr. Maclagan being "definitely sentenced" to the Archbishopric of York and £lO,OOO per annum, with perquisites for the rest of his natural life.

The Government are in an awkward position with respect to the Training Colleges (Ireland) Bill. At the commencement of Tuesday's sitting of the House of Commons the Itlsh members, through Mr. Healy, privately intimated their intention, should the Bill be abandoned, to "take it out of the Irish Estimates, of which there remained a considerable block. On the contrary, if Mr. Balfour sticks to his Bill, and insists on carrying UAL T. W. Russell, hacked up by Colonel Saunderson, has plainly in- timated his intention of using all the forms of the House to obstruct it.

It was entirely owing to tne Queen that M. Wad- dington went to Hatfield to meet the German Em- peror, as it was really her Majesty who pulled the strings in that matter, and the free expression of her commonsense views about the ill-advised visit of the Empress Frederick to Paris has dispellled the sullen resentment against France which the Emperor William has been nourishing during the last five months. The Queen has rendered a valuable service to Europe by cooling down her grandson, and she ought to get the credit both .of his Guildhall speech and of his unexpectedly friendly demeanour to the French Ambassador, as she directly inspired both the one and the other.

Heligolanders have been a little puzzled during the past few weeks owing to some balloon experi- ments which Captain von Forster, of the German Marine Service, has been making on and about the island. Ascents have taken place by day and night with the object of ,holding communication sea- wards with the island, and for balloon signalling. The appearance of the balloons amazed the adult population, and gave infinite delight to the lilveniles, for a balloon is a rare sight in Heligoland. Many improvements have been made on the island, and the services of some skilled German artizans have been requisitioned for the purpose of well- :inking in the upper part of the place.

The Crown Princess Sophie of Greece, it will be remembered, recently went over to the Greek Orthodox Church, and some Berlin papers tell an extraordinary story in connection with her conver- sion. The Orthodox ritual requires all converts to undergo total immersion, but in the Princess's case this part of the ceremony was dispensed with. She was only sprinkled on the head and forehead. The Patriarch of Constantinople, it is said, is now mak- ing energetic protests as to this concession, declar- ing that the Princess must be regarded as a heretic till the whole ceremony has been performed with- out curtailment. In the Orthodox Press the Patri- Arch of Athens and the Holy Synod are severely reprimanded for their indulgence.

It has been a good deal noted that on recent bright afternoons the attendance of members of Parliament on the terrace of the House of Com- mons has been much larger than within the House itself. The phenomenon may be explained by the fact that the terrace is one of the most select and pleasant promenades in town, and that ladies may be brought there. Teas are served out on little round tables, and, members and their lady friends pass the time very pleasantly, without much thought of the business which may be transacting within. These parties have been growing in num- ber of late, and it is said that the Speaker has directed his attention to this "excessive entertain- ment" of ladies by members who should be in per- formance of their duties elsewhere. Some new re- gulations restricting the liberty of ladies within the House are expected next Session.

The workings of an uneasy conscience appear clearly traceable in the three "cracker mottoes" which were found upon Mitchell, the young clerk who has just been convicted of forgery and of robbing the Saltley Bank. The first of these which he had so carefully preserved is from" Macbeth" : Things without all remedy Should be without regard ; what's done is done.
The second is also Shakespearian, from "Richard
I have not that alacrity of spirit Nor cheer of mind that I was wont to have.
The last which is stated to be "from Byron's Lucrece,' a poem which is not familiar to the poet's admirers, is : No perfection is so absolute That some impurity doth not pollute. _ _
The melancholy foreboding which these mottoes indicate has been only too literally fulfilled in the sentence of this youthful offender to ten years' penal servitude.

An amusing story of the late Archbishop of Can- terbury is told by Mr. Boyd in his reminiscences of that prelate in " tongman's, Magazine." It is vouched for as literally true, the writer's authority being Dean Stanley, who related it in Archbishop Tait's presence at a Bishops' dinner at Lambeth. On one of his latest visits to a certain country house in a Scottish county, Dr. Tait went alone to the post office to send a telegram to his brother. He wrote it out. "The Archbishop of Canterbury to Sheriff Tait,' and handed it in. The sceptical old postmaster read it aloud in contemptuous tones. " The Archbishop of Canterbury ! " and added, " Wha may ye be that taks this cognomen ? " The Archbishop, taken aback, remained silent for a moment. The morning was cold, and he had a woollen comforter wrapped round his neck; but on second view the postmaster thought he looked more respectable than on the first, and added, "Maybe ye're the gentleman himsel'." Tait replied modestly. "For want of a better, I am." On which the good old Scot hastened to apologise for his first suspicion of Imposture; adding, "I might have seen you were rather consequential about the legs." Then he added- words of cheer,which Tait said truly were vitally Scotch : "I have a son in London, a lad in a shop; and he gaed to hear ye preach one day, and was verra weel satisfeed."

div.head: EXAMINER, SATLRDAY, AUGUST 1, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATLRDAY, AUGUST 1, 1891.
ACROSS THE ATLANTIC.
BY "TOWNSMAN." YII.-AMONG THE AMERICANS.

THE MOVING MONTH.—THE PEOPLE.—THE POLICE, May is the "moving month" in America, and I arrived in the great Republic just in time to see what we Britishers are apt to regard as almost an impossibility—houses on the move. All tenancies across the Atlantic are yearly,and commence on the first of May. On this date, therefore, furniture removers have as much work as they can get through, and for the next week nearly every other vehicle you see contains furniture. There are no covered removal vans such as we have, as it would not pay to keep them doing nothing 51 weeks out of the year; but the furniture is removed on bug- gies, and as the weather is fairly settled at this season no necessity arises for covered vans. But the greatest novelty is to see a house removed. If a man has built a house on a plot he has rented, , and he becomes dissatisfied with his location, he finds another plot and removes his abode just as it stands to the new pitch. Oftener than not, it happens that the new location is two or three I streets away, and then it is you see the house fairly on the move. Frame houses are laid on a brick or stone foundation, and the first step towards the re- moval is taken by masons,who knock holes through • the foundation. Through then holes beams, the length of the house, are inserted, and under these are placed powerful lifting jacks. When all the beams and jacks are in position, the remaining portion of the foundation is knocked out, and the house settles on the beams. Rollers are then put under the beams, and with the aid of chains and a , windlass worked by a horse,the dwelling starts on its I travels. Along the streets are laid planks on which the rollers travel, and when the windlass is fixed at the end of a long street or avenue a good opportun- ity is afforded of witnessing the operation. It is a strange sight to see an eight or ten roomed house on its way down a public street to new quarters, and stranger still when one sees, as 1 did in Chicago, a cage bird swinging in its wire prison as the house rolled and creaked along to its destina- tion. The houses are smartly moved from one location to another, but the whole operation from start to finish i occupies a month. I saw several houses, in big and little cities, on the move, and it is no wonder that all through May the first ques- tion, after the usual greetings have been exchanged between friends, is, "What's your address ?" THE PEOPLE. - Without - exception, the, people of America are eminently social and hospitable to the stranger, and especially to the Englishman. In the course of my travels, I came across representatives of the various nations that in the aggregate go to make up the great American commonwealth,and whether Welsh, Irish,Scotch, Dutch, Swedish, French, German, Ital- ian, Russian, or native American—with all of whom I conversed—one and all treated me with the great- est kindness and consideration. In his intercourse with the polite European nations, Brother Jonathan has caught some of their polish, and he uses it with becoming dignity at all times. As all Americans are considered to be upon a social equality—whether millionaire or mudlark—every man addresses his fellow citizen with proper respect, and even the children on the streets behave quite differently to what English children do. Not but what I have seen citizens provoked. I have heard them asked questions that an Englishman would answer by quickly referring the enquirer to the door, but in every case the American returned a civil answer, and bowed the questioner out with some show of politeness. The people too are exceedingly respect- able. You see none of the dilapidated, drink-satu- rated individuals, such as roll about the streets of English towns, advertising the potency of some brewer's production and their own capacity for imbibition. No loafers obstruct the street corners, whilst tramps are arrested on mere suspicion, and "sent up" for 60 days. Everybody seems to have work to do, and to be bent on its accomplishment. Money is plentiful amongst the people, and it is spent as freely as it is earned. Native- born Americans manifest the liveliest in- terest in things English. They are particularly concerned as to the incomes of the wage- earning classes, and the cost of living in the old country. When you have satisfied their curiosity on these points they thank their stars they.live in a bigger country, even in the matter of salaries. They delight in hearing descriptions of the natural beauties of England, but can hardly realise that, they are not quite on such a very extensive scale as the picturesque panoramas of America. For all that, they all express a desire to see Europe for them- selves. The people are early risers and hard workers. American morning trains are as crowded at six o'clock as ours are at ten o'clock. The morn- ing milk is delivered at half-past five, and at seven the butcher calls to see what joint is wanted for dinner. It must not, however, be inferred that Americans are all work. They stick to work while it is about,but they appear as a general rule to take life easily. They can all find time for recreation and for reading the numerous morning and evening papers that are published. There are papers for everybody and in every language. The boys who hawk papers on the streets appear to have broken out of boarding school, they are so well dressed in comparison to the English boy newsvendors. Though American citizens speak every language under the sun, English is the prevailing means of comMunication, and there is unbounded scope for the spread of our mother tongue. The general feel- ing about immigrants, and one which they them- selves quickly recognise, was forcibly expressed by a Canadian at Niagara. Seeing him critically surveying a car load of fresh arrivals, mostly Ger- mans, who had been deposited on the depot to make change of cars, I approached him, and remarked that one needed to be a linguist to get along with new corners. "It isn't at all necessary," he replied. "Thank God, they've all got to learn English to do any good." The juvenile portion of the community are clothed quite differently to English children. Up to about six years of age all the juveniles wear long cfothes with sleeves, which strike the stranger as very peculiar, and which seem to make the child- ren prematurely old. It is, however, a very wise custom, as it protects the little folks much better from the weather than the English style of juvenile clothing does. When the novelty of the thing has worn off, it is a positive treat to see the young folks tripping along the sidewalks, and the old-fashioned I manner in which they pick up their dresses when they want to run is really very amusing. To the new comer every action of the juveniles is very comical, and they remind him very forcibly of Kate Greenaway's charming little pictures of miniature men and women. THE POLICE. Armed as they are with long staves, the. ‘3,;erica,n police are not very awe-inspiring. Dress;''f _in dark blue tunics, grey trousers, and grey helmelts with turned down brims, they are a somewhat round- shouldered lot of officers, who slouch about in a very suspicious manner, and give you the impres- sion that they are nothing but sneaks them- selves. The Impression is heightened by the fact that the turned-down-brimmed helmets fit too mulch, and the wearers seem to have pulled them down over their faces to conceal their ident- ity. They try to do as little as they can for their money, and like all other Americans they are in- veterate smokers. The police wink at all sorts of offences, and to such an extent that the citizens of many cities have to form themselves into Com- mittees of "Law and Order" to insist upon the police carrying out the duties they are paid to per- form! The pride and glory of an American " Bobby " is his staff, which is twice as long, as an English policeman's truncheon,. and which he constantly, carries in his hand. It is pitiable to see him on a hot day with his inseparable companion. He carries it first in one hand, then in the other, then he swings it by the ,cord, then stands at !ease with it across his arms, then he grips it with a ferocity that seems to indicate he would like to use it on some fellow's skull just by way of variety; then he seems to relent of his sinister idea and goes through all these manoeuvres once more. As the day wears on the baton, seems to become a bar of hot iron, it changes hands so often,and it is scarcely surprising that when the day's duty is done, the officer is so anxious to flee from this instrument of torture that he so far forgets himself as to monopolise the best seat on the car. The Americans generally also pride themselves on their. Policemen's equipment in the matter of staves, and the national vanity is further fanned by the newspapers, which print long articles comparing the armament of the police of the vari- ous nations of Europe with that of their own. Naturally the palm is awarded to Bro. Jonathan's guardian of the peace simply and solely because his staff is the longest and most freely used.

GENERAL BOOTH'S DEPARTURE.

General tooth sailed from Southampton on SatuKday afternoon in the new Union steamer Scot, for Cape Town, on the first stage of his journey round the world. The General was escorted from the station to the quay by a large procession, and the special tender which conveyed him to the Scot was followed by a flotilla of steamboats gaily decked with flags and crowded with enthusiastic passengers.

div.head: TIIORNTJN.
div.p: TIIORNTJN.
BY LOUISA BIGG. AUTHOR OF "CLARE WELSMAN," ETO.
CHAPTER X.

The night of Dillon's lecture arrived, and the coffee-room and reading-room were full by half-past seven, while by eight o'clock the passage was full also, though there were only five or six of its occupants who were at all likely to hear one word of the proceedings. In one of the seats near the platform sat Jessie Grayson, looking radiant in a black lace bonnet and crimson roses, with her Cheeks flushed and dark eyes sparkling with excite- ment. Mr. Delafield, in the intervals of keeping a general supervision, sat by her, but he was looking absent, and replied rather at random to her gay flow of talk. There was a sound of a horse's rapid footsteps, and Lmtitia's little brougham drew up at the (loon
Mr. Delafied hurried out, and in a few moments ushered in Miss Thornton, Miss Prisey, and Dillon. _ _ .

"I am afraid we are rather late," said the former lady; "you must lay the blame on vousin Priscy, for Robert and I have been ready for ages." The fact is that at the critical moment of start- ing, Miss Prisey had mislaid her umbrella, a favourite implement adorned with a carved ivory rose, ailed no entreaties could induce her to start without it, although there was no sign of rain and they were going all the way in a closed carriage. Dillon was not altogether sorry for the delay, for being a young orator he was sensitive to outward conditions, and preferred plunging at once into his subject, to sitting to be stared at for ten minutes by a roomful of people. In a few well-chosen words Mr. Dela6eld intro- duced the lecturer, and then took his seat by aetitia as if he had a right at her side. Several of the audience smiled as he did so, but not Jessie Grayson; the light faded out of her face, and she sat looking dimmed and chilled; if anyone had happened to watch her he would have wondered at the sudden change' but fortunately no one took any notice of her. Least of all did Letitia, nestled in dark green velvet and furs, guess how much her friend was suffering at her hands. "Oh, it is too hard—she has everything, all the riches ancrall the love," poor Jessie was crying in the bitterness of her heart : "Of course, he will marry her; it is no wonder that he likes her the best.

It did not occur to Jessie that any woman upon whom Mr. Delafield vouchsafed to fii: his affections could possibly be indifferent to the honour. Tom Jenk inson was also watching the party from the Firs with some dissatisfaction. He was a young man with thin light hair, a retreating chin and fosehead, and an over-weaning sense of his own abilities. He held strong opinions on the in- equality of the sexes, and had an uncomfortable suspicion that Ltitia did not recognise her own inferiority, but he was anxious to gain her favour notwithstanding. As I have said, his one object in life was to attain "a position," and he considered that Lretitio, and her coffers would be important factors in the process of arriving at the wtshed-for consummation. A good number of the regular frequenters of the Institute and their friends were present, but as a rule they would have felt a more lively interest in the entertainment if Dillon had promised a few rousing pictures of headless-corpses and impaled prisoners, or even if he had arranged to appear in Mussulman costume or to dance a war- dance.

A few youths of the better class, having heard warm praises of Dillon from their lady friends, cherished a vague hope that, being an unprofessional lecturer, he might break down or otherwise render himself ridiculous and amusing, but were soon con- vinced on seeing hira that their expectations were vain, and relapsed into a settled melancholy. With this last exception it was a decidedly sympathetic audience. For nearly an hour Dillon related his adventures as war correspondent, and fairly riveted the attention of his hearers by a succession of anecdotes, first humorous and per- sonal, but gradually deepening in colour till at last he laid before them a battle field in all its horror; then another, and another, with all their adjuncts of burning villages and plundered and outraged peasantry. There was no imaginary detail; every scene he spoke of he had witnessed and it had burnt itself into his memory. "Year by year that I have lived," he said, "has added its weight of evidence against this hateful evil of our race; this hideous wrong that men phrase a necessity. It is no necessity if the leading spirits in a nation would will to put it down, as slavery was put down. Ido not say peace at any price; for I remember Leyden and I remember Dunbar. There may be times when the Lord is a man of war, but in nine cases out of ten it is not the Lord but the Devil. War is a Christianizer of heathen nations, we are often told ; possibly, but for my part I have no great faith in apostles of a gospel of peace whose feet are red with blood, and I have often observed that we are chiefly anxious for the salva- tion of tribes that happen to possess a gold coast or a diamond field. I lately read these words, written by .a gallant English Officer I have no hesitation m saying that five-sixths of our Afriean wars, and a still larger proportion of our Indian wars, in America, have had their beginnings in wrongs done in the first instance by white men upon natives.' What an indictment against a proud nation like ours—a nation boastful of its moral culture and high moral civilisation 1 It is time that we awoke to the fact that robbery, and murder do not cease to be crimes when committed by a nation instead of a man. It is tine that we who would fain rank with the first nations of the world, should once for all unlearn the doctrine that might is right, and cease to slaughter men and women merely because they have a preference for their own faiths and their own rulers. War should be no other than a giant police force; the police force of a Court of Justice for the nations guch as may one day be founded. I shall be told that the scheme of such a court is Utopian. So is everything worth working for, till men are shown that it can be done. Was not the steam-engine ; Utopian? the abolition of slavery? the discovery of the Americas? I have sometimes thought that ridicule is the hall-mark of a good cause. Let every man and woman think this question out, and let us band ourselves together and make this Utopia a solid reality. Every leading nation in Europe must be influenced, working from the masses upward, till at last it shall be no longer possible for one man to lead on a nation to slaughter another nation with which it has no quarrel. The poor man then would no longer die fo win the rich man a place, and the subject would not perish because the king pleased. Faith only is wanted to move the mountains that shut out the sun of peace and when we sit with folded hands and vow that wars are necessary we help to make them necessary. "There is a conviction abroad that to love peace is to be but a poor creature. It may he so. For my part with the world as it is, I love war, I love fighters; but, we have need to learn what to fight and that the gun and sword are clumsy weapons for civilised man. • The war-spirit is inherent in us and is necessary to us, but the higher we rise in :he scale of humanity the more surely will our warfare be with spiritual weapons, and our foes not our fellow men, but the crushing evils that distract our world—Tyranny —lnj ustice—iguor- ance—Bigotry. "One word in conclusion. No one admires more than I the self-sacrifice, the endurance, and bravery of the &oldies, but the more I admire him the more I grudge the shedding of his blood that private ambition or lust of power and wealth and insular arrogance may be sated." I give a mere outline of Dillon's speech, but this is the summary of what he said that night, and when he sax down there were some hearty clapping and stamping of feet and one or two short speeches. Old Major Williams was sitting near the plat- form and as soon as the audience began to disperse he made his way up to Dillon and shook hands with him warmly, saying, to the gratification of the latter— "'A very good speech, and I agree with nearly everything you have said. It makes me in a rage when fellows come round and cb.ll us butchers and all kinds of names; it is hard upon an old soldier, sir; as if it was our fault. Ido not like war, and I hope you'll get us all done away with as soon as you can. While there's any fighting to be done for the country—well, do it, but every good soldier, every patriot, would rather have peace than war; why, the Iron Duke himself hated war." Several others came up, and a working man or two stood shyly near the door to shake hands with the young lecturerias he went out. "What a splendid night I' cried Ltetitia. "I think I will walk home if you will take care of me, Robert." So, having safely deposited Miss Priscy in the carriage they set off for a quick walk over the hard ground, with a million ef stars looking down upon them.

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE.
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE.
DEPARTURE FROM LOWESTOFT

Mr. Gladstone left Lowestoft at one o'clock. on Tues- day, for London, travelling by special sal^on carriage attached to the express. A great crowd gathered at the station to see him off, and the Mayor and Town Clerk were on the platform in their official capacity to bid the ex-Premier good-bye. Mr. Gladstone said he was quite recovered from his recent illness, and that he had greatly enjoyed his visit to the locality.
LABOUR CANDIDATE FOR WIGAN.

At a crowded and representative meeting of the Wigan Liberal Three Hundred on Monday evening, presided over by Councillor Richard Johnson, Mr. Thomas Aspinwall was enthusiastically adopted as the Labour and Liberal candidate for the borough at the next election, in opposition to Mr. F. S.Pow- ell, Ii .P. Mr. Aspinwall, who is a miners' agent for the Wigan district, submitted his views oif leading political questions, declaring himself in favour of Home Rule for Ireland, Church disestablish ment in Wales, one man one vote, and, in fact, the whole programme enunciated by the National Liberal Federation. A resolution thanking Mr. Aspinwall for his address, and urging his acceptance as can- didate, proposed by Councillor J. Wilson, J.P., sec- onded by Mr. Richard Lee, J.P., and supported by Councillor M'Quaid, leader of the Irish party in the borough, was adopted with cheers.

The increasing prevalence of premature baldness is a fact now recognised by the medical profession. According to Dr. Joseph Tyson's remarks in "The Lancet," the principal cause, although not the sole one, seems to be the frequent covering of the head. Women notoriously lose their hair less often. The cause is found in the comparative lightness of their head gear. Coming to practical remedies, or pre- ventatives, we are told by this authority, that children should as much as possible do without caps, and that hats, when worn, should be of the lightest descripzion. The chimney-pot hat cannot, we are aware,be too strongly condemned. In win- ter a light felt, well ventilated and unlined, is best. Washing the head more than once a week is deem- ed harmful ; continual brushing with hard brushes is also tv be avoided. Greasing the hair, once so general, is now considered yulgar, but a little sim- ple grease or oil applied after washing would, we are assured, be beneficial.

div.head: CONGREGATIONALISM IN WALES.
div.p: CONGREGATIONALISM IN WALES.

MEETINGS AT WREXIIIAM, The annual meetings of the Union of the Congregational Churches of Wales have been held this week at Wrexham, and were initiated on Monday night with an enthusiastic temperance meeting, presided over by Mr. E. Phillips, ex- Mayor of Aberavon, South Wales. At the conclusion of the temperance meeting the following resolution,proposed by the Rev. D. John Thomas (Liverpool), and seconded by Alderman T. Williams, J.P. (Merthyr), was unani- mously passed :—" That this meeting of the Welsh Con- gregational Union desires to express its deep gratification at the decision of the House of Lords in the case of Sharpe v. Wakefield '—a decision that has proved in the most emphatic manner that the magistrates have power to withhold any license to sell intoxicating drinks. It also rejoices in view of the awakening in many districts of the licensing question, and appeals in the most earnest manner to the justices of the country to make use of their powers to decline granting any new licenses, and also to reduce the number of licenses already in force, thereby assisting to save our nation from the intemperance and drunkenness that is so disastrous to it politically, socially, and morally." On Wednesday resolutions were passed on the ques- tion of Welsh intermediate education and the charges brought by the Bishops of St. Asaph and Llandaff that "Welsh Nonconformist ministers were knocking at the door of the Established Church and applying for admis- sion.'
..-......,-..-. SERMONS BY TELEPHONE.

The attempt to connect the pulpit of Christ Church, Birmingham, with the telephone system, of which we gave a detailed description some time ago, has not been suffered to become a mere barren experiment. The Telephone Company have lately perfected the arrangements, and are now supplying oral sermons at private residences on a rather extensive scale. Naturally it is the bed- ridden and the sick who most appreciate the ad- vantage of being able to hear a preacher without lattending service. A dozen yards or so of loose, flexible, cord is attached to the ordinary receiver, and a special U-shaped instrument supplied to fix on the head, with an ear-box for each ear. Thus provided it is possible, it is said, for the sick to hear comfortably while in bed. In a quiet room the tolling of the bell can be heard half-an-hour before service; the prayers can be followed, the responses emphasised, and every word of the ser- mon distinguished; while solos in the anthems are, we are assured, heard as distinctly as if one stood next to the singer. Even a casual, cough adiong the audience can be distinguished. There is stated to be a lady in Smallheath who has been bedridden for three years, and whose spiritual wants are thus supplied ; another at Egbaston, who has not been able to attend a church for seven years; and in the Birmingham jewellery district there are a dozen watchmen who, being on duty every Sunday, could never hear a sermon extept in this fashion. Twenty-four calls, representing, it is calculated,some sixty subscribers,are stated to have been received at the telephone office from Christ Church one night last week,and a similar number in , the morning. Subscribers in Manchester, Notting- ham, London, Coventry, Stafford, Wolverhampton, and Worcester have also availed themselves of this opportunity of being supplied with a spoken ser- mon at a trifling coat. LORD SALISBURY AT THE MANSION

div.head: HOUSE.
div.p: HOUSE.

Her Majesty's Ministers were on Wednesday night, en- tertained at dinner by Sir Joseph Savory, Bart. (Lord Mayor), and the Lady Mayoress. The banquet took place in the Mansion House, the Lord Mayor and Lady Mayoress receiving their guests in the saloon. Lord Salisbury, speaking in reply to a toast said they were at the close of a long seesion—a session full of anxiety and fatigue, but he was thankful to think it had been a session which the people would recognise as of hard and valuable work. The Government had made two great experiments. They had passed a Free Edu- cation Bill, and by doing so they did not bate one particle of their hope and belief that they had added to the strength and influence of that great system of edu- cation which distinguished this nation among the nations of the world. The other great experiment was that the Government had done their best to apply not a temporary but a permanent cure to the evils with which Ireland had been afflicted for generations. Look- ing back five years, when they were fresh from a general election, he believed that the voice of the people of this country was then irrevocably expressed against any severance of the two nations' and that in the end there could be to doubt that this kingdom would remain a United Kingdom to sustain the glory and the power which the United Kingdon had won. With regard to foreign affairs, he never knew a period wher. there was less of foreign difficulty or trouble to ripple the tranquil surface of the times. He never knew-European politics so tranquil as they were now. ili they wished for anxiety they had to go over to 'America. In the North things were happily quiet, but in the South it was not so. They had constant disturb- ances and recklessness of revolutionary finance, but it was no part of our duty to interfere. The prospect in Europe was much more satisfactory. The Eastern ques- tion was not settled, but the rapid progress of Egypt and Bulgaria furnished a hope that from the centres of civilis- ation which they constituted would issue the influence and the spirit by which the Eastern question would be solved in the only effective and permanent manner. Re- ferring to the visit of the German Emperor, his Lord- ship said the pacific sentiments expressed by him must have carried conviction to all who heard them." A few weeks hence we hoped that we should welcome in our harbours the fleet of the great French Republic, and that we should see in that event a renewed ond most welcome guarantee of peace and amity between the two- great countries represented. Our allies were all those who desired peace.

"I wanted to speak to you about the lecture," said Lmtitia, frankly; "why did you never tell us what you thought about these things? I suppose you considered that we were only women, and should not care for anything sensible." "It was you who stopped me, Letitia; I have wished to tell you a hundred times, but I fancied you would say that I was amusing myself with philanthropy, like Delafield." "Oh, is it possible, is it possible that you have understood me so little ? ' said Ltitia, forgetting how secret she had kept all her longings on Dillon 's behalf. She had been so open with herself that she could not realise how reserved she had been with him, and that he could have no clue to her hidden thoughts. Somehow he felt-it more difficult to begin talk- ing of his projects when alone with Letitia than to speak of them to a crowd of strangers, and he said almost timidly: "Then you think it is worth while to try and make the world better in this way, even if one should fail?"

"It is worth giving your whole life to it. I did not know people had great aims now; my world is so small, and I have grown so sceptical of motives; I thought every one was the same, and only cared for what they could get-" she panted out with difficulty, so excited and glad was she. Psyche had found the treasure she sought, but as yet she could hardly believe it. "I mean to give my life to it," said he, gravely. "There are others who think as I do, and we must persuade the world to believe with us. It will be slow, but we must hold on, and never lose hope. Think, Letitia, of the greatness of a work like this! A good that may touch all nations through- out all time to come. The vision of it carries me away till nothing else seems worth the doing." "You will let me help you? at least I can give some money, and I have more than I know what to do with."

"I wish you had less," said Dillon, impulsively, instead of answering her. "You think it is not good for me ?" "I think it is bad for me ?" "Bad for you? How can that be? I do not understand you." "If I were only rich—like Delafield, for instance —1 I never cared about money before, bat now I see how much it can do." _

" It seeews to me of very little consequence com- pared to cater things," said Lmtitia. They had reached the garden and nothing more was said then, but each felt that the relations between them were changed, and that they had not known one another till that night. The two ladies went to their rooms early, leaving Dillon, who was feeling sleepless with excitement, to think over the events of the day by the dining- room fire. He had fallen into a deep reverie, and was startled when someone gently turned the handle of the door anti came into the room. There was a large screen stretching half across the room, and he had watched anxiously till the mysterious visitant came from behind it, expecting he knew not what. It was Lmtitia, and a spirit from the other world would scarcely have surprised him more. He rose and set a chair for her, for she was crossing the room towards the fire, and her busi- ness, whatever it was, was evidently with him. She did not sit down, however, but stood on the hearthrug, holding something in her hand. "Do not look so frightened at me, Robert," she said, laughing nervously, "I am not-crazy or walk- ing in my sleep. I brought you this, for I kept thinking about it, and wanted to get it off my mind to-night. You will need money to carry out your plans—l mean about a court of justice for all nations, and the rest—and I do not know how else to help you." She put a cheque for a hundred pounds into Dillon's hand, and turned to leave the room. For a few seconds he stood looking stupidly at the piece of paper with Lretitia's clear decided handwriting running across it, and could say nothing. lhen he held it towards her and told her that he could not take so much.

"But it is my own," she pleaded, "and it will please me so much ' • you must keep it." The voice of the woman he loved, her childlike confi- dence in him, her sweet sympathetic face, over- came him altogether. He forgot all his scruples and hesitations, and remembered only La3titia and his love. He seized her little cold hands and kissed them with all his heart in the kiss.
"I will only keep it on one condition," he mur- mured, "you must give me yourself too." She slipped away without a word, but she had not said no.

div.head: CHAPTER 7.1.
div.p: CHAPTER 7.1.

It was the day after the lecture and Lretitia was in her roou, reviewing her winter dresses, which were strewed about in picturesque confusion. This year she had grown very fastidious in her attire, and was feeling a new pleasure in delicate colour and graceful folds. Life had acquired a fresh value in her eyes, and it was worth while to take pains with it and lovingly study its details. This morning she was especially happy, and while her hands were busied with light necessary labour, her heart swelled with generous thoughts and longings. She was free, too. Last night had oomAeted her emancipation and she had no more doubts whether she should marry Mr. Delaiield. "I wonder what cousin Prisoy will think of it 1" she was saying to herself, when a rap at the door startled her out of her reverie. The housemaid came in and announced that Miss Grayson had called to see her. "Is she alone?" asked Lmtitia.
"Yes, Miss," said the maid, "and Miss Priscy is down the village and Mr. Dillon out some- where."
"Oh, ask her to walk upstairs; she will not mind.' _ _ _

In a few minutes Jessie appeared, looking pinched and wan, for weeping passionately at night does not improve the eyes or complexion, and she had indulged for half the night in that unprofitable employment, and had finally gone to sleep only to dream that Miss Thornton was showing her her wedding-dress which suddenly turned into dead leaves.

"I am so glad to see you, Jessie," said Letitia, "for I was just in need of a guide, philosopher, and friend; sit down, if you can find a chair, and tell me whether this silk is fit to wear or what I shall do with it." _ - -

It was a golden brown dress which Jessie had often eyed admiringly. "Fit to wear! why you should see my best silk," cried JeKie, "this looks to me as good as possible. But perhaps you want to have every- thing new," she added with a tremor in her voice; all of a sudden a determination had come over her to face the worst and have it over. Miss Thornton noticed her odd manner, and looked up bewildered. "Everything new!" she exclaimed, "why should I? What do you mean, Jessie '/ " "1 meant—l mean "—stammered Jessie, " jf what people say is true." "And pray what do you say ?" asked Lmtitia in her haughtiest tones. Jessie was very white, but tried hard to speak lightly: "Nothing treasonable; only that you are going to be Mrs. Delafield."

Leatitia laughed merrily, for she was too hapi, to be offended, and besides that was an old story, and a pardonable one; she had feared she hardly knew what, and Dillon had come into her mind. "Never, Jessie • tell everybody that it is a delusion; Mr. Delafield and I are the best of friends, but never shall be anything more. The colour came back to her friend's face and the light into her eyes, and she ran over to Lastitia and suddenly kissed her. "You are not offended with me for telling you of it, are you, dear ?" she asked. The room seemed glorified to her, and Detitia's dresses the prettiest garments that ever were seen; she was afraid of betraying herself if she stayed much longer, and after a few minutes she hurried away, leaving Miss Thornton in a state of astonished incredulity. It had never once occurred to her that Jessie could care for the lover whom she her- self held so lightly. Jessie and Mr. Delafield—it was the strongest of combinations, and altogether inexplicable, but she was as sure that Jessie loved him as if she had heard her confess it in so many words. It was a very pleasant idea if only Mr. Delafield could be persuaded of its pleasantness. "How can she care for him when he has never given her any reason to," thought Lastitia ; "per- haps I am mistaken; but yet her manner was so strange, and she looked so unlike herself. Poor Jessie ! I never dreamt of this." She could not go on with her work after this extraordinary discovery, and put OR her hat and jacket to walk down to the village and meet Miss Priscy. Her great care should now be to avoid any declarations on the part of Mr. Delafield, and to transfer his affections from herself to Jessie Gray- son, if possible. She was sincerely sorry for her, and respected her for so well preserving her unhappy secret, but the affair had its comic side, and Letitia smiled to herself more than once as she tripped down the lane. "She would make him a delight- ful wife, and I should make him horribly uncom- fattablc," was. her_ retlectien as she saw Mr.

De'afield entering ;the Inititiite in close etinvetsa. tion with Miss Priscy. They had not seen her, so she did not join them but went through the village and into the churchyard, pausing by poor Tom's grave. As she stood there, thinking deep thoughts on the mystery of death and the unfathomable spring of life, she saw Dillon coming towards her, and her whole heart went out to him. How bright he looked! lbw brave and good and true! She felt as they walked back together, happier than ever in her life before. The world had been so unsatisfying before he came, and its problem had oppressed her in a way which no one guessed. Now all was made right and happy solutions to those problems possible—nay, confidently to be hoped for. She reposed in his love like a child in the sunshine. When Lmtitia and Dillon entered the Hall the letters from the second post lay upon the table.
"One for me, two, and a paper," said Laltitia, "and this one for you, Robert." They went into the drawing-room where Miss Prisey, was basking by the fire, and opened their letters.
"This is marching orders for me, I suppose," said Dillon; "By Jove! I shall have to go to America."

" When ?" asked Letitia, turning pale. "At once; I must catch the next train for Lon- don, settle my affairs there, and start for Liverpool by the evening mail." What do they want in 4merica ?" asked Miss Priscy. "I would not go at 'l. moment's notice, if I were you." "I am used to it, cousin," said he; "I am sorry it has happened just now," and he glanced mean- ingly at Lwtitia, "but it cannot be helped." He hurried through his preparations and then with a strange sinking at heart, bade them both good- bye. "You will wait for me, love ?" he contrived to whisper to Miss .Thornton, "I shall not be gone long.' "Do not be afraid," she whispered back; "I shall be always looking.. for you..". _

Jessie mee.itwhile reaChed her own room and had sat down to consider the situation. The first glow of comfort brought to her by Miss Thornton's frank declaration had faded, and though her state of mind was less hopeless than before, she could not hide from herself the fact that she was really no nearer the love she coveted than before. Of course if she had been a model young lady she would have kept her heart under lock and key till such time as its surrender should be demanded; but model young ladies are very scarce; and Eros is a youth more difficult to manage than any of the naughty boys in the whole domain subject to her Majesty's School Inspectors.
(To be continued.)
THE DOCTORS SHOOK THEIR READS.

"I would give a million dollars for a, stomach," said a wealthy American recently. Now, a million dollars, £200,000, is a deal of money,but he was not able to buy the article at that price. Mr. Thomas Gaskin, of No. 3, Poplar Row, Darley Abbey, near Derby, is not so rich as many, being a gar- dener, but he was ready enough to give all he had for one thing he had not got. Here is his story, and he shall tell it in his own way. Mr. Gaskin goes on to, say: Up to eight years ago I had never lost an hour's work through sickness. In December, IEB2, whilst living at Beeston, near Nottingham, my appetite fell away, 1 had dreadfuVpain after eating, a bad taste in my mouth, which would fill with water and slime,.the latter so thick and sticky that I had often to remove it with my fingers. MIT chest used to 'fill up' and my throat would swell so I couldn't button my shirt at the neck. I vomited a great deal, chiefly a yellowish green phlegm. I had a racking ceugh, and would cough and 'strain till I bled at the nose, and the blood rushed out of my ears. I became exhausted and short of breath, and had to call the doctor, and was in bed five or six weeks.

"I then went as an :out-patient to the Nottingham Hospital, and after attending there for six months, was very little better. I got so thin that I was like a ghost walking about, and my friends said it was Al up with me. For eighteen months I kept getting better, then worse, and at last the doctors recommended me to try a change of air. So I came to Darley Abbey and my for- mer master gave me an indoor recommendation to the Derbyshire Infirmary, _Derby. I found, however, that all the beds in the hospital were full, and I saw my club doctor and also two doctors at Derby. The first one said, you are in a galloping consumption, and must dis the other doctors, after sounding my lungs and chest, said nothing bat shook their heads. " Getting a trifle better my old master allowed me to do what little I could in his gardens and grounds; and some days I worked a little, and then would be away for a few days. Things went on like this until Decem- ber, 1888, when I caught cold, got very short of breath, and broke down completely. I was Ilways coughtng and spitting up phlegm, sometimes as much as a tea- cupful at once, and was afraid to go to sleep for fear as phlegm would choke me. At this time the whites of my eyes turned yellow, and my eyes were bloodshot. My lips and mouth were dry and parched and I often broke out into a cold clammy sweat. 14 tongue was like a piece of brown leather, and I could keep nothing down. I lost over a stone weight in three weeks. "I managed to get up for a few hours at a time, but was so weak I had to take hold of the furniture to move a few yards. I was always tired and weary,. and sit- ting or lying, was never at ease and got no real rest. Too weak to read I often sat for hours looking at my hands —nothing but skin and bone, and was so nervous I couldn't bear the least noise, and the children at play quite upset me. "The doctor kept on attending me, but he said, 'I can do you no good; I can only patch you.upibecause your lungs are diseased. I then gave over-taking this medicine and tried everything I could hear of. * One thing was a cough cure from London that costs 225. a bottle. But nothing did any good,and my friends who came to see me said, Well, you won't cough mnch longer; youlave merely to prepare for another world.'

" About the middle of March, 1889, a neighbour named Joseph Tatham, who works in the paper mills at Darley Abbey, said to me, Tom did you ever try Jrother Seiyers Syrup ? ' and told me how he had been cured after being in the hospital. He spoke so much in praise of this medicine I sent my wife to Derby and got a bottle at Mr. Smith's Stores in Victoria Street. After the first dose I had an evacuation black as ink, and vomited. Then I fell asleep and felt rested when I awoke. After taking the medicine for three days my breathing got easier, my food kept down, and in a few days more I was able to go oat for a short walk. By the end of a fortnight I went to see my master, who asked what had wrought the improvement, and I told him, as I tell every one, that Mother Seigel's Syrup had saved my life. I commenced work at once, and have never It,ql- day's work since. "Of course my strength did not return all at once, but , after taking Sei.gel's Syrup for six months I was as strong as ever in my life and have continued so ever since."

In giving his consent to the publication of this remark- able statement, Mr. Gaskin requests us to refer all doubters to him or to Mr. Beetley, Head Gardener, Dar. ley Abbey, who is acquainted with all the facts alleged. Mr. Gaskin has lived at Darley Abbey 22 years and bears an excellent reputation. Now, what was the complaint from which he suffered ? Not galloping consumption, certainly (as one of the doctors thought), or he would have galloped into hie grave in less titan three 'months, instead of growing worse for seven years. His complaint was chronic initamma- tory dyspepsia (or chronic gastric catarrh), which has lung symptoms like consumption, for which it is so often ignorantly mistaken and wrongly treated. When the right remedy, Mother Seigel's Syrup, was used the dis- ease yielded, as all diseases of the digestive tract do yield, to that magnificent preparation. We heartily congratu- late Mr. Gaskin on his recovery, and commend the facts of his case to all thinking people.

IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter past four. Nnw PEERS.—Lord Mount Stephen (Sir George Step- hen) took the oath and subscribed the peers' roll of Par- liament on his elevation .—Lord Masham (Sir Cunliffe Lister) also took the oath and his seat on his eleva- tion. Mn. STOREY AND THE SILKSTONE EVICTIONS.—Lord LONDONDERRY drew attention to the statement made in the House of Commons by Mr. Storey in reference to the Silkstone Colliery evictions. Mr. Storey said the money for the prosecution was found by Lord London- derry, the owner of the colliery, and this charge his lord- ship now emphatically denied. Tun VACCINATION Am.—Lord DE RAMSEY informed Lord Herschel! that when a person was imprisoned for the non-payment of a fine inflicted for the breach of the Vaccination Acts he was treated as a criminal, but he was treated as a debtor when incarcerated for not paying costs. Bnas ADVANCED.—The reports of amendments to the Sale of Goods Bills and the Public Health (Scotland) Acts Amendment Bill were received and agreed to. The Turbary (Ireland) Bill, the Metalliferous Mines (Isle of Man) Bill, and the Post Office Acts Amendment Bill were read a second time.—The Penal Servitude Bill and the Local Registration of Title (Ireland) Bill were read a third time. The House adjourned at 5.45. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. NEw MEMBER.—Mr. Arthur Brand, the newly-elected Gladstonian member for Wisbech took the oath and his seat amid loud Opposition cheers. He was conducted to the table by Mr. Arnold Morley and Mr. Halley Stewart. MR. ATKLNSON SUSPENDED. Mr. ATKINSON called attention to the statement in the journals of the House on Saturday that he had frivol- ously called for divisions in connection with the debates on the Railway Rates Bills. He explained how he came to oppose those Bills, and protesting against the accur- acy of the entries in the journal, moved that they be expunged, or that a Committee be appointed to consider his conduct. The SPEAKER maintained the accuracy of the journal, and complaining of the manner in which Mr. Atkinson had attacked him by letter, appealed for the protection of the House. Mr. GOSCHEN thereupon moved that Mr. Atkinson be suspended for the remainder of the session, but after some debate, in which several members urged extenuat- ing circumstances, it was finally decided unanimously that the period of suspension should be only a week. Tint LATE MR- MMENRY.—Mr.MArranws in answer to Mr. Cobb, said the analysis of the contents of the stomach of the late Mr. M'Henry pointed to death having resulted from natural causes. GOVERNMENT Busimess.—Mr. Goschen's motion that for the remainder of the session Government business should not be interrupted by any standing order regulat- ing sittings of the House was agreed to. INDIAN DISTRESS.—Sir J. FERGUSSON replying to Mr. Buchanan as to the distress in India, said several relief works were already going on, and every precaution would be taken to deal with any destitution. SUPPLY.—The suspension of the twelve o'clock rule for the rest of the session having been agreed to the House went into Committee of Supply on the Civil Service Esti- mate. On a vote for prisons, Mr. Parnell moved a re- duction in order to demand that the sentences passed on certain men now in English convict prisons for alleged complicity in dynamite outrages ought to be revised,and in doing so made an attack on police and Home Office administration, to which Sir William Harcourt and Mr. Matthews replied. The amendment was defeated by 95 to 64. HOUSE OF LORDS—TuEsDAv. '• ROYAL ASSENT.—The House met at eleven o'clock for the purpose of receiving the Royal Assent by commission to various bills. The sitting was resumed at a quarter past four, when the Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack. MISCELLANEOUS.—The Redemption of Rent (Ireland) Bill was read a first time. The Cotnmons's amendments to the Lords' amendments to the Irish Land Purchase Bill WPro azrp.d to. The Public Health (Scotland) Acts Amendments Bill was read a third time. The Turbary (Ireland) Bill, the Metalliferous (Isle of Man) Bill, and the Post Office Acts Amendment Bill passed through Committee. PEERS IN THE COMMONS.—Lord DE MAULEY moved that a Peer giving notice of his intention to offer his ser- vices to a constituency to represent them in the Rouse of Commons should be excused attendance in the House of Lords during the existence of the Parliament..—The Marquis of SALISBURY did not think it necessary to move the previous question on a motion of this kind. The change proposed no doubt involved a great constitutional change, but if the noble lord (Lord de Manley) chose to offer his services to a constituency there would be no danger of his being summoned to the House of Peers during that Parliament. (Laughter.)—Lord de Mauley's motion was negatived, and the subject dropped. The House adjourned at a quarter to six o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY. The Speaker took the chair to-day at eleven o'clock, the early sitting being a formal one to receive the Royal Assent to a numberpf Acts of Parliament passed by both Houses. The House resumed at three o'clock. MISCELLANEOUS.—The Lancashire, Derbyshire, and East Coast Railway Bill was ordered for third reading. The Channel Tunnel (Experimental Works) Bill was withdrawn. THE INDIAN DROUGHT.—Replying to a question as to the threatened famine in India, Sir J. GORST said the latest reports were most reassuring, timely rains having arrested the drought in various districts. MINISTERS AND PUBLIC COMPANIES.—Mr. GOSCHEN in- formed Mr. Labouchere that members of the Govern- ment were not prohibited from being directors of public companies. IMMIGRANT AmEns.—ln answer to Lord H. Bruce, Sir M. HICKS BEACH said the total number of aliens who had arrived in this country during last month was less by 220 than during the same period last year. THE FRENCH FLEET.—Lord G. HAMILTON told Mr. Gourley the French fleet would arrive at Portsmouth next month, and that the visit would be spontaneous on their part. The exchange of international civilities would be marked on the occasion. SUPPLY.—In Committee of Supply, Dr. CLARK moved a reduction by £lOO of the vote for the Crofters' Com- mission, as a protest against the crofters' holdings be- ing too high and sufficient arrears not being taken off. The motion was, however, negatived, and the vote agreed to, as was the vote to complete the costs of lay charges and criminal prosecutions inlreland, the vote for the Irish Supreme Courts of Judicature, and several others. The House rose at 2.43. ' HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at a quarter past twelve o'clock. • MISCELLANEOUS.—The Elementary Education (Con- tinuance Schools) Bill and several others were with- drawn. The Lords' amendments to the Irish Land Pur- chase Bill were read, their consideration being deferred until next day. IRISH Vonts.—ln committee on the Civil Service Esti- mates, on the vote for the Royal Irish Constabulary, Mr. Sexton complained that the cost of the force steadily increased as the people grew poorer and less numerous, adding that no Minister had carried so far as the pre- sent Chief Secretary the policy of rewarding those members who had been the most violent, inso- leut, and unscrupulous. Mr. Balfour defended the Con- stabulary, declaring that so long as it was necessary to have a police force in Ireland there could not be a better one. Mr. Healy and other Irish members offered some criticisms, after which the vote was carried. The vote in regard to Irish prisons, which was also carried, pro- voked some severe comments from Mr. Healy, Mr. Sex- ton, and Mr. O'Brien, as to the treatment of political prisoners. BILLS ADVANCED.—SeveraI Bills were advanced, and the debate en the second reading of the Clergy Discip- line (Immorality) Bill was adjourned. The Foreign Mar- riages Bill was read a third time and passed. The House adjourned at 20 minutes past seven o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THURSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at a quarter-past four. Bitis ADVANCED.—The Earl of Dudley took the oath and subscribed the roll on his accession to the title. The Railway Rates Bill passed through Committee, a pro- posal by Lord Belper to reinsert words providing for higher maximum rates on certain lines in North Wales being negatived. The Sale of Goods Bill, the Highway and Bridges Bill,the Turbary Bill, the Metalliferous 'Mines (Isle of Man) Bill, and the Post Office Acts Amendment Bill were read a third time and passed. Lord DE RAMSEY replied to Lord Herschell reganding the treatment of persons committed for non-compliance with the vac- cination laws. The Hcuse adjourued at 6.35 p.m. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THunsnAY. The Speaker took thechair at three o'clock. QUESTIONS.—Mr. MarrnEws, answering a question put. by Mr. Cobb as to the recent "glove fight" between Smith and Pritchard, said the police informed him that the only injury they observed was a small swelling on Pritchard's face. If evidence were forthcoming that a fight was of an illegal character he should not hesitate to take proceedings, whether it was with or without gloves.

—Roplying to Sir Henry James, Mr. Goscum said that 'until they had made further progress in Supply he was not sure whether they would be able to take the Factories and Worshops Bill on Monday. Tim EDUCATION BILL.—The House proceeded to con- sider the Lords' amendments to the Elementary Educa- tion Bill. In clause 4, which provided that the free education accommodation should be efficient and suit- able, the Lords had struck out the word "suitable." Mr. MUNDELL!. moved to disagree with the Lords' amend- ment. He said that if the Government were to refuse to restore the word they would be guilty of something nearly equivalent to a breach of faith. Sir W. HART- DYKE asked the House to maintain the Lords' amendment. Sir W. HARDOURT said this amend- ment had been inserted at the instance of men who hated free education, with the object of hamstringing the bill. Mr. E. Stanhope contended that the word "suitable" was introduced for the purpose of bringing in the religious difficulty. On a division the numbers were :—For the Lord's amendment, 110 ' • against 86. A good deal of discussion took place on the House of Lords' amendment in reference to the grouping of schools, and the debate was adjourned.
THE FRIGHTFUL RAILWAY
DISASTER NEAR PARIS. 50 LIVES LOST.

PARIS MONDAY MORNlNG.—Between nine and ten o'clock, last night an appalling disaster occurred at St. Mande station, a few miles to the ncrth-west of the capital, and close to the celebrated Vincennes Forest. A choral fête had been held at Joinville, which is on the Eastern Railway Comps ny's line, and owing to the im- mense attendance, due largely to the delightful weather, several supplementary or special trains were run. One of these had reached St. Mande heavily leaden, and the signals being against it, the train was brought to a, standstill beside the platform. However, while the train was still in the station a second and equally crowded train, also from Joinville, dashed up at high speed, and before any alarm could be raised had crashed into the stationary train with frightful force. The impact was such that the engine of the second train was forced on to the top of the rear van of the stationary one and the adjoining carriages. The awful results can- not well be described. Fire and steam burst forth in terrible volumes, and the driver and stoker were practically burned to death on their box. The greater calamity was, however, caused by the engine striking he cap of a reservoir over a first-class carriage in which he gas used for illuminating the train-was stored.. The gas exploded with a deafening report, and.a few seconds later four carriages were seen to be enveloped in flames. Panic seized upon those who had escaped from the lead- ing coaches, and even the few officials who were in the station were rendered helpless by sheer fright. Thus the fire rapidly consumed the fittings and upholstery of the carriages, and the shrieks of the imprisoned and burning passengers were heartrending beyond description. It was not until the carriages had been furiously blazing for some minutes that the telegraph was nut in operation, and in due course soldiers, firemen, and gendarmerie as- sembled in force. The work of extricating the injured and the bodies of the dead was as painfully slow as the spectacle was saddening. Everybody worked with des- perate energy, but all danger of the fire spreading had passed, and the principal labour was to convey the more seriously wounded to hospital. ARREST OF STATIONMASTER AND DRIVER.

PARIS, TIIESDAY.—The number of deaths by the disas-, ter at St. Mande has now increased to 50. It appears that 44 persons were killed on the spot, and 33 bodies were identified in the hall of the Marie at St. Mande ; the remainder, comprising seven women, two children, and two men, all so terribly charred as to make recogni- tion almost impossiblePbeing taken to the morgue yes- terday evening. The death-roll of 50 is completed by five of the suffers of St. Antoine Hospital and one woman at Vicenne,s Hospital succumbing to their injuries last night. This morning papers confirm the arrest of M. Deguerrois, assistant stationmaster at Vincennes, and Caron, the driver of the second train. Several persons have been missing since the catastrophe, and it is feared they may have been in the ill-fated train, although their names are not among the list of the injured.
