Shrews- bury's average is 41.47, Gunn's 40.90, and Bean's 36.75. The average' of some of the Lancashire players reads as follows :—Briggs, 2052; Yates, 20; Barlow, 1836; Baker, 18.35 ;A. N. Hornby, 1731; and A. Ward,17.31. Surrey still keeps the first position for the championship of the first-class counties. It has played eight matches and won all of them. The other counties stand in the following order :—Notts, won 5, lost 2, drawn 1 ; Kent, 2,1, 3 ; Lancashire, 4,4, 1 ; Scmerset,2, 3,1; Middlesex, 4,5, 1 ; Sussex, 2,4, 2 ; Yorkshire, 3,6, 0 ; Gloucester, 1,6, 3..

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS:,
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS:,

The English football team in South Africa played, their sixth match on Saturday against a fifteen of Port Eliza- beth. The weather was all that could be desired, and there was a large attendance of spectators, but unfor- tunately the game was very one-sided,the-visitors carry- ing off the victory by six goals and four tries to nil.

At the Paddington Recreation Ground, on Saturday, the National Cyclists' Union (London centre) champion- ships were competed for, but were not by any means an unqualified success. In the twenty-five miles tricycle championship race only three competitors took part, and for the first seven miles the pace was a mere crawl. At this point Branson's machine went wrong, one of the tyres bursting. His two opponents were, however, suffi- ciently imbued with the chivalry of sport as to slow up and wait until he had procured another machine and re- joined them. Had they gone on, Branson could never have caught them, but their success would not have been the result of merit, but would have been occasioned by another's misfortune. In the event Branson won easily when the actual racing took place. in the last mile. The time, was, however, only slow. It is pleasant to record such an act of courtesy, as the one just mentioned.

A good deal of interest was centred on Saturday, in the road match between the Manchester Wheelers and the Sefton and Dingle C.C. The distance was 50 miles on the road, starting from Grappenhall, thence via Mere, Tabley, Knutsford, Congleton, back to the eighth mile- stone from Knutsford.' A. Mancunian, J. Reilly, had the honour of being first man in, but when the points were counted the Liverpool club were victorious by 22 points.

Mr. William Sachtleter and Mr. Thomas Allen, the bicyclists who started from New York, and have been through Ireland and England on wheels, have traversed Europe. They passed through Stamboul, and then went on to Angora, Sivaz, and Erzeroum, and have now ar- rived at Tauris. It is said they are going to Bokhara via Teheran, Meshed, and Samarcand.

The ten wickets defeat of Surrey by Derbyshire is one of those unexpected and inexplicable reverses which always occur in the course of a season. The Surrey men were perhaps a trifle stale, but candid critics admit that the champions" were fairly beaten, and that the de- feat would have been more decisive than it was if all the chances given Jiad been taken. Porter and Davidson were toe good for the Surrey cracks, and Bagshaw and Chatterton made themselves very merry at the expense of Lohmann and Skarpe. A few years ago' when at the height of success, Surrey were most cruelly defeated by Essex ; and similarly in 1888, Leicestershire beat them by eleven runs. All the counties suffer at times from these aberrations, but they never fail to cause extreme surprise. The great match with Notts on Bank Holiday will tell us whether the defeat was an ac- cident or whether Surrey is really losing form. Not- tinghamshire is an easy second in the race for the cham- pionship, and with the ability her representatives are showing just now, a very close ight may be ex- pected.

The Clyde shipbuilders have received an intimation from the Newcastle Executive that if they remain firm, the latter will send money to support 6,000 men. PRESENTATIONS TO ASSISTANT MASTERS.

Mr. J. H. Wright and Mr. H. Gorse then ascended the platform, the former carrying a handsome silver teapot in his hand and the latter a silver salver. Addressing the Rev. H. G. Smith, Mr. WRIGHT tegeed his acceptance of the present as a small token of the esteem and affec- tion which had been entertained for him during his ten years' connection with the school. When, some few weeks ago, the news came of his presentation to the Rectory of of Halewood, there were few among them— especially those in the 6th and sth, with whom Mr. Smith's work was more intimately connected—who did not feel a selfish pang of regret amid the many congratu- lations which their master received. With regard to the old boys, if any proof was required of their good will, it was amply afforded by the very hearty and liberal man- ner in which they had come forward and helped with regard to the present. (Applause.) Mr. GORSE then presented the salver to Mr. Hollowell, in appreciation of his nine years' services in the school. It was needless for him to enlarge upon the very grgat interest Mr. Hollowell had always shown in everything connected with the school, but they should dike to be allowed to offer him their heartiest congratulations upon his appointment to the headmastership of the West Kirby Grammar School and their most sincere wishes for hisfuture success. (Applause.) The Rev. H. G. SMITH, who was received with ap- plause, said it was with very mingled feelings that he accepted such a beautiful and farewell gift. It was also with mingled feeling that he now addressed them for the last time as second master of the school, which position he had held for ten years and three months, dur- ing which time it had been his happy lot to work among them. He did not need any gift to remind him of the kindness which he had always received in the school, or to awaken memories which would never die. He had one more favour to ask, and that was that they would shoi, the same confidence and the same loyalty and sym- pathy to his successor as as they had shown to him. (ApplausQ.) Mr. Hottowerx said he felt somewhat in the position of a candidate for Parliamentary honours who begged to say "ditto "to the eloquent speech which had just been made in his hearing. He (Mr. Hollowell) could say " ditto "to much that Mr. Smith had said. It was quite impossible to find words to thank them sufficiently for the handsome gift which had been made to him, and for the good wishes that had accompanied it. He was look- ing forward to his work at West Kirby with much pleasure and hope, although he would feel the severance from the Warrington Grammar School. His work had always been exceedingly pleasantl and his relations both with the head master and the assistant masters and the boys had been most happy. (Applause.)

div.head: HEADMASTER'S ADDRESS.
div.p: THE HEADMASTER'S ADDRESS.

The Rev. G. WILLcocKs, M.A., in his address said :It is usual for me to open the proceedings this afternoon by laying before you a statement of the work done in the school during the last year, and to give in detail the re- cent successes of the past and present members of this old foundation. Last Christmas we sent in ten candi- dates for the Cambridge local examinations. All passed, and were distributed as follows :—Two in the Ist class, two in the 2nd, and three in the 3rd of the honours division, and three in the pass divi- sion. Distinctions were gained in religious knowledge, Latin, Greek, German, and mathematics. H. Gorse, the first " Beamont " scholar, has been elected 'after open competition to an entrance scholarship of £4O per annum at Queen's College, Cambridge. J. S. Place has heen successful in obtaining the third place in order of merit in the recent open competitive examination of candidates for boy clerkships in her Majesty's Civil Service. R. E. Kenyon has been elected to the "Edward Rathbone " memorial scholarship at University College, Liverpool, Victoria University, of the value of £25 per annum for two years. C. S. White has passed the army preliminary examination. J. W. Isherwood has won both the " Rogers " scholarship and a Hulme exhibition at Owens College, 'Victoria University. W. A. Stone, scholar of St. John's College, Cambridge, (1) has been placed in the first class in his college examinations, and (2) has been elected to a Goldsmith Company's exhibition of £5O per annum. J. C. Fisher, of Brasenose College, Oxford, has graduated B.A. in the second class Final Science Honours School. A. S. Kidd, exhibitioner of St. John's College, Cambridge, has been placed in the first class in his college examina- tions, F. C. Scotson, of Owens College, Victoria Univer- sity, has passed the primary examination for the fellow- ship of the Royal College of Surgeons, London. J. G. Gornall, 8.A., of St. Catherine's College, Cambridge, and St. Thomas's Hospital, London, has passed the necessary final examinations to qualify him for the degrees of Bachelor of Medicine and Master of Surgery of the University of Cambridge. E. A. White has obtained the third place in the first class in the final examination of the Incorporated Law Society, with a prize from the Honourable Society of New Inn. (Applause.) Not only have the boys done credit to themselves and to their school,but three of our teaching staff have this year been promoted to leading and responsible spheres of action. (Applause.) It is with mingled feelings of regret and pleasure that I have to state that the Rev. H. Gibson Smith, second master, has been presented to the Rectory of Halewood,and thereby severs his long connection with us, extending over a period of more than ten years. I cannot let this opportunity pass without expressing my warmest thanks to him for the assistance he has rendered me in raising and maintaining the efficiency of this school. (Applause.) Ho has always made the interests of the boys his own, and many of them will, I am con- fident, hereafter acknowledge that they owe much of their success in life to his unwearied patience and zeal in their behalf. He carries away with him the best ; wishes of all those with whom he has been so longintim- atelv connected, and our hope is that he will be as much appreciated in his new calling as he is in his old one. (Applause.) Mr. W. Hollowell, who for the past nine years has been one of our most able and painstaking assistant masters, has just been elected out of a large number of candidates to the head mastership of West Kirby Grammar School. (Applause.) This in itself is a fitting recognition of his energy and ability. Much as I personally regret his loss as one of my colleagues, I join most heartily with all his friends in wishing him as much success--(applause) —and happiness as he himself would desire. Mr. A. S. Shurrock, late assistant master in this school, was appointed last autumn to the head mastership of Tarvin Grammar School, and I under- stand that he is making his way and is mah esteemed. (Applause.) I have secured the services of Mr. L. B. Radford, scholar of St. John's College, Cambridge, as Mr. Smith's successor. Mr. Radford comes to us with the highest recommendations. He has graduated first class in part I. of the classical tripos, and also obtained a first class in part 11. (Applause.) The HEADMASTER added that he held in his hands the Examiner's report. It was too long to read to them in extenso, but he would give them an extract, with which he concludes his report :—" I have come to the conclusion that generally the school is in a highly satis- factory condition. While Warrington possesses the inestimable advantage of a school in which a high stand- ard is aimed at in the old branches of ecrlication, I have satisfied myself that the instruction is on the best approved modern lines, and that no subject of import- ance is overlooked. It is always a difficult problem in a school of this size to combine the advantages of the classical and the modern sides, but as far as possible this is being done here with considerable success. The tone of the school is all that can be desired, and I recommend the good work being done to the favourable judgment of the governors of the school and the parents of the pupils." (Applause.)

div.head: ADDRESS BY THE DEAN OF MANCHESTER.
div.p: ADDRESS BY THE DEAN OF MANCHESTER.

The DEAN of MANCHESTER remarked that he was thoroughly pleased to see that the- masters and boys were thoroughly loyal to the Headmaster. (Applause.) He Could conceive of no sounder foundation upon which any school might rise. Without that foundation he was persuaded there could be no satisfactory superstructure; because unless that spirit prevailed the old proverb would come true, "A house divided against itself can- not stand." Happily, they had in their headmaster one who was celebrated for the earnest interest, the almost painful interest, which he took in the welfare of the school, and he felt it to be as much their school, the boys' school, as his own. (Applause.) The Warrington Grammar School had certain credentials of its own. Their school had not merely a history, butan educational history, and he noticed with pleasure that it was based upon a very broad foundation, and that a successful attempt was made to generalize the scope of the educa- tion given within the walls of the school. They had, therefore, a right to look for highly cultured minds among those taught in the school. (Hear, hear.) Some of the boys had not received prizes, but he would tell what they had got, which was, after all, the greatest pzize—he meant their own entity or own being. They had got that which could form for them, and was form- ing, their character. That was, after all, a matter of the highest importance. They could not- all receive a prize. He had been toLd ny one distinguished master that there was one class of boys he dare not openly declare his sympathy for but for whom he felt much sympathy. They were the boys who might In the first instance be dull; but they must not be discouraged. Some brains came to perfection before others, and if the brains of some of them had collo to perfection at an early age, they must take good care not to overwork them. If others found that their brains had not yet arrived at a full development, let them have a little play, and let their brains take their chance. But brains or no brains, let them use the talent God had given them, and those boys who had not received prizes must not feel discouraged. (Hear, hear and applause.)

div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of th is Board of Guardians was held at the Workhouse, Warrington, on Wed- nesday. Mr. Balharry presided, and there were also present Messrs. Heaton, Davies, Diggle, Dobson, Hood-Wright, Aukland, Harrison, Mather, Humph- reys, J. Houghton, Clarke, A. Jolley, W. Hough ton, Smith, Ratcliffe, Dignum, Hibbert, Kilshall, Kil- shaw ; J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), C. H. Ward (workhouse master), and H. M. Mines (superintendent of Padgate Schools.)
A NEGLIGENT OFFICIAL,

On the reading of the accounts, Mr. CLARKE asked if there was not a bill from the registrar of Newton.—The CLERK replied that it was a great inconvenience to him as superintendent registrar that the registrar at Newton had not,as a rule, produced his papers by the last day pro- vided by law for the purpose.—Mr. HARRISON said that was a great irregularity.—The CLERIC said that when the papers were not sent in at the proper time they pro- bably came at a time when it was next to impossible for him to give proper attention to the work.—Mr. HARRISON thought it was too bad for an officer to accept an office and then neglect to do the duties of it.—Mr. RATaIFFE moved that the Newton registrar be requested to come before the Board to give an explanation.—Mr. HEATON seconded this proposal which was agreed to.

div.head: SCROOLS.-ANOTHER RESIGNATION.
div.p: THE SCROOLS.-ANOTHER RESIGNATION.

The Schools: Committee reported that Miss L. Ben- nett had sent in her resignation as mother of number 3 home. Mr. T. PoHitt, of Oldham, had been appointed assistant master.—Mr. W. THE ILLNESS OF MR. T. JONES.

In moving the confirmation of the minutes of the School Fees Committee, Mr. Dignum referred to the ill- ness of the Chairman of the Committee, Mr. T. Jones, and on behalf of the Committee expressed a hope that Mr. Jones would be spared to his family and his ser- vices to that Board. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: DEFAULTING RELIEVING OFFICER.
div.p: A DEFAULTING RELIEVING OFFICER.

The CLERK said he had to read to them the following report as a result of a conference at Newton of the New- ton District Relief Committee:—" At a meeting of the Newton District Relief Committee, held at their office, Town Hall, Newton, July 23rd, Mr. W. Balharry presid- ing, it was unanimously recommended to the Board: 1. That as it is now proved that Mr. John Wm. Caldwell, relieving officer for the No. 2 district of the Union, has been guilty of wilful misconduct in connection with the administration of relief, and has made serious misrepre- sentations to the Committee in his application and report book during the last and present half years, and also made erroneous entries of payment of such relief in the same period, he be immediately dismissed from office, and that the cleric be instructed to report the circumstances to the Local Government Board. 2. That the collector of No. 1 district be appointed to collect for No. 2 district. 3. That the clerk be instructed to advertise for a relieving officer, such officer ' being further appointed to discharge other duties except those Of collector, at a total salary of £lOO per annum. 4. That beyond the usual condition that the relieving officer be required to devote the whole .time to the duties of his office, it be made a condition of such appointment that the officer be required hereafter to comply with the orders of the Board in respect of lattendances at the offices at Newton, the visitation of the I poor, and the payment of relief."—On-the motion of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr. RATCLIFFE, the above report was unanimously adopted.—Mr. HIBBERT Sug- gested that Penketh should be taken out of the district of the Newton relieving officer.—The CLERK pointed out that if they did this thgT would have to put Penketh into the district of another relieving officer who had heavier work to do than the one whose dis- trict they were taking it from.—Mr. SHEARER relieving officer, who has been temporarily in charge of the New- ton district, said he did not consider that district a heavy one at all.—Ttie Ct.aarc thought that ono of Om .I;caoai ties of the late officer was that he had not had sufficient to do.—Mr. HIBBERT said he was quite satisfied with the explanations that had been given.—The CLERK then read the following letter which he had drafted to be Sent to the Local Government Board, viz "The Guardians, at to-day's meeting unanimously adopted the enclosed report by the Newton District' Relief Committee. They dismissed Mr. J. W. Caldwell, appointed in 1888, relieving officer of the No. 2 district frpm their service and instructed me to advertise the vacancy thereby arising. They also instructed me to report to your Board the circumstances calling for such dismissal. It may be explained that, in September last, Caldwell was refused an increase of salary, and in the half-year commencing at October he misrepresented, in a few cases, the sums previously granted as out-relief. He entered one case as an ordinary case of relief in the list of Newton poor, also in the list of non-settled poor, and for the whole half-year charged in his relief lists double the sums he actually paid. He continued, in some other cases to charge, as weekly paid relief to persons who were dead or who had removed, sums not so paid. The course he thus pursued prevented discovery, at the weekly examination of his accounts, of his misconduct as the entries in my relief order book agreed with the allowances made in the appli- cation report book and with the relief list. At the recent audit, however,certain irregular entries were discovered, and viewing Caldwell's explanation to be satisfactory, your auditor determined upon adjourning the audit and conferred with me as to the tests to be applied in the interim. I attended thereon before the Newton District Relief Committee, and as a result of a private inquiry by the assistant clerk in two cases, I advised the Guardians temporarily to pay relief in the No. 2 district through their assistant relieving officer, and to instruct him to investigate and report in all cases. At the follo-wing meeting of the committee, Caldwell failed to appear and, after consideration of the assistant officers' report and examination of some of the paupers referred to therein, the Committee decided to recommend as set forth in the enclosed report. Caldwell further failed to attend the adjourned audit, and sums amounting in total to £l4 , 17s. 6d. were disallowed by your auditor on the evidence given to him that no such sums had been said. So far as inquiry thereon was practiCable it was not found that Caldwell had been guilty of doing wrong in any

previOuifialf-yeaf, but I regret to sac that in the first quarter of the present half-year he had been similarly acting and that it will be necessary to deal with the cases Of misrepresentation and fraud in that period at next audit. lam to ask your approval of the officer's dismissal by the Guardians. The Guardians do not pro- pose to continue the separate office of collector for No. 2 district, but to add the same to the duties of Mr. Basil Shearer, collector for. part of the Union, and to pay to him the rate of percentage on the sums collected he has hitherto been paid. They have, therefore, resolved ac- cordingly, and lam to ask your approval thereof. In view of the probable determination of duties, of school fees inquiry officer, the Guardians do not propose to make an appointment at a separate salary, but they wil make it a condition of such apppointment of relievingl officer that the person to be appointed will act as inquiry officer for the brief period necessary. On the other hand, the Guardians, in view of the whole time of the person to be appointed relieving officer be- ing given to their service, and in view of the fourth recommendation contained in the enclosed report, to which it is their intention to give effect, have decided to increase the salary of relieving officer for No. 2 district by the sum paid Caldwell as collector and inquiry officer, viz, to give the sum of £lOO per annum. I am to ask, so far as the several proposals herein contained require to be approved by your Board,that you will approve them. I may add that Caldwell is believed to have left the Union."—Mr. HIGINUM asked if it could be stated what was the total amount of the defalcations.—Mr. RAT- CLIFFE said they would come in two half-years. After the next audit the clerk would be able to give the whole of the amount. He added that there were cases in which poor people who were ordered 2s. 6d. had only been paid 2s.—Mr. HEATox thought the Committee should have every case before them to rectify them.— The CLERK said that in those cases it would be regarded as a fraud not against the poor but against the Union. —Mr. HEATON : And you will call upon his sureties to pay.—The CLERK: Yes.—The letter of the Clerk was then approved by the Board.
The -relief cask were next taken. —.,lfio._ BOWLS.

PILKINGTON'S PLATE WORKS v. MOSS BANK.—Played on the ground of the latter at St. Helens, on Saturday. Score :—Plate Works, 231; Moss Bank, 284. VERDIN PARK v. FRODSHAIL—PIayed at Northwich, on Saturday. At the first meeting Frodsham won by 73 points, but on this occasion the home players won by 79, thus securing a victory en the two games by six points. GLAZEBDRY.—On Saturday a bowling match for £1 a side took place on the green attached to the Chat Moss Hotel, between John Peacock and John Nimmy, both of Glazebury. The game was 31 up, and Peacock won by six points. _

WARRINGTON LDIRRAL CLuB.---The bowling green at the Liberal Club, is at present in fine condition for play, and it was on Saturday afternoon the scene of an en- counter between a team representing the Leigh Liberal Club and a team representative of the local Liberal Club. There were thirty-six visitors from Leigh and of these thirty-two played. A very interesting main was the re- sult of the meeting and in the end the local team won by 19 points. This, it should be stated, was a retutn match, 14se the Leigh playe being victorious on the pravious occa- sion. After the me the visitors were entertained to an excellent tea pre dby Mr. Mitchell, the manager of the Club, Mr. Basil Shearer, the captain of the home team, presiding. The visitors who left about nine o'clock expressed themselves much pleased with the reception they had met with, and with their enjoyable outing.
THUNDERSTORMS AND LOSS OF LIFE.

A shocking lightning fatality occurred at Lady Green, near High Wycombe, Bucks, on Monday afternoon. A flower show and cricket match were taking place when, in consequence of a sudden storm, the spectators and cricketers took refuge in tents and under trees. The lightn- ing struck a tree under which five young men named J. Eggleten, a young farmer, H. Bowler, George Adams, E. Ward, and T. Ward had gone for shelter, killing Eggle- ton, Bowler, and Adams instantaneously. The Wards, although still alive, are in a critical condition. When the accident occurred the flower show was in full progress. Lewes Stand was set on fire by lightning during a thunderstorm on Monday. The damage was confined to the telegraph office, and the flames were quickly ex- tinguished.
RELEASE OF MESSRS. DILLON AND
O'BRIEN. MR. PARNELL REPUDIATED.

Messrs. Dillon and O'Brien were liberated from Galway Gaol at 9 25 on Thursday morning. Outside the gaol some persons cried" Stick to Parnell," and others gave vent to anti-Parnellite demonstratiens. Prison life has left its traces on both gentlemen, but not to an alarming extent. After breakfasting with the Bishop, the hon. members went to the Public Hall, where they were pre- sented with addresses from local bodies and deputations rroto oriotod tenants. Both Mr. Dillon and Mr. O'Brien in response, declared in emphatic terms against Mr. Parnell's leadership. Mr. Dillon's declaration, I cannot accept the leadership of Mr. Parnell," was received with great cheering. Mr. Dillon said that he would make no further effort at conciliation. Mr. O'Brien, amidst a storm of cheering, supported to the fullest extent Mr. Dillon's statements, and declared that he was at his country's disposal for any part that it wished him to take. Mr. O'Brien urged that full reliance should be placed on Mr. Gladstone's promises to bring about the establish- ment of a National Parliament. He *called upon Irish- men to trust the English Liberals, who had made so many sacrifices for them. The hon. members arrived in Dublin in the evening, and were received with enthu- siasm.

div.head: SERIOUS ASSAULT ON A SON AT WIDNES.
div.p: SERIOUS ASSAULT ON A SON AT WIDNES.

At the Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Daniel Gilmore was brought. up on remand charged with assaulting his son, Martin, aged seven years, by striking him on the head with his fist and knocking his head against the wall, causing several wounds. Prisoner has been a soldier for many years, and has been out in India for a long period.—Dr. Miller, assistant to Dr. McLennan, stated that the boy was brought to him on the 18th inst. He found him suffering from a wound on the head; his left temple was swollen, and his ear was black and blue. The boy had recovered from the bruises, but had since been suffering from pleurisy, which would most likely be caused by violence. He was now recover- ing from that, and he considered him out of danger.— P.C. Worsfold said he was on duty in Alidwood-st., about three o'clock on 'he morning of the 18th inst., when he saw the boy Martin out in the street with nothing but his shirt on. He said he was running away from his father, who had thrashed him. He was then bleeding from the mouth.—Mr. Knowles, who defended prisoner, asked the Bench to deal leniently with him, as he was an old soldier and had suffered from sunstroke while in India, and when he took a little drink he was like a madman. When sober he was a loving father and husband. Prisoner also pleaded earnestly on his own behalf, and promised to sign the pledge if the magistrates would give him another chance. This they decided to do, and in- stead of sending him to prison fined him £5, allowing him to pay 10s. per week.

div.head: A. DARESBURY FIGHT AND IS RESULTS. ONE FARTHING DAUAGES.
div.p: A. DARESBURY FIGHT AND IS RESULTS. ONE FARTHING DAUAGES.

- - At the Liverpool Assizes, on Monday, .before Mr. Justice Wright and a.common jury, an mteretting local case was heard in the Nisi Prius Court. An action to recover damages for assault was brought, the plaintiff being Charles William ;Phillips, a licensed victualler and farmer, the Ring o' Bells' Inn, Daresbury, and the defendant Edward James Furmston, a blacksmith, of the same village. Mr. Mulholland appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Pick- ford for the defendant.

The plaintiff stated that through slipping out of a trap he had hurt his right arm, and on March 31st last he drove to the residence of Dr. Willett, accompanied by his wife. He had been on fairly good terms with the defen- dant, whose brother, John Furmston, was in the plain- tiff's employ as a yardman. When plaintiff arrived back the yardman did not come to attend to the horse. Plain- tiff found him asleep and intoxicated among some hay. Words passed between them, and John kicked the plain- tiff, who, to protect himself, struck back at John. At this point the defendant came up and took away John. As the latter was being taken away he called out, "Pay what you owe me." To this the plaintiff replied, "You owe me money, and so did your father before you." This seemed to vex the defendant, who returned and struck plaintiff a violent blow, cutting open his cheek and knocking him down. In consequence of the wound he was confined to his bed for two weeks. His wife was the sister of the two Furmstons.—Three witnesses were called in support of the plaintiff's case. The defence was that the plaintiff was using bad lan- guage, and it wal• not until he began to stnke and ill- treat John Furmston, a lame man, that defendant inter- fered to part the couple. The plaintiff then struck at him, and defendant, in self-dcfence, bit him on the face. The defendant was called, and said that both his brother and the plaintiff were drunk. He himself was sober.— The allegation of insobriety was denied by the doctor and other witnesses called for the plaintiff. The jury found for the plaintiff, damages one farthing, and his Lordship said that.while he did not say that the verdict was wrong, at the same time he did not see any sufficient reason to deprive the plaintiff of his costs such costs as the law allowed.

div.head: NEW STOCK.
div.p: THE NEW STOCK.

The Finance Committee of the Manchester Corporation have presented a report. After dealing veldt various details, as to the result of their communications with the Bank of England, they say :—" In copclusion,yourCom- mittee recommend the Council to adopt the necessary re solutions as to the creation, issue, and redemption of £1,500,000 Manchester Corporation, 1891, Redeemable Stcok, the appointment of the Bank of England as regis- trar of such stock, and the composition for stamp duty on all transfers of such stock ; and that your Committee should be empowered to carry out such resolutions and to make arrangements with-and advances to the Ship Canal Company under the powers of the Act."

div.head: SFIEBEENING AT ELLESMERE PORT.
div.p: SFIEBEENING AT ELLESMERE PORT.

At the Chester Castle Petty Sessions, on Saturday, a labourer named Hugh Jones, said to be employed on the Ship Canal,was charged with selling intoxicating liquors at Ellestnere Port without the necessary license, on the 19th inst. Mr. J. P. Cartwright prosecuted, and it ap- Ipeared that Superintendent Hindley, along with other officers, visited defendant's hut, where they saw several men, some of whom were drunk. They discovered an eighteen-gallon cask of beer on tap in the private bed room of Mrs. Jones. Some of the men were supplied with beer,and money passed between them. The magis- trates remarked that defendant had beenpreviously con victed for a similar offence, and he would be fined the same amount, £25 and costs, with the alternative of three months' imprisonment. He was further ordered to pay the advocate's fee. THE INCE MANSLAUGHTER CASE. At Chester Assizes on Wednesday, before Mr. Justice Lawrance, John Sheen (25), labourer, surrendered to bail indicted for the manslaughter of James Birnie, a fellow-workman on the Ship Canal, at Ince, on tie sth March. It was stated for the, prosecution that on the night in question the deceased man was croing on duty at nine o'clock, and asked to be allowed to sleep near a fire by which prisoner was at work, for a short time. Pri- soner, using bad language, refused to allow this, and on Birnie persisting threw a quantity of lueigen oil on the fire. The fire blazing up enveloped Birnie in flames, and his body was so severely injured that he died in the course of a few weeks at the Ship Canal Hospital, where he was at once removed.—The defence was that the oil was accidentally upset in the fire. At the conclusion of the case for the prosecution, the foreman of the jury said the jury felt that upon the evidence they had heard they would not be justified in convicting the prisoner of manslaughter, and he was accordingly discharged.

div.head: LANDSLIP ON THE LNCE SECTION.
div.p: LANDSLIP ON THE LNCE SECTION.

One of those landslips which cause so much trouble and annoyance in deep cuttings when approaching com- pletion took place on the Ince section of the canal docks on Saturday last. The point at which it occurred is opposite to the diverted course of the small stream known as Thornton Brook, which has been turned into the river Gowy, and with that river has been carried under the bed of the canal in a" double-barrelled " syp- hon, of which each tube is 12ft. in diameter. Nearly the whole depth of the canal at this point has been excavated through the blue marsh clays (locally known as "bun- gum "), which are about the most slippery and treacher- ous of the materials with whicn the engineers have had to deal. Indeed, the present is, we believe, the third slip which has taken place at this spot. Its dimension are not serious, its length being from 200 ft. to 300 ft., and its greatest depth (back into the slope) about 50 or 60ft., from the face. Somewhat sensational accounts of this slip having (as usual) appeared in a Liverpool contem- porarv,we maysav that no "embankment "of any kind has been effected by it, and that the removal of the material, which through it has been brought into the canal, will not delay the opening of the Weaver section. MR. LEADER 'WILLIAMS ON SHIP CANAL APPLI-

div.head: ANCES.
div.p: ANCES.
The conference of the Institution of Mechanical En- gineers was resumed at St. George's Hall, Liverpool, on Wedne3day morning, the president, Mr. J. Tomlinson, occupying the chair.

Mi.-E. 'Leader Williams,C.E.,coutributed a paper "On the mechanical appliances employed in the construction of the Manchester Ship Canal." In the coorse of the paper IMr. Williams said: The Manchester Ship Canal is the I largest work of its class in this country,and the mechani- cal appliances used in its construction have been on the largest possible scale, in order to minimise the employ- ment of labour and to hasten the completion of the works The number of men and boys employed on the canal ha; never exceeded 17,000 and about 200 horses have been used. As the excavation amounts to 44 million cubic yards, of which over 10 millions are sandstone rock, it is clear that any available number of men and horses wculd be insufficient to do the work in any reasonable time. Ninety-seven steam excavators and eight steam dredges of large power have therefore been employed. for this work, and for the general purposes of construc- tion, 173 locomotives and 6,300 trucks and wagons have been used. A railwaylas been laid along the whole course of the canal, in many places on both sides with numerous sidings. 'nese lines, with those laid in the bed of the canal for excavating purposes, amount to a length of 228 miles of single line. Flat-bottomed steel rails, 561 b. to the yard, with fish joints, are laid on or- dinary cross-timber sleepers. The cost was about £630 per mile of single line. The railway and its rolling stock are on a largez scale than some of the passenger and goods lines worked in this country or on the Con- tinent. The rate of excavation has varied from I mil- lion to 1 million cubic yards per month. As the work, proceeded, and the cuttings became deeper and the in- clines steeper, and as the sandstone required blasting before the excavators could remove it, the rate of excavation in the bottom of the canal is slower. There are employed on the works 124 steam cranes, .192 portable and other steam engines, and 212 steam pumps of various sizes, some being large Cornish pumps that had been brought from the Severn tunnel works. The large plant used consumed about 10,000 tons of coal per month. The grearer part of the plant was specially constructed for the works ; the remainder was principally brought frolNlr. Walker's contracts at the Severn Tunnel, and Preston and Barry Dock works. The total cost amounted ro £93,610; the whole plant, huts, & , are the property of the Ship Canal Company. No less than 58 Ruston and Proctor's steam navvies are used, being the largest number ever employed on any work. Each costs about £1,200. With this machine about 2,000 cubic yards has been excavated in one day of ten hours in good material. A fair average, however, may be considered to be 600 to 700 cubic yds. per day of ten hours. The working expenses of a steam navvy may be put at about 30s per day. The Priestinan and other grabs have been used principally for excavating foundations and other similar work. The Ship Canal Company also own four powerful steam dredgers. The" Manchester" can dredge 800 tons per hour in favourable material. The " Mersey " and "Irwell dredgers each dredge 400 tons per hour into hopper barges. The 'Barry dredger also delivers into hopper barges. There are also working on the canal three other large dredgers hired from Preston, Ayr, Dumbarton,„ and the Weaver Navigation, besides smaller dredgers. grabs, tsx., worked on barges. At Ellesmere Port there is an embankment faced with stone, one mile long, ,across an enlargement of the estuary. On each side ot the foot of this embankment close timber piling is driven, consisting of piles 13 to 14 riches square and 35 feet long. Over 13,000 of these piles have been driven through sand without any trouble by the use of the water-jet principle, Four steam pumps were used, which delivered the water at a pres- sure of about 301 b. per square inch through 21n. India- rubber pipes to the pile, where it was attached to a liin. wrought-iron pipe, which was put downi under water- pressure alongside the pile. With this assistance the steam pile engines quickly drove the pile, which without the disturbance caused by the water jets in the sand could not be driven. Steam pile engines are employed on various sections of the work.
After a short discussion, Mr. Leader Williams was thanked for his paper. TAKING FORCIBLE POSSESSION OF A RUT. _ _ _ _

At Runcorn Police Court on .Thursday, befoze Dr. Steele, a navvy named John Williams was charged with sleeping in a hut on the Ship Canal works, not having any visible means of subsistence. It was stated that the prisoner and some other men had gone to the hut and turned out the boy in charge there. The police were in- formed of the circumstance but on going there all the men had disappeared With the exception of the prisoner who was asleep. He was sent to gaol for 14 days' hard labour.
THEE SHIP CANAL DISASTER
DISCHARGE OF THE ACCUSED.

On Saturday at a special sitting of the Chester Castle, before Sir T. G. Frost, ;Mr. R. C. Roberts, and Mr. J. Thomson, George Pratt, aged 16, pointsboy,was brought up en remand charged with causing the death of James Hinton and James Heaton, together with eight other men, on the Ship Canal Works, at Ince, on the previous Saturday morning under circumstances reported in our last issue. Mr. E. S. Giles appeared to defend the pri- soner. Superintendent Walker briefly stated that Pratt, on the night of the 17th inst., was employed on the Ince cutting of the Ship Canal as a pointsboy,and an attempt had been made twice by two sets of engines to take 23 waggons up anlincline, but they failed both times. The third time they went further vp another incline to get a greater impetus. It was prisoner's duty to attend to what is called the point, which is a weighted one —that was to say, it remained in its proper position for the main line until it was moved by some per- son. Prisoner had no business to touch this point unless he received a signal, and it would .be proved that the signal was not given. On the third time down unfortunately prispner moved the points,and instead of the engines and waggons proceeding up what was called the overland route, they went into a siding, the consequence being that they fell over a precipice, a distance of 35ft. ten men being killed and four seriously injured. Various witnesses having been heard, the magistrates said they considered that no prima facie case had been made out and discharged the accused, remarking that his instructions were insufficient for so important a post, and his employment was altogether unsatisfactory. They further deprecated the employ- ment of lads as pointsmen.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY. AUGUST 1, 1891.
POLITICIA.ZTS of the - Chamberlain Home Rule for Wales.
school, with a wish that is father to

the thought, have tried to persuade themselves that Home Rule is dead. They ob- serve that the air is not full of it as it was at and immediately after the General Election, and they conclude that this means that the electors have dismissed it from their minds. But that is where they make a mistake. What has happened is, that the hour for argument has gone by, and that the people are awaiting the hour for action. It would be difficult to find a voter now-a-days, who has not come to a conclusion one way or another on the question of Home Rule; and the way in which the bye-elections have gone shows that those who once halted between two opinions are halting no longer; they have decided in favour of

giving Ireland an opportunity of governing her- self. It is true that English electors are interest- ing themselves in the next programme of reforms; and it is quite time that they did so. Ireland has blocked the way; but it having been settled that the Irish train must be the first to go through, the question is—" What next, and next ?" Mean- time, so far from the Home Rule plant being dead, it has taken root in Scotland and in Wales, and promises to become a flourishing tree. There is an association for the promotion of Home Rule for Scotland, and another for Wales, matters hav- ing got as far in the latter country as the produc- tion of a bill. Its title is the National In- stitutions (Wales) Bill; it is backed by a num- ber of Welsh members; and it has been issued amongst recent Parliamentary papers. Let those who are terrified at the words "Home Rule" and " Separation " consider as dis- passionately as they can what -are the -Objects of this measure and the means to be employed,and theni ask themselves if there is anything to be afraid of.

The Welsh Home Rule Bill seeks for power, in the first place, to appoint a Secretary of State who shall have transferred to him all the powers and duties of a Secretary of State so far- as they relate to Wales,except those of the Secretary of State for War. This means of course full control of domes- tic affairs, while matters of Imperial concern re- main untouched. For instance, there is a clause in the bill which would confer upon the Welsh Secretary of State the present powers of the Lord High Chancellor as to the appointment of magis- trates in'Wales. And why not? How is it pos- sible for the Lord Chancellor to be-properly posted, as he ought to be, with information as to the per- sons behind the names that are sent up to him with a view of their being placed upon the Com- mission of the Peace. We know what curious ap- pointments are made at times in this country ; and there is every reason to believe that in Wales the selections are often absolutely unfair. The vast majority of the people of Wales are Noncon- formists ; but in. the making of magistrates it seems to have been written up large—" No Non- conformist need apply." The grievance stares everybody in the face ; it is an insult to all that is brightest and best in the Principality; and we would put it to any fair-minded man, Tory or Liberal, if it would not be better, as proposed under the Bill, that these appointments should be made from lists prepared by the county and borough councils. Then there is the question of education. Wales, like Scotland, has shown her- self much more ready than has England to make sacrifices in order that the mass of the people may grow in knowledge and in wisdom. But every scheme having atpresent to be sanctioned by the Imperial Parliamert, the pace is slow and un- certain, and Scotland and Wales are held back instead of being encouraged to go forward. Sum- marising this portion of the! Bill, a contemporary says :

Clause 10 enables the Queen to constitute a Welsh. Education Department, and clauses 14 to 20 provide for the formation of a Welsh National Council and for its procedure: Clause 21 defines its power, which includes inquiry into the management of Crown lands, application for a charter for a Welsh University, and for establishing a national museum, and the passing of railway and other bills of the second class relating to Wales. Clause 22 enables the Secretary (with consent of the Government ' department affected) to transfer powers of adminis- trative nature to the national council. Clause 23 directs that provisional orders made by the Secre- tary shall be confirmed by the national council in lieu of Parliament. What is there, we would ask, in these proposals to disturb the nerves of the strongest upholder of the unity :of the Empire? The matters to be dealt with are not Imperial; they are national and domestic, and should, be dealt with by national and domestic Parliaments. The Imperial Parliament would have quite enough to do if it were kept to Imperial affairs. At pre- sent it tries to do everything, and the result is that a great deal is, every Session,, left undone, whilst that which is done often bears upon the face of it evidence of hasty and bad workmanship. The arrears of Parliamentary legislation are so large as to be a discredit to us as a nation; and, what is worse, they are growing. This does not, to be sure, concern the Tories,for they are disposed as the representatives of class interests and class exclusiveness to keep things as they are. But it is otherwise with Liberals; and it is for them to grow with the growth of the world; to break down all barriers which hinder the progress of the people ; and to establish such institutions as will

give to each and all equality of opportunity. To this end, we need to press for Home Rule earn- estly, steadily, and persistently—Home Rule not for Ireland alone, but England, for Scotland, and for Wales.

IT would seem that a great deal Woman's Freedom. of sympathy has been wasted upon Miss GREENFIELD, who, it was alleged, had been carried off by Kurds and was held in captivity by them at So-uj-Bolak ira Persia. The Kurds refused to give her up, and. asserted that she had changed her faith. Threats were resorted to, but this made no difference. Possession was nine points of the law with theta..; and theymaile it clear that they would fight rather than give up the girl. The acting British Vice- Consul, Mr. PATON, vigorously supported the mother in her efforts to obtain the release of her daughter; and it was at last arranged that an inquiry should be held. This inquiry took place,on. Tuesday,in presence of the mother,the Consul, and the commander of the Persian troops ; and Miss GREENFIELD settled matters by saying she was the wife of Aziz, one of the Kurds, and that she was now of the Mussulman faith. " De,sdemona's " fondness for " Othello " was regarded as a case of "nature warring against herself " ; and Mrs. Greenfield will probably take the same view of the conduct of her daughter. But further inter- ference is now out of the question. The young lady has had freedom of choice, and she has exer- cised it. As she has made her bed so must she lie; and who knows ? this extraordinary, love thatch may prove to be a happy match after all. Marriage is a lotteryrand it is just possible, that there may be a prize- amongst the Kurds. Miss • GREENFIELD, unlike Mrs. Jackson, did not desire to be rescued.

Going still further 'Mist, we find that the Jack- son case is having effect at the Straits Settlements.. The centre of Government of this Crown Colony is at Singapore ; and the law so far as it applies to the Malays is based on the English Judicature Acts. A few weeks ago in one of the courts, the magistrate,in reference to a case before him,said'of a woman who had left her husband that "she was , entitled to live with her husband or not according as it suited her fancy." This application of the ruling in the Jackson case-seems to have caused; some .excitement amongst the Malaya; and , Tungkee Allum, a person of the highest rank amongst them,is appealing:to the Colonial Govern- ment for an expression of opinion on the subject.. He anticipates trouble ; and says that some hun— dreds of women are already thinking of leaving their husbands. That is pretty much- how matters stood in this country soon after the Jackson de- cision; but some of the English women who thought of leaving their husbands have "thought. better of it," since they learned that if they left their husbands in this way, they would have to . keep themselves. It is not unlikely that it will.be the same at Singapore : the bulk of disappointed wives will stay at home when they find that their husbands under such circumstances cannot be called upon to contribute to their support.. Still, the wife has the best of it under this new reading of the law; for if the husband take it into his head to leave his wife he is by no means free of the matrimonial yoke: he can be called upon to maintainthe woman he has left behind him. This can scarcely be said to be fair ; the tendency to- - wards equality between the sexes is in this respect producing an inequality:. What is required from people who—cannot possibly life -happily togetner is, not merely judicial separation, but greater facility for divorce. We do not say every facility; there is a golden mean between the harmfully rigid and the harmfully lax; and that golden mean ought to be made the basis of our marriage laws.

Strikes WAR and rumours of wars be- at tween masters and men seem to St. Helens. be the order of the day at St. Helens. After a long spell of idleness, owing to disputes in the building trade, work has been resumed by the carpenters upon the basis of the award of the Mayor, Councillor JOHNSON, who was called in as arbitrator. As is usual in these cases,. he found there was something to be said on both sides, and his award is in the nature of a corn- . promise. Unfortunately the masons were not un- der any obligation to be bound by the arbitrator's . decision; they do not accept it, and they are still out. They do not object to the proposed six. months' notice being given of alterations of rules; but they hold that the notice should expire on the first of May, as VMS the case nth the three months' notice. The point is one of considerable moment to them, seeing that their. earnings are chiefly made in the summer months; but why object to arbitration in the matter ? As a rule, workmen have shown a good example to employers in their willingness to submit disputes to arbitra- tion; and lit is to be regretted that the masons of St. Helens do not see their way in this, instance to this reasonable course. T-arning to, another important branch of trade, a strike. amongst chemical workers is,. unhappily, threat-- ened.. Notice has been gigen by the Alkali Union of reductions, and, of alterations. of the basis of payment which the workmen say are equivalent to reductions. It appears, that the workmen will be satisfied to accept the prices paid at the. Globe Works ;;and this being the ;case there should be no difficulty about coming to, an understanding, for we do not suppose that. the Alkali Union will want to make fish, of one set of men and flesh of another:. Judging from thestate- ments.made at the men's meeting, on DiesdaY night, some objection appears to have bem taken to treating with Mr. El. J. KING, the pald repre- sentative of the men.. But if the men think fit to employ someone to act for them he ought to be met as their representative, whether- he be a lawyer or a layman, Some of the 5.21311123 in the present dispute are of a complicated character, and it may be that the men have, formed:at wrong esti- mate of the loss they would sustain, by the altera-- tions which are. proposed. There. is every need; therefore for fell discussie3,,and for the exercise, of patience and moderation. Why not lay the whole of the facts, in this. case, before an arbitra,. tor, and agree to accept his decision, whatem. may be ?

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

The life of the Speaker of the House of Com- mons would not be worth living, if there were a -dozen members in the House as full of complaint and fume and fret as is Mr. Atkinson. He seems to have lost his head, and his suspension for a week will give him time to find it. He who would govern others must first learn to govern himself.

When Charles Valentine Smith met three of his wives in the Central Criminal Court, on Tuesday,it may be said to have been a case of courting extra- ordinary. He was sentenced to fifteen months' imprisonment for his bigamies; but wouldn't it have been more of a punishment if he had been compelled to live with his thrde wives?

Mr. Parhell has been seeking to set aside the notice calling upon him to pay Captain O'Shea's costs in the divorce proceedings; but he has failed. His way of ignoring all that has happened " wasn't good enough" for the Bankruptcy Court. There seems to have been some difficulty about. proving his English domicil& but it has been done. "Mr. 'Fox" has at last been run to earth.

There is a disposition to commiserate France because her population is not advancing as ,fast as that of other European countries; but there Is no need. The peasantry with small families have less care and anxiety than those who have large families. The aim of existence ought to be increase of happiness rather than increase of'numbers ; for, as Emerson says, most men and women are merely one couple more.

"Tommy" Burns and Professor Vivian are get- ting up a little advertising steam by challenging each other to dive off bridges ; but, as the Professor is going to America, nothing is likely to come of it. " Tommy " says that he has dived off Runcorn Bridge when there was only six feet of water. But that feat has been over-topped by the man who dived off a bridge when there was no water at all. He broke the record of course—and himself.

A forge labourer, named Charles Carney, was sent to prison for three months by the Warring- ton magistrates, on Tuesday, for stealing a watch and chain. He had taken them from a bedroom in the house in which ho lodged—to repair, he said, and he forgot to take them back." With men like Carney about afflicted with ,awfully bad memories—it is necessary to act on the advice of the wit who wrote :
He who his watch would keep, two things must do: Pocket his watch, and watch his pocket too.

The Salvation Army was worsted in an encoun- ter with the Police at Eastbourne on Sunday. It is stated that the action of the Police in stopping the band and dispersing the " soldiers " was loudly cheered. The inhabitants of Eastbourne are not opposed to salvation,; but they do object to so much noiSe being made over it on a Sunday. The Salvationists have something to learn; order should be earth's as it is heaven's first law.

"Truth" says:—" I understand that the Duke of Rutland and Lord .Cadogan are to be invested with their respective Garters at Osborne, by the Queen herself, in the course of next month." The dukes will feel very pleased, no doubt, when they have "got 'em on "—as pleased as the Chowbent lad was, who, as a special favour, was allowed to wear his" Sunday garters" when he went to the Michaelmas Fair.

. - Another relieving officer gone wrong. This time it is Mr. J. W. Caldwell who had charge of the Newton District,. It was remarked at the meet- ing of the Warrington Board of Guardians, on Wednesday, that he was far from being over- 'worked; and "Satan finds some mischief still" Btc. There is a good post for somebody, and it is to be hoped agood man will secure it. It is soon all.up With a INlieving Officer when he takes to relieving himself at the expense of the ratepayers.

Thero is no falling off in the interest which at- taches to the presentation of Warrington Grammar School prizes. On the contrary, the interest is increasing, as shown by the large attendance at the Public Hall, on Tuesday afternoon, every seat be- ing occupied. There was an extra attraction this year in presentations to two masters who are leav- ing—the Rev. H. G. Smith and Mr. Hollowell. The head-master, the Rev. E. J. Willcocks, knows how to keep pace with the times, and the result is seen in the success of his pupils in the various public examinations.

Lord Salisbury indulge in a restrospect of the past five years in his speech at the Mansion House, on Wednesday. The chief point which he sought to make was that the Government had been success- ful in that period in restoring law and order in Ire- land. But he forgets that Ireland was so peaceable when Mr. Gladstone went out of office that he and his friends, on coming in, allowed the Crimes Act to lapse. All he can claim is that he is where he started; and if everything is so satisfactory in Ire- land to-day, why is the present Coercion Act in force? Let Lord Salisbury or his nephew tell us that.

The House of Commons sat from Thursday afternoon until half-past four on Friday morning, a fierce battle being waged over the proposal of the Irish Secretary to devote certain moneys to the training colleges of Ireland. It was "a spectacle for gods and men" to see Mr. Balfour furiously attacked by Mr. T. W. Russell and other Ulster members, while he was supported by the Nationa- lists. The struggle ended for the moment by a motion to report progress, Mr. Balfour intimating that he should not permit obstructive tactics to defeat him in the end he had in view. "The quarrel is a very pretty quarrel as it stands."

But the funniest thing in the Premier's speech is the statement, in face of recent bye-elections that the decision of the country on the Home Rule question in 1886 is "an irrevocable decision." He does indeed refer to the next general election as possibly giving "a passing decision in the op- POsite direction." Why " passing ?" Is it not more likely that it is the next decision which will be irrevocable? It is really amusing to see hew Lord Salisbury speaks of that as irrevocable which IS on the eve of being revoked. He is like the Woman who, finding herself in a difficulty, is most emphatic in asserting her opinion when she is most in doubt. Can it be that the Prime Minis- terhas been amongst the Primrose Dames?

Mr. John Warburton may thank his stars, and the generosity of Councillor Jenkins of Warring- ton, that he is not at this moment contemplating the inside of a prison wall. The series of libels which he has published upon Mr. Jenkins as a solicitor were simply intolerable; and could only end, as they have ended, in criminal proceedings. The defendant has been well advised in pleading guilty; and escapes well in paying £35 costs. But the sword of Damocles hangs over him in the shape of a sentence of imprisonment in case he repeats his eccentric performances. Let him take warning; and secure peace by living in peace with all men.

Mr. Justice Smith, in charging the Grand Jury, at thQ Liverpool Assizes, on Monday, referred to the marked -diminution of crime throughout the Country. With regard to the causes of this im- provement, there can be no question that the national education of the past twenty years has been one of the most important. There need be no fear, then, that things will grow worse under a ystem of Free Education, which, so far as the State is concerned, must necessarily .be secular. There is less talk, however, than there used to be about "godless education " ; like "disintegration of the empire" it has hs,d its day, and almost Ceased to be.

THE VYRNWY WATER SCHEME. On Thursday.on a visit being paid to the crossing Works at Fiddler's Ferry, in connection with the 7Yrnwy water scheme, it was found that the state Of affairs continued to be fairly satisfactory. The Water from Wales was passing through the tempor- ary pipe-lines laid across the river, and it was as- certained that the divers who had been engaged in the work of preventing leakages had concluded their labours in that direction.
LOCAL NEWS.
GOSPEL MISSION _SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN

The anniversary services in connection with this school were held on Sunday, when two sermons were preached, afternoon and evening, by Mr. William Tharme, superin- tendent and missioner of the Liverpool Evangelistic and Temperance Mission to Railway men and others. On Monday evening a sermon was also preached by the Rev. J. P. Williams, of St. John's Church. There were good congregations, and appropriate :music was sung by the choir and children. Collections were made in aid of the school funds.

NATIONALISTS AND THE COMING MUNICIPAL :ELECTION. The adjourned meeting of the Irish Nationalists of Widnes, was held in the League room,St. Paul's-chambers, on Monday evening, presided over by Dr. O'Keeffe. There was a good attendance. Addresses in favour of conducting the election on political lines, and of amalga- mating with the Liberal party, were delivered by the Chairman, Messrs. Whelan, Healy, Duffy, and Flynn, and eventually a Committee was appointed to select suitable candidates as representatives- of the Nationalist party, which will be submitted to a future meeting. WRINGING THE WANE LEATHER AT THE WRONG TIME. At Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, Annie Johnson, White-st., was summoned for assaulting Sarah Shaw- cross, on Friday afternoon, the 24th inst.—The com- plainant stated that at 3.30 on Friday afternoon she was passing the defendant's house, when she threw a quan- tity of water over her from the bedroom window, which completely saturated her, besides damaging her clothing. The defendant insulted her every day she went out.— The defendant denied that she threw the water over complainant. She simply wrung the wash leather with which was cleaning the window, and did not know com- plainant was passing at the time.—The defendant was ordered to pay 55., and 10s. costs, or in default Of pay- ment seven days.

div.head: EXCURSION OF MESSRS. GOSSAGES EMPLOYES.
div.p: EXCURSION OF MESSRS. GOSSAGES EMPLOYES.

The employes of Messrs W. Gossaze and Sons, at the Widnes Soap Works, held their annual excursion to Southport on Saturday, when over a thousand of the workmen and their wives and sweethearts took advant- age of the generosity of the above firm to visit this charming town. Three trains had been chartered for the purpose, the first starting from Widnes Central Station at 7.45 in the morning, ten minutes each dividing the trains, the last arriving in Southport shortly after nine o'clock. The people spent the day in visiting the several places of interest, arrangements having been previously been made for their admission at a reduced rate. The return journey was commenced at 7.30 in the evening, the last train arriving in Widnes at nine o'clock. The trippers were accompanied by the Widnes Sscap Works Brass Band, which discoursed music both going and returning. J. &. W. DUTTON 8 SUMMER SALE now on. Sankey Street, Warrington.—Advt. • ANNUAL SERMONS AT RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH.

OnSunday the annual sermons on behalf of the choir fund were preached in the Parish Church before large congregations. In the morning the Rev. F. W. Willis, M.A., rector of Warrington, preached en excellent ser- mon before which the choir gave an able rendering of Dr. Roberts' anthem' "Seek ye the Lord," the solo be- sung sun with much taste and feeling by Mr. James Lit- tler, the honorary choirmaster. A flower service was held in the afternoon, when the Vicar (the Rev. Canon Wood, M.A.) gave a most interesting and instructive address on the subject 9f flowers. The pulpit in the evening was occupied by Canon Dodd, M.A., Vicar of Stretton, who preached an eloquent sermon. The an- them was Dr. Elvey's " Wherewithal shall a young man cleanse his way ?" which was admirably sung by the choir, the solo being taken by Mr. D. S. Garner, in a praiseworthy manner. Mr. Johnson presided at the or- gan. The collections for the day amounted to upwards of £lB. WIDNES NISH NATIONAL LEAGUE.

The weekly meeting of the above branch was held in the League rooms on Sunday afternoon, under the presidency of Mr. P. Whelan. Mr. J. Druery, son of Mr. Thotbas Druery, Widnes, delivered an eloquent address on "The present political situation in Ireland." He ad- mitted that both sections of the Irish party were faulty, but Mr. Parnell was responsible for the present con- troversies amongst the Irish people. He then went in- to details, in which he explained, to the satisfaction of all present, that Mr. Parnell had deceived the people of Ireland. It was nonsense for people to say that morals had nothing to do with politics. He concluded by ex- pressing the hope that the people of Ireland would never accept for their leader a man who on account of his immoral action was dragged through the Divorce Court and proved to be a vile adulterer. Mr. Druery was loudly applauded, and the motion of Mr. H. O'Donnell, seconded by Mr. J. F. Kenny, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the lecturer, to which he replied in a suitable manner. SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT WESTON QUARRIES.

Mr. J. E. Worsley, district coroner held an inquest on Saturday at the Prospect Inn, Weston, near Runcorn, touching the death of William Lawrinson, 35 years of age, a native of Tarvin, near Chester. From the evidence it appeared that the deceased was employed as a labourer by the Runcorn and Helsby Stone Co., at their Weston stone quarries. On the Thursday morning, about half- past seven, he was engaged with two other men, named Thomas Lloyd and Henry Weston, taking a truck to a crane for the purpose of having it unloaded. This was done, and in returning they had to descend a slight gradient. The men pushed the truck with unusual force and jumped on. It went down the incline with great force, and they were unable to stop it. The result was that the truck ran over the points,and on to another line, where it came into collision with some waggons. The deceased was crushed between the buffers and sustained serious injuries to the abdomen, death resulting the same day. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." RUNCORN PARISI CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOLS TREAT: The scholars attending these schools had their annual outing on Tnursday, the place selected being Mersey View, Overton. A special train had been engaged, and the party, numbering 450, left Runcorn shortly after one, accompanied by the Rev. G. H. Kingston, 8.A., Mr. Jordan (superintendent of the boys' school), Mrs Tonics (superintendent of the girls' school), and the teachers. The Vicar (Canon Wood) and Mrs. Wo)d joined the party at Mersey View, and the afternoon was ple*antly spent in the numerous ways known to this popular resort, not forgetting the excellent tea provided, which the hill-climbing and other pastimes caused to be thoroughly enjoyed. The return journey was made shortly after eight, the party safely reaching Runcorn after a most enjoyable day. The thanks of the party are due to Mr. Smith (stationmaster) and his staff for the excellent manner in which the train arrangements were carried out, and for their unremitting care for the welfare of the scholars. The whole of the arrangements were in the hands of Mr. John Littler, secretary of the schools.
ROBBING A DRUNKEN WOMAN.

At Widnes Police Court on Monday, Mary Tarpey, no fixed abode, was charged with stealing a purse contain- ing 15s. from the person of Mary Lloyd, of Runcorn, on Saturday night.—A boy named Holligan, who gave his evidence in an intelligelit and straightforward manner, stated that he was on the market ground on Saturday night in company with a lad named Hopkins. Mary Lloyd, who was then "nearly drunk," came up to them and asked them to show her the way to Runcorn Bridge. They both proceeded with her towards the bridge ; on the way, however, she fell down. The prisoner Tarpey then came up to them and assisted the woman to get up, at the same time taking the woman's purse from her hand, telling her that she would take care of it for her. Tarpey then sent the boys for a policeman to take Mrs. Lloyd to the Police Station. When she was at the Police Station she said that Tarpey had taken her purse from her.—P.C. Worsfold said he arrested Tarpey about an hour after this. When he charged her with stealing the purse she replied, " Oh, yes." She had not got the purse in her possession wheifsearched.—Prisoner denied the charge, but the Bench found her guilty, and fined her £1 or 14 days. Prisoner went to gaol. BMIGRATION.—Intending emigrants to New York, Boston. Philadelphia, San Francisco, Canada, China, Japan, Aus- tralia, or New Zealand, should take tickets (lowest rates) at the" Examiner" Office, by Cunard, Onion, American, Aus- tralian, Oriental, and other lines.—John Walker, agent. ."
