div.head: rITW EXAMINER, SATUTWA. AUGUST 1, 1891.
div.p: rITW EXAMINER, SATUTWA. AUGUST 1, 1891.
THE WIDNES MAGISTRATES AT FAULT,
There were two cases of drunkenness to be heard at the Widnes Police Court yesterday, but in consequence of no magistrate being obtainable they had to be deferred till to-day.
GOSSAGES' BAND
Last Friday, this band won the first prize at a brass band contest at Crosby.
A SUCCESSFUL WIDNES ATHLETE.
On Saturday, at the Wirral Harriers' meeting, H. Peters, of Widaes, wlto had 22 yards start, won the quarter mile handicap, the time being 49 3-5 secs.

ANNIVERSARY AT RIXTON. The Sunday school anniversary was held in the Rixton Wesleyan Chapel on Sunday. Councillor Mycock, of Stafford, preached two excellent ser- mons during the day. The evening service especi- ally was well attended, the preacher taking for his subject "Christ, the great teacher." The singing of the choir, under the leadership of Mr. William Shaw, shows signs of improvement. Special an- thems and choruses were rendered. The collections in aid of the funds amounted to .E 7 Gs. Gd. BLssEgirrrEs.—J. S. Garland, Ironmonger; 51, ,Bridge-st., Warrington.—Advt.
surees hands was £326 2s. lid.; and there were some small amounts to pay • and £5 was thereupon voted to the Clerk on petty cash account.
MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.
The Medical Officer reported two cases of scarlet fever at Aston and at Frodsham and a case of croup at Halton.

div.head: RUNCORN COUNTY COUItT,
div.p: RUNCORN COUNTY COUItT,

_ The cause list at this Court on Tuesday contained 31 original summonses, two default summonses, and five judgment summonses. There were no contested cases of public importance. THII NEW WIDNES POLICE INSPECTOR.

Ex-Sergeant Cooper, of New Brighton, entered 'upon his duties yesterday at Widnes in place of Inspector Bowyer, who the same day assumed the office of Inspec- tor in the Egremont constabulary division. CRONTON NI.:ESLEYAN SUNDAY SCLIOOL. The annual treat to the 'scholars attending this school took place last Saturday, in a field at Cronton lent by Ur. Jos. Taylor. There was a large number present, including friends and parents. Tea was provided in the chapel. PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, SIMMS' COOSS, WIDNES.

Special services were held in this place of worship, on Sunday, when two excellent sermons were delivered by the Rev. E. Ball, of the Prince's Avenue Church, Liver- pool. There were good congregations on both occasions. Collections were taken.in aid of the trust fund. , RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH CHOIR. The junior members of this choir had their annual trip on Monday, the place selected being Blackpool. The party, numbering 30, accompanied by Mr. James Littler, the hon, choirmaster, left Runcorn in a special carriage at seven o'clock, arriving at Blackpool shortly after ten. The party again reached Runcorn safely at ten o'clock, after a most enjoyable day.

div.head: WLNDOW BREAKER SENT FOU THREE MONTHS.
div.p: A WLNDOW BREAKER SENT FOU THREE MONTHS.

On Wednesday at the Liverpool Assizes, before Mr. Justice Smith, Catherine Hynes (221, was indicted for having at Widnes, on July 20th. maliciously broken a plate glass in the window of the Waterloo Vaults,belong-t ing to Peter Walker and Co., Limited, and valued at £7 103. She was found guilty, and committed for three months.

DEATH OF MRS. THOMAS HAZLEHURST OF RUNCORN. We regret to record the death of Mrs. Thomas Hazle- hurst, widow of Mr. Thomas Hazlehurst, Beaconsfieli, Higher Runcorn, which took place on Wednesday, in her 79th year, after a short illness. Deceased and her late husband were well known in Runcorn and neighbour- hood for their generosity in various ways, find particu- larly in the buildiug. of numerous Wesleyan Chapels in Runcorn, Widnes, Halton, Frodsham, and Halebank.

div.head: RUNCORN FREEMASONS AT HAWKSTONE PARK
div.p: RUNCORN FREEMASONS AT HAWKSTONE PARK

On Thursday about 30 of the members of the Elles- mere Lodge (758) of Free and Accepted Masons, Run- corn, with their wives and female friends, held their annual picnic to Hawkstone Park. The party left Run- corn by the 8.40 a.m. train, and on arriving at Wein, proceeded to Hawkstone Park, by 'buses, accompanied by the W.M., Bro. James Little. After visiting the various places of interest the return journey was com- menced, some of the party returning by the 8.30 p.m. train from Wem, and some by the 10.27 train.

div.head: SWING ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN.
div.p: SWING ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN.

On Monday evening, an accident, which, fortunately, has not been attended with fatal consequences, befel a youth named William Rushley. 19 years of age, residing mith his parents at 24, Trinity-st. It appears that whilst in one of the swing boats on the fairground, he overbalanced himself and falling coming in contact with a plank, breaking it into two pieces. He was picked up in an unconscious condition and immediately placed un- der the medical treatment of Dr. McDougall, under whose care and skill he is now making satisfactory pro- gress towards recovery. •

div.head: NEW WESLEYAN MINISTER.
div.p: THE NEW WESLEYAN MINISTER.

The Rev. T. Law, superintendent of the Widnes Wesleyan Circuit, goes to Nuneaton after the present Conference. The Rev. W. Kidman, of Stockton-on-Tees, was selected as his successor, but owing to ill-health he has been accorded a twelve months' holiday. In the second draft, which was issued last Saturday, it was- stated that the Rev. A. French, of Seacombe, who has been superintendent of that circuit for three years, was planned for Widnes. This selection will, however, have to be confirmed by the final draft. Mr. French has the reputation of being a capital preacher.

div.head: WIDNES FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE,
div.p: WIDNES FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE,

The ordinary monthly meeting of this Committee was held at the Town Hall on Wednesday afternoon. Dr. O'Keeffe presided, and there were also present Messrs. F. H. Pankhurst, W. Sadler, D. J. Brookes, T. Craik (law clerk's assistant), S. Hoyle (accountant), and Miss Walker (assistant librarian).-Accounts amounting to £l6 123. 7d. were passed for payment.—Mr. Craike re- ported that the General Purposes Comtnittee of the Local Board had decided to leave over the matter of pro- viding a temporary room for boys for the present, as they had found that the expense would be more than they were prepared to incur.—The Chairman said he was very sorry at that decision, because the room was greatly required.

div.head: DRATII FROM BURNS AT WIDNES.
div.p: DRATII FROM BURNS AT WIDNES.

Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, held an inquest yesterday morning, at the Widnes Accident Hospital, on the body Id the infant child of Antomious and Ann Smith, 15, Water-st. The parents of the child are Poles, and the evidence of the mother, which had to be taken through an interpreter, was to the effect that on Mon- day nigl.t the child (vito was two years of age) was left alone in the parlour of the house, where there was a fire. Soon afterwards the mother returned and found the child's nightdress in flames, and these were extinguished with the aid of some of the neighbours, not, however,' before the boy had been severely burnt. He was at- tended at the Widnes Accident Hospital by Dr. Hutchin- son, but death resulted on Wednesday morning. A ver- dict of "Accidental death" was returned. Muss PLANTS AND CANARIES IN A CHEMICAL YARD.

A Liverpool contemporary says :—lt may be interest- ing to readers to learn that in the works o,f W. PiMing- ton and Sons, Widnes, there are musk plants growing which measure about forty inches in height, and of a very healthy appearance, produced by a manure ma'au- factured in the fertilizing department of the above-named firm. The room where this plant is to be seen growing -is known as the foreman cooper's office, and is adjacent to the bleaching powder departments. The plants have a very healthy appearance, the stems and leaves being proportionately large in comparison with the height of the plant. It is a curiosity, as it is sqch a tender plant, to find it growing in the centre of a chemical yard. There are also to be seen in the same room several nests of young canaries, which are very attractive, but the greatest object of interest are the musk plants.

div.head: PROPERTY SALE
div.p: PROPERTY SALE

On Wednesday afternoon, at Wilson's hotel, Runcorn, a number of important lots of shop and other pr*perty were put up by auction, as follows :—Lot 1. A large double-fronted shop and commodious dwelling-house, No. 77, Bridge-street, Market-square, Runcorn, bought by Mr. Alfred Buck, chemist, the tenant, for a 1,400. Lot 2. A large double-fronted shop and house, No. 79, Bridge-street, with outbuildings and yard, bought by Messrs. Tyler aud Sons for £BOO. Lot 3 a large double fronted shop, and house, 81 and 83 Bridge-st., with out-buildings and yard,bought by Messrs. Tyler and Sons for £750. Lot 4 two freehold messuages:3 and 5 Duke-st., bought by Mr. John Canning, for £3OO. Lots 5 and 6 two freehola messuages, 7 and 9 Duke-st.,and two houses fronting Bold-st., not sold, the reserve price not being reached. Lot 7, two copyhold houses in Main-st. Halton., with gardens, stable, and coach-house; bought by Mrs. W. S. Pritchard for £4OO. Mr. Fred. A. Lake was the solicitor for the vendors of most ot the property.
APPOINTMENT OF MATRON TO WIDNES HOSPITAL.

A special meeting of Widnes Local Board was held, at the Town Hall,on Thursday afternoon, for the purpose of confirming an appointment as matron of the Infectious Diseases Hospital made by the Health Committee. Mr. Wright presided, and there were also present Messrs. Sadler, Nail, Taylor, Timmis, and Openheim (clerk).—The Health Committee reported that there had been 21 appli- cations for the post. Five applicants were asked to ap- pear before the Ccmmittee, who afterwards resolved to recommend for the appointment, Miss Milburn, of Leeds, at the salary of £3O per annum, with uniform.—The Chairman, in moving the confirmation of tke minutes, said he thought they had selected a very capable matron. Since her selection Miss Milburn had had a better pffer by £lO a year fram Bournemouth, but she had deciAd to accept the Widnes appointment, and the Committlia had promised that in case of' their being mutually satisfied, they would, in a short time, ask the Board to consider the question of increasing her salary.—Mr. Timmis seconded the proposal of the Chairman, which was agreed to.—This was all the business.

RUNCORN SONS OF TEMPERANCE, AND INDEPENDENT ORDERS OF RECHABITES UNITED VILIGANT COMMITTEE. On Monday evening the members of the above Com- mittee were entertained to an excellent supper, provided by Mr. and Mrs. Heesom, to which ample justice was done. Among those present were Messrs. T. Lea, D. Bisbrown, T. Clarke, J. Johnson, E. Key, W. C. Cooke, J. Bisbrown, T. J. Holt, T. Heesom, R. Harrop,T. Cooke, S. M. Temperley, J. W. Rovle, W. Cartwright, J. Lea.J. Owen, J. Booth, J. Jones, J. Sales, and J. Taylor. The tables being cleared, Mr. Thos. Lea was unanimously elected to the chair, when several matters of importance were duly considered and discussed, amongst othei:s,the one of chief importance being the forthcoming election of Commissioners. After due consideration,it was unanim- ously resolved to run two temperance candidates. Several names were then submitted to the meeting, the choice falling to the selection of Mr. Thos. Lea, the successful temperance candidate at the recent election of poor law guardians, and Mr. Daniel Bisbrown, of Greenway-road, a much respected life teetotaller. It was unanimously resolved that this meeting pledges itself to support the two candidates named, and to use every legitimate means to secure their rettirn as !members of the Board. It was also resolved that a petition on behalf of the two orders be drawn up. to be presented at the forthcoming Brews- ter Sessions, praying for a reduction in the present license. Mr. Ed. Key was appointed president of the Committee for the ensuing term, and Mr. R. Harrop and Mr. J. Lea vice-presidents, whilst Mr. Thos. Cooke and Mr. G. S. Leadstone were appointed joint secretaries. A vote of thanks to Mr. and Mrs. Heesom for the excellent repast provided, brought the meeting to a close.

div.head: RESCUED BY A WARRINGTON REPORTER.
div.p: RESCUED BY A WARRINGTON REPORTER.

On Sunday afternoon, Mr., Percy Wright, repor- ter, of Warrington, was out with a pleasure party on a flat on the Wigan canal, and had jumped off on to the bank when a youth of about 14 years of age, who was standing there attempted, out of bravado, to get into the craft as it was reaching land. As a coneequence he fell into the water, and would have been drowned had not Mr. Wright. seized him by the hand and kept him up until another youth arrived on the scene, and with his help he was drawn out.

div.head: POST OFFICE, EXPRESS DELIVERY.
div.p: POST OFFICE, EXPRESS DELIVERY.

On and from to-day (August Ist) the Post Office will deliver messages, letters, and parcels, by special messenger in all parts of the town and rural district. The fee for express delivery will, in addition to the ordinary inland postage, be 2d. for the first raile and 3d. for every succeeding mile or part of a mile, when a public conveyance (i.e., tram- car, railway or omnibus, &c.) is available in both directions. The following offices in the district will be opened at the outset as express delivery offices :—Warrington, Frodsham, and Lymm.

div.head: RAINHILL HORTICULTURAL SOCIETY.
div.p: RAINHILL HORTICULTURAL SOCIETY.

The fourth annual flower show and exhibition of canaries, under the auspices of the Rainhill Horti- cultural Society, was held in a field at Rainhill, lent by Mr. Joseph M usson, on Saturday at ternoon. The arrangements were carried out by a committee, of which Mr. H. Flower was the chairman and Mr. J. L. Watkin secretary. The prizes offered in the floral department amounted to about .E:l3 in value, and there were about 300 specimens exhibited. For canaries the prizes were valued at .C 6 and 50 birds were shown. The flower judges were Messrs. Smetham, Norris, Rawlinson, and Johnson ; and Mr. James Lucas (Prßscot) officiated as judge of the canaries. During the afternoooti the field was visited by a large number of persons, and the Hay- dock Brass Band rendered a selection of mule. J. & W. DUTTON'S SUMMER SALE now ou. Sankey Street, Warrington. —Advt. SALE OF WORK AT HUTTON.

In furtherance of the project {of erecting a new church to meet the growing needs of the working class population in the Huytou Quarry portion of the parish of Huyton-cum-Rody, and in compliance with the terms of bequest of the late Miss Lucy Ashton, daughter of a former vicar, of £2,000 towards its endowment, on condition that the church was erected within five years, a sale of work was held on Saturday in the grounds of the vicarage, tents being pitched on the greensward. The articles were the product of Mrs. E. M. Sander- son's working party. The fancy work stalls, taste- fully arranged in a large marquee, were attended by Mrs. M'Seen, the Misses Fieldwick, Langdon, and Blezard, and Miss Hughes and pupils; the flower stalls by Mrs. Ihler, Mrs. G. Ihler, and the Misses Ihler, E. Felton, and Barber. Mrs. Wilton presided over the refreshment stall„assisted by a number of ladies. By the kind permission of the vicar, the Rev. E. M. Sanderson, the gardens of the vicarage were thrown open to the large number of visitors. The church is estimated to cost £4OOO, towards which £2,000 has been promised. The sale realised over £lOO. ' J. &W. DUTTON'S SUMMER SALE now U. Sankey Street; Warrington.—Advt. THE FATALITY AT COLLIN-4 GREEN.

On Saturday morning. Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquiry at the Pear Tree Inn, Burtonwood, relative to the death of Daniel Yates, 39 years of age, a gang rider, employed at the Collins Green Colliery. Mr. Henry Hall, Government inspector, was present. The evidence showed that on Wed- nesday morning the deceased was scen to leave a landing to go down a slant, in charge of 14 full tubs of coal. It was his duty to walk in front of the tubs, but a boy who was engaged at the colliery stated that he had often seen the deceased riding on the 4.nbs. When the tubs got to the end of the slant the underlooker (William Jones) saw that three of the tubs were off the rails, and on going down the slant he found the deceased lyino. on the ground, suffering from injuries, and 18 yard's further on he found his lamp and cap, and it was evident he had been dragged that distance.—Mr. Hall stated that on examining the place and questioning the witnesses, he had satisfied himself that the deceased had been riding. He always took the opportunity of preventing gang riding. It ought to be prohi- bited by law, but it was not. He should like to say that if the officials did not know that the man was in the habit of riding, they ought to have known.—The jury returned a verdict of "Acci- dental death." LAWN movrEßs.--Gariand, 51. Bridge-st., Warrington. and at Earlestown.—Advt.

div.head: WINNINGS OF ST. ITELIINS VOLUNTEERS.
div.p: WINNINGS OF ST. ITELIINS VOLUNTEERS.

Below appears a statement of the winnings of the members of the 2nd V. 8., South Lancashire Re- giment, who took part in the various competitions at the National Rifle Association's annual meeting at Bisley. There may be a few other small prizes which may fall to the local men when the report of the National Rifle Association is issued, but it appears that the local men have won £9l in money besides several badges, and a pair of pic- tures which were won by Lieutenant White in the "Graphic " competition. This result compares un- favourably with that or previous years' and there is a great decline in the prowess of the St. Helens re- presentatives at the range bf the National Rifle As- sociation. Last year they won £122, besides a num- ber of valuable jewels, crosses, and badges, and in 1889 they won £143 and a number of badges and one gold jewel. While they had no men in the hundred last year they had two this year, so that they have done better in this respect. In 1889, however, they had two in the sixty, in 1888 three, and in 1887 five. Last year they only won £l3 in the Queen's, while this year the winnings in that competition amount to £l4. The individual win-, flings this year were as follows :—Lieutenant White Queen'sl prize, £3, "Graphic " £5, English Twenty Club £2, Alexandra £2, All-Corners' Aggregate £2, Grand Aggregate £2,Association Cup £2; Armourer- Sergeant West, Queen's, £l2, English Twenty £1; Private R. div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held at the Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday after- noon. There were present Messrs. John Mclntyre (chairman), J. Edwards, H. E. Heywood. J. Parr, J. Brandreth, P. Hall, J. Hall, W. Whittle, J. Ashton (clerk), G. Ashton (assistant clerk), Dr. Adams (medical officer), and J. Farrington (inspector).

div.head: SEWERAGE IMPROVEMENTS.
div.p: SEWERAGE IMPROVEMENTS.

_ A report was read from Mr. L. B. Wells, C.E., respec- ting the sewer in Moss-lane, Moore, also the sewer at Stockton Heath and Sea Flats outfall at Frodsham.— The report was considered and adopted.—The Inspector applied for and obtained an order to have the defective sewer in Northwich-road, Wilderspoot-road, opened and improved in as economical a manner as possible, as it would most likely have to be re-laid in a very short time.—Permission was granted to the Ship Canal Co. to divert the sewer situated near the Twenty Step Bridge, Stockton Heath. as a temporary arrangement until the siphon under the canal is completed.—The Inspector said he had again visited the sewer outfall on the wes- tern side of the river Weaver, and feund that the work was in hand, and that the siphon at the western works was discharging freely through the wooden shoot which had been put in until better provision could be made. SUTTON VILLAGE WATER SUPPLY. The Inspector reported that the Committee appointed at last meeting to deal with this matter had met, but as nothing definite could be concluded as to the best means to be adopted to defray the cost of improving the sup- ply, it was decided to adjourn the meeting so that the agent to the estate might be interviewed and the rate- payers consulted on the subject.

div.head: RESIGNATION OF A VACCINATION OFFICER
div.p: RESIGNATION OF A VACCINATION OFFICER

The Clerk read a letter from Mr. Coleburn tendering his resignation as vaccination officer. He had, he said, held the appointment for many years, ever since the passing of the vaccination act, and he took this step in consequence of increased duties caused by increase of population resulting from the makinc, of the Ship Canal, and feeling that he was growing old—The Chairman in reply to questions, said Mr. Coleburn did not say when his cessation of office commenced, and he was bound to give a month's notice.—The Clerk, in answer to a Guardian, said the salary of the office was £l5 a year, and the vaccination fees came to £l2 12s. id. during last year.—On the motion of Mr. Speakman, seconded by Mr. Parr, it was resolved that the resignation be accepted, as from the end of the quarter.

div.head: COUNTY COUNCIL EXPRN:iES.
div.p: COUNTY COUNCIL EXPRN:iES.

The Clerk produced an abstract of the County Council accounts for the year ended March 21st, 1890, and said this proved that the opinion he and the Chairman of the Board had held that the expenses would be redui!ed was not correct.. The account up to March 31st, 1891, was not yet out. The analysis prqduced showed that there had been an increase of expenditure, chiefly upon main roads.—Mr. Aaron: Does it give how much more has been spent for travelling expenses and salaries ?—The Clerk: It does. There is not very much alteration in that. There is another item. The River Weaver Trus- tees instead of paying £15,000, now only pay £lO,OOO. —Mr. Aaron said for a certainty the salaries and travel- ling expenses were £l,OOO a year more, as four more men had been appointed at £2OO a year each.—Tho Clerk: That is since this account, which only goes up to March, 1890.—Mr. Parr: instead of being about £BO,OOO it is nearer £300,000 expenses.—Mr. Aaron: We shall want a proper balance sheet before we pay any more. —The Clerk said he had been to see the auditor, who said the accounts for 1891 were very complicated, and would not be out for some time.—Mr. Aaron: You have got your accounts out twice a year, or you would very soon be shipped away from here, and we want the same from the County Council.—The Clerk (laughing) : .Yes, but we can't insist upon that.—Mr. Speakman ad- vised the Guardians to direct their attention to the fin- ancial statement which would be given at the next meeting of the County Council, and would be of very great interest to them. He wished te correct any sup- position that the County Council accounts were hot in order.—Mr. Whitlow said it was stated that the extra expenditure was chiefly on the roads, but he could not see that they were one penny the better for the County Council having charge of them.—The Clerk pointed out that the total average county expenditure for the last three years was £101,354 145., and the expenditure for last year £132,348.—Mr. Whitlow said he did not see much yet for the £21,000 increase.—Mr. Speakman said the expenditure seemed to be increasing at a great ratio ; but pointed out that £81,912, contributions from the exchequer must be set against the total.—Mr. Parr: Mr. Speakman may paint it as bright as he likes, but they are a very expensive body of men. _ _ THE BOARD'S FINANCIAL STATE. _
Mr. Brandreth pointed out that the Board had in the bank £1,289 17s. Bd., and after paying amounts due, would have £929.
VOTES OF THANKS. were accorded to the vicar of Runcorn for a present of flowers for the [louse. and Mrs. Marsden for treating the children at Aston.

div.head: STEALING TIMBER AT WIDNES.
div.p: STEALING TIMBER AT WIDNES.
CHARGES AGAINST WORMIEN.

At Widnes Police Court on Monday, Joseph Gerrard, 3, Castle-st., John Rigby, 7, Chatham-st., licnry Rigby, 52, Albert-road, were charged with stealing a quantity of timber on the 22nd inst., valued at 155., the property of the United Alkali' Company. James Marsh, 198, Warrington-road, and Nathaniel Blake, Gorsey-road, were charged with receiving the same, knowing it to have been stolen. —Joseph Haddock, a joiner at Messrs. Pilkington's works, Widnes, said he was on the high level, at these works, on the 22nd inst., when he noticed two or three pieces of new timber in a waste waggon, which was being taken to the waste tip at Cuerdley. As his sus- picions were aroused, he informed Mr. David Horabin, foreman joiner, of what he had seen.—David Horabin was then called, who said that he repeated Haddock's statement to Mr. Tallon, manager, and from in- I formation which he afterwards received he went I to the Cuerdley Manure Works, and there saw the man Nathaniel Blake. He told him he had come to measure the timber that had been bought there. Blake replied "I don't know anything about it." Hora- bin told him it was no use for him to deny it, as he had witnesses to prove that the timber had been sent there. Blake then told witness that someone had been there on the previous night inquiring about some thnber. It had not then come, but on the morning of the 22nd inst. it arrived and he put it into the works, but was not aware that it had been stolen. In a tiort time a lad with a donkey and cart came to fetch the timber. He did not know the man who inquired about the timber.—Peter Cullen, foreman labourer at Messrs. Pilkington's, who was in comnany with Horabin when he went to the Manure Works, corroborated that witness's statement.— Thomas Giller,engine driver atMessrs. Pilkington's,and he tookthe train of waste waggons to the tip at Cuerdley. When he was opposite the Cuerdley Manure Works he saw John Rigby, the brakesman, throw some timber from one of the waggons. He did not see the i timber put in the waggon, neither did he know t was there until he saw Rigby taking it out.— Henry Jones, labourer, stated that he saw Rigby throwing some timber out of a waggon near the Manure Works.—Mr. P. Tallon, manager at-Messrs. Pilkington's said that he sent for John Rigby, the brakesman on the train, and Thomas Giller, the driver, and then asked them what thy knew about the timber. Rigby replied that Gerrard told him he had bought it from the foreman joiner, and that Harry Rigby had put it in the wagon. He then sent for Joseph Ger- rard and Henry Rigbv,and cluarel them with taking the timber. Gerrard said he tho4ht he would not be able to buy it, so he took it, but he was very sorry it should have happened.—J. H. Saxe, aged 12, stepson of pri-

soner Marsh, said Gerrard had asked him to fetch him some timber from Cuerdley Manure Works. He did so, putting it in Marsh's pantry, as requested by Gerrard.— Sergeant Me3rregor stated that he went to Marsh's house on Saturday, and there found the timber'Produced. He took Marsh to the police station, and there charged him and Blake. whom he had previously arrested, with re- ceiving the stolen proporty. They both replied that they did not know it had been stolen. This ended the case for the prosecution.—All the prisoners with the ex- ception of Gerrard, pleaded "not guilty." He also said that the other prisoners knew nothing at all about it.— The Chairman said that as the charge was not suffi- ciently clear against the prisoners John Rigby, H. Rigby, J. Marsh, and M. Blake, they would be discharged, and taking into consideration that it was Gerrard's first offence, he-would only be fined 405., or one month in default.

div.head: MERSEY MISSION TO SEAMEN.
div.p: MERSEY MISSION TO SEAMEN.

The annual tea party in connection with the Runcorn branch of the above mission was held on Tuesday evening, in the Mission Room, Bottom Locks. Upwards of 40 sat down to tea, which had been provided by the Committee. The tables were pre- sided over by Mrs. Shaw and Mrs. Mack. After tea, Mr. William Shaw (missionary), in the absence of the chaplain, took the chair. He called upon Mr. Richard Shaw to make a presentation to ohe of the workers who had taken an active part in the work of the Sunday School, and had lately been married. The presentation took the form of a Bible and a Sankey's hymn book, and inside each book bore the following in- scription :—" Presented to Miss Helena Mars Garratt,on the occasion of her marriage, 14th July, 1891, by the Sunday school teachers in connection with the Runcorn branch of the Mersey Mission to Stamen, as a token of their esteem and well wishes for her future spiritual and temporal welfare." Mr. Ebbrell, on behalf of his wife, begged to thank the subscribers for their very handsome present. A collection was made at the close on behalf of one of the workers of the Mission who had been con- fined at home through sickness for 40 weeks, and amounted to upwards of 18s.

VACCINATION AT ST. HELENS.—SERIOUS CBARGES OF IRREGULARITIES.—The Clerk read the subjoined letter: —" Local Government Board, 21st July, 1891.—Sir,—I am directed by the Local Government Board to advert Ito the inquiry recently made by their inspector, Mr. 'Thompson, into the circumstances of the death of David Cathcart, certified to have died from vaccination diffuse cellulitis, and pneumonia, and I am to state for the in- formation of the guardians of the Prescot Union that in view of the length of the interval which elapsed between the vaccination of the child and the appearance of the disease, which afterwards proved fatal, there would not appear to be sufficient evidence of the operation being concerned in the fatal result. am at the same time, to state that the Board learn from their inspector that this inquiry as to the case in question brought to light the fact that at the St. Helens station,where the child was vaccinated ,the conduct of public vaccination had recently been attended with serious irregularities. It appears that in many instances vaccinations have been entered in the vaccination register as performed by the public vaccinator and the entries initialed by him, which were in reality performed by an assistant, whose employment Its his deputy the board had not authorised. It also appears that as regards 52 cases investigated by Mr. Thompson, all the children vaccinated by Mr. McNicoll or his assistant were entered in the register as having been duly inspected at the vaccination station by the public vaccinator on the Bth day of their vaccination, although a considerable number of them had never been inspected at the station or elsewhere either by himself or his assistant, and that he gave and presumably received payment for certificates of successful vaccination in res- pect of cases where owing to his failure to inspect, he had no knowledge Of the success of the operation. These irregularities appear to the board of so grave a charac- ter that it becomes n•ecessary for them to consider whether, with due regard to the proper administration of the Vaccination Acts, they can allow Mr. McNicoll to act any longer in the capacity of public vaccinator. They request, however, in the first instance that this letter may be communicated to him, and they will be ready to consider any representations which he may submit to them on the subject.—Yours, &c., C. N. DALTON, assist- ant secretary."—The Clerk said that he forwarded a copy of that letter to Dr. McNichol, and he had received the following reply :—" St: Helens, July 23, 1891—Mr. Mann, Dear Sir—l have received your letter enclosing copy of letter from the Local Government Board with respEct of the matter of vaccination in my district. In reply thereto I beg to say (1) that although it is quite true that in such instances vaccinations have been entered in the vaccination register as performed by me, when the actual hand that made all the luci- sions was that of my assistant, yet I was personally present upon all such occasions, and assisted and supervised. It was simply for the purpose of giving him experience that I allowed the assistant to take part in the operation that he did. (2) As to the state- ment that my abistant was not duly appointed as my deputy, I beg to state that on July 30, 1889, I wrote to the Board of Guardians asking that Dr. W. C. Dale might be appointed my deputy as medical officer to the union, and that he was so appointed. . (3.) In many cases the parents of children will not bring back the children for inspection, and as the gurdians when asked to prosecute in such cases refused to do so, I was powerless to prevent them. My long experience had taught me that I was nearly always successful. I made it my practice some time ago to go to the houses and inspect the children who had not been brought back, but the inspector of vaccinations from the Local Government Board said that the practice was not good, and it would lead the people to think that it was not necessary to bring the chil- dren to the surgery. I am, of course, quite willing to undertake that for the future no case shall be signed up unless the child has been brought back to the surgery. In conclusion, I would remind you that I have held the I office of pill )lic vaccinator for more than 40 years, and that I hay- probably performed the operation for over 30,000 ca,a..;, and that this is the first occasion on which any complaint has been made,and I venture to express the opinion that,with such a record, it is ailittle hard that the concluding paragraph of the Local Government Board's letter should be so severe, and I trust that they will be satisfied with my explanation and ...undertaking.—l am, yours faithfully, ROBERT MCNICOLL, public vaccinator." —The Clerk said that a copy of Dr. McNicoll's letter had been sent to the Local Government Board, but lie had not heard anything in reply.—The Guardians decided to await another communication from the Local Govern- ment Board before taking any further steps in the matter. TIIE SALARIES OF VACCINATION OFFICERS.—the Local Government Board wrote acknowledging receipt of the reignation of Mr. P. Chorley, vaccination officer for the St. Helens district. They remarked that they considered Mr. Chorley's remuneration namely 4cl. per case of suc- cessful vaccination was much below the average.—The Chairman said the salary was fixed at that amount owing to the exceptionally large district and the great number of cases that were registered. FREEING THE LIBRA.IIY.
RENOVATION AND IMPROVEMENTS.

On Tuesday next Warrington Public Library will be made free, in the fullest sense of the word, to the inhabitants of Warrington, for on and after that day no subscriptions or charges of any kind will be levied for the loan of books. In view of the change, and of the probable large accession to the number of readers, several ALTERATIONS AND RENOVATIONS have been made at the library, and some alterations have also been made in the rules for the lending department. For a few weeks past the work of cleaning and repainting the library and reading room has been carried on, and a considerable improve- ment in appearance is the result. The large reading room, in addition to the cleaning and re-painting, has had its walls hung with paper of a light and cheerful tint, and this does away to a large extent with the previously rather sombre aspect of the place. The floor, too, has been covered with a thick cork carpet, which will be a boon to readers as it will very much lessen the noise made by persons walk- ing about. In the library, the counter has been raised, and lengthened so as to prevent readers in the future from walking amongst the books to select the volume they want. That, it is obvious, is a privilege which could not be extended to a much enlarged circle of readers without causing inconvenience to the librarian and his.assistant The new arrangement cannot, however, be regarded as a hardship, as a much better way of finding the book one wants is to make use of the very complete and admirably compiled catalogues which are at the disposal of every one at the library. Another alteration that it has been deemed advisable to make is with regard to

div.head: ISSUING OF BOOKS.
div.p: THE ISSUING OF BOOKS.

Hitherto an account has been kept with each sub- scriber, but in future, an account will, so to speak, be kept with each book; that is to say, instead of keepipg a ledger of cards, one card or each bor- rower, there will be one card for each book. Inside the cover of each book, a little pocket has been placed to contain the card when the book is in the library, and when the book is issued the pocket will be useful for keeping the membership card of the borrower who has taken it out, especially as this card would have to be produced every time a book is borrowed. There is also pasted inside the cover of each book a sheet on which will be entered the date on which the book been issued—an arrangement which will enable each borrower who has kept a book beyond the regulation period of a fortnight to calculate the fines that will be due from him when he takes the book back. And it may be added, here, for the benefit of those who are remiss in these matters, that the fines—which are not very heavy, it is true, but mount up if the book is kept long enough, will in future he vigorously exacted, no credit being riven.
A NEW CODE OF RULES

has been issued by the Museum and Library Committee, and it may be worth while noting a few of the alterations that have been made. In future, children under the:age of 14 will not be admitted to the read- ing room except by the permission of tha Librarian this is a rule which the older and more staid frequenters of the rsadinz room will not, we are of opinion, be in- clined to cavil at. In addition to the other occasions on which it has been usual to close the lending department, it will also, in future, be closed at 1 p.m. on Thursdays. The new rules as to borrowinc, provide that books shall be issued free of charge to *borrowers residing or em- ployed in, or rated for, the borough; a ticket entitling to borrow books, will be issued to each person over the age of 12 years who shall present a guarantee signed by a burgess of the boiough, but a burgess may borrow on his own guarrantee. Another rule, which, we believe, is made more for the purpose of protecting too popular burgesses than for any other reason, is that no burgess shall act as guarantee for more than six borrowers. It may be added that at the end of last year the lending library contained 10,873 volumes, the reference library, 11,280, and these, together with pamphlets and mami- scripts amounted to a total collection of 25,803. THE FREE LIBRARY AGITATION.

As our readers will be aware the agitation in Warring- ton for the freeing of the library was commenced about 1885, and has been kept up more or less until the an- nouncement that it would be made free by taking power under the late local Act of Parliament for levying another *d. in the £. The agitation was commenced by the editor of this journal who, in various articles pointed out the injustice of levying a penny in the pound fora free library and still continuing to take subscriptions, instead of making the library free as contemplated by the Public Libraries Act. Various correspondents took the matter ' up warmly, and a committee—composed principally of working-men—was formed with the object of freeing the library. Mr. Thomas Morris acting as chairman. Know- ing that the difficulty was a financial one, it was sought in the first instance to get the subscribers as far as pos- sible to consinue their:subscriptions, and to levy a volun- tary rata of half-penny in the pound; but, as this pro- posal was not supported by the Museum and Library Committee, the agitation from that point took the form of pressing for the lending library being made free apart from any question of subscriptions. Two town's meet- ings were held, and both adopted resolutions in favour of the library being made free. The question was again raised during the year of the Queen's Jubilee, 1887. Alderman Pickmere, who was then Mayor, called a meeting to determine how the jubilee should be celebrated in Warrington, and amongst the pro- posals discussed were the founding of a technical institute, and freeing of the library, and the taking down of the wall and laying out the ground in front of the Town Hall. The final decision was between the library scheme and the Town Hall wall scheme, the lat- ter being adopted by a narrow majority. Curious to say, however, the adopted scheme was never carried out, very few showing themselves willing to contribute to such a project. One concession which was made, as a result of the agitation,was the decision to lend out books at the 'rate of a penny per volume to thoss who were unable or unwilling to pay the quarterly or annual sub- scription. As an evidence of the desire amongst the poorer classes for obtaining books, it may be mentioned that this change practically resulted in doubling the I number of books taken out of the library for home read- ing. Two years or so afterwards, the Town Council re- solved upon applying to Parliament for a bill for autho- rity to purchase the Waterworks, extend the boundaries of the borough, and forother purposes. Up to this time the committee which was working for the freeing of the library had objected to the suggestion to accomplish this telaject by adding to the rates, seeing that this could not be done without a special Bill, but when it was found that a local Bill would, in any case, be proceeded with, Mr. John Walker saw Mr. Robert Davies, who was then chairman of the Library Commiitee, and two or three of the principal officials of the Corporation, and at his sug- gestion it was decided to introduce a clause giving power to levy another id. in the pound with the object of free- ing the library. It was afterwards a moot point whether power should be taken to levy an extra ld. or an extra id., but it was ultimately decided, at a special meeting of ratepayers, that the limit should be another halfpenny in the pound, making the library and museum rate ltd. in the pound. On this basis, so far as the library was concerned, the Bill became law in the course of last year, but the freeing of the library was deferred until the August of this year in order that the Library Committee might have a little in hand to meet the extra cost of preparing for the change. That

div.head: TM? FUNDS
div.p: TM? FUNDS

tinder the new arrangeinent-W-illbe fully sufficient for the purpose is pretty evident upon comparing the returns from the library rate with the added subscription. In 1886, when the agitation was in full force, the penny rate realised £530, and the subscriptions to the library £l5O, giving a total for library and museum purposes of £6BO. In 1890, the total from the rate was £549 and the amount received from subscriptions £l2l—total £670. The penny rate up to March of this year realised £567, and adding the id in the pound which will be taken from the poesent year we get a total of £B5O, or £/80 more than was realised from the penny rate and the subscrip- tions for 1890. This surplus of £lBO will be more than sufficient to cover the extra cost of making the library- free, and will enable the Committee to make some pur- chases in the way of new books and additions to the museum. It is a matter of course to expect that the public will make full use of the boon which 19 being cop- ferred upon them, and we anticipate that during toe coming reading season there will he a much i-az,s,ve.r demand for books than has ever previously been aspen- enced at the Warrington library.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

RUNCORN BONK WORKS COMPANY.—The anmual excur- sion of the employs of the company took place on Satur- day. The workmen with their wives and friends left Frodsham Station by an early train for Birkenhead via Chester, where the day was partly spent, the remaining portion being taken up by visiting Liverpool, New Brighton, &c., and in the evening the party returned arriving back beforenine &clock, after spending an enjoy. able day.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
A RAILWAY STOWAWAY.

At the Warrington magistrates' court on Saturday, before Alderman Burgess (chairman) and Councillor Voisey, Albert Greenwood was charged with riding from Liverpool to Warrington on the London and North- Western Railway Company's line, without a ticket. Railway-Detective Atkinson said the prisoner reached Bank Quay station by the train arriving there at 7.5 p.m. on the previous day, and a porter on opening the door of one of the carriages, found the prisoner lying under the seat. He asked him what he was doing there, and he replied that he had no ticket and no money.—The prisoner now stated that he was a groom, and belonged to Manchester. He was out of employment and had walked from Birmingham to Liverpool in search of some. —He was allowed the alternative of paying 20s. and costs or going to jail for 14 days. OBSTRUCTING THE STREET WITH HAMPERS.

At the magistrates' court, on Monday, John Buckley and Wm. Mason, greengrocers, of Church-st., were charged with obstructing that thoroughfare by allowing hampers to stand in it an unreasonable time, and were both ordered to pay the costs of the summonses. BREACH OF THE WILD BIRDS PRESERVATION ACT. Patrick Garity, the Ship Yard, was charged by In- spector Dowty at the Warrington Police Court, An Mon- day with being in possession on July 21st, of a young thrush during the close season. He was discharged on payment of Is.

div.head: BRUTAL SCOUNDREL
div.p: A BRUTAL SCOUNDREL

At the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, Peter Garrit, 21, Tilley-st., labourer, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Fennell-st., on Saturday night, and with assaulting Isaac Millington, on the same occa- sion. Millington appeared in court bandaged.—lnspec- tor Spinks deposed to .finding Millington with a severe wound on his eve, and to learning that it had been caused by the defendant kicking him. Witness dressed the man's wound and sent him to the Infirmary.—The complainant said about 11 o'clock on Saturday night he heard the prisoner using some very nasty language to his wife because she would not give him a cup to drink some beer out of, and witness was crossing the street to remonstrate with him, when the prisoner, who thought witness was going to strike him, struck witness and knocked him down, and kicked him on the eye as he lay. Two other witnesses gave eviden,:e,:one stating that the complainant's wife threw herself on the top of him to protect him and that prisoner kicked him as he lay under her.—The Mayor remarked that it would not be sate to be out in the town if such men as the prisoner were allowed to be at liberty, and he was sent to prison for three months' hard laboar. THEFT OF A BOOK.

At the Warrington Police Court on Wednesday, John Driver who appeared clothed only in shirt and trousers, was brought up on remand chargsd with stealing from the shop of the "Observer," Printing and Publishing Company, in Sankey-st., on Saturday afternoon, a book value 9d. It appeared from the evidenceof Miss Beatrice Gaunt, who was in.charge of the shop at the time, that the prisoner went in,and said he wanted to see some reli- gious books to ease his mind. She showed him some, and then went to serve Police-Sergeant Doyle, of Frodskam, who was also in the shop, and who was watching the prisoner. The Sergeant saw him put the book into his pocket, and took it from him ; and gave him into custody. P.C. Corbett who gave evidence as to prisoner being taken into custody, said he had torn all his clothes up in the tells.—Mr. Hunt said prisoner when first charged was suffering from the effects of delirium tremens and he was considered hardly responsible, therefore he was re- manded, but he was not so bad as he would have the bench to believe. He was sent to prison for seven days.
THEFT OF A CLOAIL

At the Police Court, Warrington,on- Thursday, Rose Roberts, a young widow, was charged with stealing cn the 19th of June, a lady's waterpro9f cloak, value 255., theproperty of Mrs. Gilroy, wife of George Gilroy, residing at that time in apartments with his wife at Mrs. Smitton's, 3, Golborne-st., but now living in Paul-st. The prisoner was doing some charring for Mrs. Smitton, and at the time that Roberts was in the habit of coming to do this workthe cloak was missed. On Wednesday Mr. Gilroy saw her at Bank Quay station wearing a water- proof cloak,and at his request she came to Mrs. Smitton's where it was identified .by her as Mrs. Gilroy's, Mrs. Gilroy herself subsequently identifying it. The prisoner was given into custody. She stated that she had only borrowed the cloak, and had intended to bring it back. The prosecutor said he had no desire to press the case, and the prisoner was discharged with a caution, a con- viction being recorded.

div.head: DIRET FROM A DRAPER.
div.p: DIRET FROM A DRAPER.

James Hope, was charged at the Warrington Police Court yesterday, with stealing on Tuesday last, six cot- ton shirts, the property of William Coates,draper, Friars' Gate.—Peter Leicester, assistant to Mr. Coates, said he was told that prisoner had stolen the shirts from inside the shop door and followed him up the street, and asked him where he was taking the shirts to, and he replied, "What did yola hang them out for ? " Witness took the shirts from him and let him go.—Mary Webster deposed to seeing the prisoner take the shirts, put them under his coat and walk away, and to entering the shop and in- forming Mr. Coates what she had seen.—Detective- Sergeant Monaghan said he apprehended the prisoner on Tuesday, and he was identified, and admitted the theft. He was committed for trial to the Quarter Sessions.
DAMAGE BY CHILDREN.

At the Warrington Police Court yesterday three little girls, named Lily Williams, Bobette Praeger, and Lily Rigby were charged with doing damage to the amount of 405., to potatoes the property of Elizabeth Green, on ground adjoining Bank Quay mission cricket field, Lovely-lane, on the 21st of July.—The complainant's son deposed to seeing the children rooting up the potatoes. He also stated that he was about to apply for summonses against some boys who had torn the cricket tent to pieces on Thursday night.---Frank Williams was/ called by Mr. Praeger and denied that Williams was on the ground, and that the other children were long enough to commit the damage described. Rigby was dismissed, and the other children ordered to pay Costs. ANOTHER WOMEN'S MELEE. At the Magistrates Court yesterday Mary Madden, wife of John Madden, 3, Cloth Hall-yard, was charged with assaulting Winifred McGuire, Stone-yard, on the £4th of July, George McGuire, labourer, husband of' Winifred, was charged with assaulting Mary Ann Madden, and Winifred McGuire was charged with assaulting Maria Mannion, on the same date. Mr. Brown appeared for the McGuires and said Mary Ann Maddon was the daughter of a Mrs:Farrell, who had recently lost her license as a lodging-house-keeper; and it seemed the Maddons accused McGuire as being the cause of this, which was utterly untrue.—Mannion on* the night of July 25th went to the McGuires' house called out to Mrs. McGuire-" Evictor," and the latter pushed her back,upon which Mannion rushed on her, and then the Maddens in a crowd invaded the house, overturned and smashed the paraffin lamp, and set the place on ire. Mr. Brayshaw came in and put the fire out, and Mrs. McGuire had her eye blackened.—Mrs. MeGuire corrobo- rated, and said Mannion got her by the hair of the head, and then all the Maddons ran down, and the reeults were as described.—Mr. McGuire confirmed her evi- dence.—Mary Maddon said Mr. and Mrs. McGuire came to her house when she was in bed, and tbreatened to kill her, and dragged her by the hair, and knocked about her little girl, Mary Ellett Maddon who was coming into the house. Witness came out and interfered, and Mrs. gcquiFe bit her on the thigh,—Dr. Peacock° deposed to

finding teeth marks on Mary Maddon's leg.—Mary Ellen Maddon deposed to the assault upon her, and her sister gave confirmatory evidence. It appeared that Mr. McGuire had been lying asleep on the sofa, when the crowd came into his house, and he took no part in the row. He was, therefore, dismissed, but the other de- tendants ware bound over in the sum of £lO to keep the peace for six months, and ordered to pay costs, Bs. 6d. each.—Maria Cohen, 9, Stone-yard, was charged with threatening Winifred McGuire, on the 26th July. Mr. Browne appeared for prosecutrix. She was dismissed on payment of 4s. 6d. costs.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH .EOLICE COURT,

MoNDAy.—Before- the Mayor (Alderman R. W. Fran- comb), Alderman Harrison, and Mr. J. Fairclough. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—WiIIiam Butler, 12 Ashton- st., was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Winwick-st., and attempting to rescue Thomas Blair from the custody of P.C. Harrington. The prisoner both struck and kicked the constable in trying to release Blair. He was fined 20s. and costs ;in default a month's hard labour.—Thomas Foy was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Horsemarket-at. on Saturday night. The prisoner had quarrelled with a man he had bought some strawberries from in the street, complain- ing that they were not proper weight, and flew at him, both going down on the ground. On being apprehended he became so violent that the police had to carry him to the station.-ss. and costs.—Daniel Higham, drunk and 'disorderly in Sankey-st., on the 18th of July, ss.—Wm. Caskev, 12th appearance, drunk and disorderly in Knuts- ford-road, on Saturday night, IN.—Samuel Lomax and Henry Dagnall, drunk and disorderly in Friar's Green on Saturday night, ss. each.—Michael Preston, aged 21, 12th appearance, who now appeared with his head cut, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bank- st. on Saturday night. The prisoner who kept reiterat- ing that he meant to turn a different life up alto- gether," was discharged on promising not to come again. —John Scott, labourer, of Acton Grange, for being drunk and disorderly in Dial-st., on Saturday night and assaulting Bridget Kimbling, 20s. and costs.—William Edelsten, drunk and disorderly in Buckley-st., on Satur- day morning. 10s.—Alfred Hoyles, in Sankey-st., on the night of July 18th. He was first disorderly at the per- formance of the Midget Minstrels at the Empire Theatre, then in the street, 10s.—Charles Fudge, canal labourer, and Mary Ann Fudge, his wife, were charged with being drunk and disorderly near his house in Green's Court on the night of the 18th. The defence was that he had a portrait of King William hanging on his wall, and some people came to the door and called King William an Orange bastard, and threatened to smash the picture, and one of them threw a bucket of water in. This aggravated the defendants.—The Mayor: How do you think the canal will ever be finished if you men carry on like this P—They were discharged on payment of ss. i —Thomas Hardman, drunk and disorderly n Green -at., on July 18th, ss. 1 Drumm—John Warburton, in Peter-st., on Saturday night. and John Whittle in Bridge-st., on the night of the 16th. ss. each.--David Plinston, in Wilderspool-road, on July 20th, 205., including costs. DRUNK AND INDECENT.—James Hayes and Susannah Finders, drunk and indecent in Friars Green, early on Sunday morning, ss. and costs each. BAD DANGUAGE.—Kate Cowell, for using obscene lan- guage iii Winwick-road, on the 16th of July, was fined ss. _

GAMBLlNG.—Frederick , Chadwick, Thomas Howard, Peter Harper, and Wm. Legh, lads, for playing at pitch and toss on the fair ground, on the 19th of July, were fined 23. 64. each.—Frederick Dickinson, James Fogg, John Barton, Samuel Wearing, George Wearing, and Wm. Jackson, for playieg with cards for money on the same date, were fined ss. each. CRUELTY TO HORSES.—Isaac Pearson, a Yorkshireman, was charged with cruelty to a horse by travelling it whilebsuffering from a strained tendon and ringbone on the 18th of July, and Wm. Pearson, his father, was charged with causing the horse to be so treated.—lsaac aas fined ss. including costs, and William 205., includ- ing costs.—Abraham Chadwick, farmer, of Bolton, was charged with committing a like offence on the same date, and was discharged on payment of ls.—lnspector, Dow ty, R .S. P.C. A. , prosecuted in the three cases. Morrrwth—Martin Kelly and Joseph Corcoran were summoned on a charge of fighting in Bank-st., on the 21st of July. Kelly was bound over in the sum of £5 to keep the peace for six months, and had to pay the costs 13s*. 6d., and a warrant was ordered for Corcoran, who did not appear.—Thos. Blair was charged with being drunk and disorderly and assaulting P.C.'s ',Harrington and Leathwood in Winwick-road, on Saturday evening. On being apprehended by Harrington for the first offence,the prisoner kicked and struck him and on Leath wood coming to his assistance kicked him also. He was sent to jail for a month with hard labour TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. Robert Garnett (in the chair) and E. M. Crosfield.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Catherine Pearce, in Butter- market-at. on the previous night, she having broken several windows, was committed to gaol for 14 dvs.— Mary Ann Steadman, in Bank-st., discharged on promis- ing to leave the town. STEALING A WATell AND GUARD. Charles Carney, forge labourer, last from Liverpool, was charged with stealing from a bedroom in the dwelling-house of William Woodhouse, spade maker, of 16. Keen-st., on the 20th June, a silver Geneva watch and guard, of tHe value of £l.—The Chief Constable said the prisoner came to Warrington about six week ago, and lodged with the prosecutor. On the morning of the 20th of June he went into prosecutor's bedroom and took the watch and guard from a nail and remarked "I will take the watch and get it repaired for you." He, however, was never seen again until Monday night, nor was anything heard of the watch and guard. In the meantime, information was given to the police. On Monday night the prosecutor was in Bridge-st., when he saw the prisoner, whom he pointed cut to Constable Evans. The officer went to the prisoner and said" Where are the watch and guard you took ? " The prisoner replied "I will tell the truth. I stole them. Here's the guard, but I have had the watch stolen from me." The prisoner was taken to the Police Station, and charged with the offence, and his reply was, "Well, I took the watch to be repaired, and I forgot to take it back. lam sorry for it."—He was committed to gaol for three months with hard labour. INSANITARY PREMISES.—Thomas Hogan, Thomas Shel- don, and James Lee, all living in Cambria-place, were each fined a shilling for allowing their outbuildings to be in an insanitary condition. IkEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Holmes, Alderman Chandley, and Mr. J. Fairclough. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—WiIIiam Lewis, drunk and disorderly in Scotland-road, the previous night, was fined ss. and costs; in default seven days' imprisonment. THIIRSDAY.—Before Major Pickmere. (chairman) Alder-

man Sutton and Captain Ridgeway. DRUNK AND Disoßmutx.—Thoma,sLoydon, drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-st., on the 29th of July, and Alice Gill, in Corporation-st., on the same date, were each fined ss.—Mary Turner in Bridge-st., on the same day, whose excuse was that she was celebrating the birth of her child. Ss.• ASSAULTING HIS MOTITEIL—WiIIiam Foy, of 7, Walsh's Yard, Latchford, was charged with assaulting on July 29th his mother, Bridget Foy, with whom he lives. The defendant had dropped half a crown out of his trousers pocket, and lost his temper about it, striking the complainant.—The Chief Constable said the police were frequently complained to about the defendant assaulting her.—The defendant, who denied the charge, was bound over in his own recognizances of £/.0 and a surety ot £5, to keep the peace for six months; in default a months' imprisonment. 4 FElDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison (chairman),and Dr.

div.head: Gornall.
div.p: Gornall.

ASSAULTS.—James Mooney, labourer, 6, Ship Yard, was charged with assaulting Bridget Rabbitt, on the 25th of July.—The defendant was bound over in the sum of £lO to keep the peace for six months, and ordered to pay the costs.—Sarah Brown was charged with assaulting Sarah Ellen Armitage on the previous Thursday, and Monday, and Sarah Eden Armitage was charged with assaulting Sarah Brown. Mr. A. Browne appeared for Brown, and Mr. P. Davies for Armitage. Both parties lived in Orford-lane, and are the wives of ironworkers ; and both of them were bound over in the sum of £5 to keep the peace for six months, and mulcted in the costs. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Catherine Mooney, charged under a warrant with being drunk and disorderly on Cropper's Brow on April 20th, was dismissed on promis- ing amendment.

DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS. TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. J. C. Parr (chairman), J. Marson, and W. Long. DRUNK.—Martin Delaney and John Muriay, 29th of June, at Moore, is. and costs each. DRUNK AND DISORDLAILY.—Sames Doyle, at Grappen- hall, on the 4th of July, 2s. 6d. and COSIS. DRUNK AND REFUSING TO QUlT.—Joseph Morris, la- bourer, of Norton, was charged with refusing to quit the licensed premises of J. L. Jones,Red Lion Inn ,Moore, on the 29th of June. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the prosecution, and said the licensing laws were at present in a very precarious condition, and it was, therefore, the duty of. every licensed victualler to protect himself to the utmost. He did not, however, press for a severe Penalty. The defendant was fined ss. 'DOGS AT LARGE.—John Murphy, bricksetter's labourer, 9 Wainwright's Yard, Warrington,was fined is. and costs for allowing his dog to be at large unmuzzled, at Preston Brook, on the 13th of July.—William Pierpoint, .and Charles Bryant, tanners, of Latchford, for having two dogs at large unmuzzled, in Thelwall-road, on the 27th of June., were fined is. and costs each.

NO NAME ON HIS CART.—Percy Grange, contractor, Padgate, was charged with being owner of a cart which was used at Stockton Heath, on July 2nd, without having his name and address painted thereon. The name had been written in blue chalk on one side, and three weeks after he was summoned, the name and address were put on in paint.—The defendant had to pay the costs, 3s. 6d. ASLEEP ON HIS LURRY.—Thomas Profitt, carter, of Warrington, was fined 2s. 6d. and costs for being asleep on his furry, at Sevenoaks, on the 27th of July. BREACH OF A NEW LAW BY A COAL DEALER.—John Darbyshire, of Warrington, was charged with committ-

ing a breach of an Act recently passed by selling from his cart at Appleton, on July 6th, bags of coal without having a metal label on each denoting the weight in the bag.—P.S. 179, who proved the case said the defen- dant had two empty bags with labels on.—The defen- dant said the labels he had been using broke off, bu t he now used better ones that would keep on. The Chair- -man remarked that the case was the first of the kind that had come before that Bench, and the defendant was fined 10s. and costs. CHARGE OF ASSAULTING A FARM SERVANT.—George Priestner, farmer, of Whitley, was charged with assault- ing Thos. Murphy, his farm servant, on the 26th of , June. The complainant said the defendant told him to ' milk the COWS, and he, having got wet, replied that he must change his clothes first. Then his master kicked him out of the shippon ; and on his coming for his wages on two following days, kicked him again each time.—Richard Woodward said the complainant refused to milk, but his master never touched him.—The defendant, who referred to a diary to refresh his memory, said he did not assault the defendant. He " sacked " Murphy on his refusing to milk, and re- fusedto give him a week's notice. He offered him money next morning, but he would not have it without the week's notice, and witness told him to go to the County Court for it.—The defendant concluded by exclaiming "What could I do with a man like that ? We are simply a tool in their hands." The case was dismissed. CHARGE OF PERJURY AGAINST A WOMAN.—EIIen Green- ough, a married woman residing at 29,New-road, Latch- ford, was summoned at instance of Elizabeth Gleave, on a charge of having committed wilful and corrupt per- jury in her evidence in an affiliation case in which Elizabeth Gleave was the complainant and Henry Green- ough, the son of Ellen Greenough was the defendant. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the prosecution in the pre- sent case, and Mr. Riley, of St. Helens, for the defend- ant. Mr. Brown stated that on the hearing of the affil- iation case the present defendant was called as a witness as to the payment by her of 2s. per week towards the maintenance of the child for 2 years, to Mrs. Gleave, the mother of the defendant in the affiliation case, in accord- ance with an arrangement come to between them. Mrs. Greenough, had the audacity to swear on the 30th of June when the case was heard that she never paid any such sum and never purchased any boots from Mr. Jenkins's shop in Warrington for the child,and that the money she ii ad paid every week was for washing for her son Henry. But he (Mr. Browne) was prepared to call Mrs. Gleave, Frank Gleave, Mr. Jenkins and another witness who would prove that these statements were untrue. Mrs. Gleave had only done washing for 12 months, and then there was only a matter of a few pence per week for washing Henry Greenough's collars. Mr. Browne stated that he had a witness who would prove that Mrs. Green- ough had admitted to her having-paid £l3 towards the child, but she could not come that day as she was ill. He applied therefore that the case might be heard at Warrington.—Mr. Riley objected to this, and urged that Mr. Browne must either apply for an adjournment of the case or go on with it now.—Mr. Browne accordingly applied for an adjournment.—The magistrates acceded, and the case stood adjourned till next session. • NON-ATTENDANCES AT SCHOOL.—Robert Braban and Thos. John Ormesbv,were at the instance of Mr. De Prez, school attendance officer, fined for not sending their chil- dren regularly to school, the former 10s. and the latter 15s. STEALING FLOWERS.—James Smith was charged with stealing flowers, on July 10th, from various gardens at Walton. A police sergeant saw him on the date named with a quantity of flowers in his possession, and he said he had bought them in Warrington market. Peter Kirk- ham a gardener, however, identified them as from his master's garden; and it was found that flowers were missing from other gardens, and the prisoner was arrested. He was now fined 10s. and casts; in default a month's hard labour in jail.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. H. Reynolds (chairman) and Major Hazlehurst. A STONE THROWER FINED. A boy named William Dyer was summoned for throwing stones in Greenway- road, Runcorn, on the 18th inst, and pleading guilty, he was ordered to pay 55., including costs. QUARREL AMONGST NEIGIb3OIIRS.—Sarah Ann Snow- ball was summoned for assaulting her neighbour, Tryphena Inman, on the 18th inst. Mr. T. J. Peters pro- secuted, and Mr. Lake defended. Mrs. Inman was also summoned for assaulting Mrs. Snowball on the same day.—The evidence adduced concerning the first charge was to the effect that the complainant and defendant re- sided next door to each other in Lower Sewell-st. On the day in question Mrs. Inman's boy, about four years old, rubbed a piece of brick upon her doorstep, but Mrs. Inman, seeing this, immediately had the step cleaned. Mrs. Snowball then commenced to use very obscene lan- guage, and challenged her out to fight. About eight o'clock the same evening, as complainant was going down the entry, defendant got hald of her by the hair with one hand, and with the other struck her several times on the head with a stone, which caused her to bleed very much.—John Inman, husband of the com- plainant, deposed to seeing Mrs. Snowball assault his wife with the stone produced. Mrs. Snowball threatened she would " lay " on him, as well as Mrs. Inman.—Mr. Lake, on behalf of Mrs. Snowball: denied the assault, and said the whole affair appeared to have arisen through petty jealousy. He accused Mrs. Inman of having been the aggressor. This assertion was borne out on oath by Mrs. Snowball and her daughter, and eventually the Bench -ordered both complainant and defendant to be bound over to keep the peace for six months, or in de- fault of finding sureties to go to gaol for seven days. AN INTOLERABLE NUISANCE."—Thos. Wood,Fredrick Dutton, and John Johnson, three youths, were sum- moned for obstructing the footpath in Greenway-road on the 18th inst.—P.C. 258 proved the charge, and said he saw the defendant knock several people off the foot- path.—The defendant pleaded guilty in answer to the charge.—The Chairman said the offence was an intoler- able nuisance. As that was their first offence, they would each be fined ss. including costs. ALLEGED• DRUNKENNESS.—Sarah Price . appeared in answer to an adjourned summons charging her with be- ing drunk and disorderly in Bridge-st., Runcorn, at 11 o'clock on the night of the 19th inst. The defendant, as on the last court day, pleaded not guilty, and called four witnesses to prove her innocence.—The magistrates held there was a doubt in the case, and dismissed it. RESISTING A CANAL CONSTABLE.—A boatman named Thomas Rothwell was charged with resisting a Ship Canal constable named Wm. Doe, whilst in the execution of his duty. It appears that on Saturday the defend- ant's boat was causing an obstruction on the top lock of the Bridgewater Canal, and when requested by the con- stable to remove his boat he refused tb do so. Whilst the constable was removing it he was interfered with by defendant, and had subsequently to bring him to the Mice Station because of his conduct.—Defendaut was fined 2s. ed. and costs, or seven days in default.
WIDNES POLICE COURT.
SaTunDaY.—Before Mr. H. Wade Deacon,

--- --- . - DRUNKENNESS.—James Baxter and Thos. Williams, of no fixed abode, were charged with being drunk on the highway at Widnes, on Friday, and were each fined ss. and costs, or seven days. MONDAY.—Before Messrs. F. H. Gossage and H. Wade-
Deacon.

DRUNRENNESS.—Mary Lloyd, Runcorn; Ann Docherty, Dock-st.; Edward McCulloch, 64, Lugsdale-road ; and George Burns, Parr-st., were each fined ss. and 6s. 6d. costs for being drunk at Widnes, on Saturday night.— John Haggarty, Rainhill, was fined 7s. 6d. and costs, or ten days, for a similar offence. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Joseph Riley, Water-st. ; Patrick Cochran, Nelson-st. ; James McMullen, Welling- ton-st. ; Caleb Kendrick, no fixed abode • Michael Cain, Margaret-st. • Mary Smith, no fixed abode; John Walsh, no fixed abode, were fined 53. and costs each, or seven days, for this offence. BREACH OF THE PEACE.—For this offence Mary Cumasky Cromwell-st., was bound over in her own surety of £lO, and £s,to keep the peace for a month,or in default seven days. ASSAULTING THE POLlCE.—Thomas Cumasky pleaded guilty to a charge of assaulting P.C. Hudson by striking him on the head with his fist whilst he was taking prisoner's mother to the police station for causing a dis- turbance. He was fined 10s. and costs, or ten days' im- prisonment in default. Therr OF A WATCH.—Edith Holden, no fixed abode, was charged with stealing a watch valued at 45., from the dwelling-house of Mrs. Townsend, in March. last. Prisoner came to Mrs. Townsend's house, and asked for relief. As she seemed very respectable Mrs. Townsend took her in and gave her some tea, and allowed her to stay all night. Prisoner left about eleven o'clock next day. In a short time afterwards she missed the watch, and followed prisoner to St. Helens. She was unsuccess- ful in finding her, so she came back and gave information to the police at Widnes. Nothing more was heard of prisoner until she was arrested at Garston for felony. She was then sent to gaol for a month, and on her release was apprehended by P.C. Lord, of Widnes.—She now pleaded guilty of the theft, and was sent to gaol for one month.

WOUNDING A FELLOW WORKMAN.—Patrick Martin, 60, Moss-st., was charged with wounding John Kelly, Moss- Bank, on Saturday last, by striking him on the head twitn a small bar of iron while following his usual em- ployment at the British Alkali Works,Widnes. Dr. Hu- dson said witness came to his surgery on Saturday night. He examined him, and found a large wound on the left ' side of the head penetrating to the bone. It had, to all appearance, ' been caused by a blow with some blunt instrument.—As Kelly is not yet out of danger, Superin- tendent Noblett asked fc!r-a remand until Monday next, which was granted, prisoner being allowed bail.

DRUNKENNESS .—The following persons were fined ss. and costs for drunkenness :—Thomas Roach,commercial traveller; Mary Tobin, Sankey-st. ; Elizabeth Jones, Nelson-st. ; John Tansey, Railway-st. ; Mary Walsh. Bold; and Bridget Green, Lee-st. Rose Kelly was fined 10s. and costs or 14 days. A COAL DEALER FlNED.—William Wiles, a coal dealer, of Salisbury-st., was charged with having in his posses- sion scales for weighing coal which were 2lbs. 12oz. against the purchaser. Inspector Kilpatrick deposed to

examining the scales on one of the defendant's lurries in Violet-st., and to finding the scales to be light as stated. Mr. Knowles appeared for the defence. A fine of 2s. 6d. and 12s. costs was imposed. LIGHT BREAD.—Richard Webster, grocer, Widnes-rd., was charged with selling bread which was not the weight represented. Inspector Kilpatrick said he had seen de- fendant's servant delivering loaves in Egypt-st. He weighed six of the loaves which had been delivered to Mrs. Beesley, and found each of them to be 2oz. short of 41bs. A fine of 2s. 6d. and 13s. costs was imposed. Johnson and Woods pleaded guilty, but Cooney denied the allegation.—Cooney was dismissed, and the other two were fined 6th each and is. 6d. costs. ASSAULT BY A WOMAN.—Maria Moores, Lee-st..was sum- moned for assaulting an old woman, named McQwyer, of Lee-st., and she was bound over to keep the peace for three months.
CHIMNEY ON FlRE.—David Roberts, of Pear-st., was fined is. and 4s. costs for having allowed his dwelling- house chimney to be on fire.

UNMUZZLED Doo.—For allowing his dog to be at large unmuzzled, Thomas Haynes, Charlotte-st., was ordered to pay Costs. BREACH OF THE PEACE.—EIIen Jones, David-st., was. bound over for three months tor having committed a breach of the peace.

WARRINGTON V. BIRKENHEAD PARK.—The recollection of the close victory gained by Warrington over Birken- head Park in the first match this season was sufficient inducement foran attendance above the ordinary at the Arpley ground on Saturday. The Birkenhead club have a good record so far this season, having defeated the majority of their neighbouring clubs around Liverpool. Winningthe toss, the visitors elected to bat, Messrs. Holden and Pickworth being the first representatives. Lee and Clark had prepared a capital wicket, but the light was not of the best, and ere five runs had been totalled Holden was badly run out, after being called for an impossible run. This was a serious disaster for the visitors, but 'Pickworth and Black made a better stand. However, after Black had put together 13, J. J. Crosfield got the Cheshire footballer in two minds, and the scor- ing board read as 25-2-13. Aspinall was caught at the wicket six runs later, and Smith next joined Pickworth. For a time this pair defied all efforts to separate them, so at 38 Smith relieved S. M. Crosfield. The change worked immediately, as in his second over Smith bowled Pickwortn with a yorker for a good 29, the total now being 55. Madden looked like staying, but after he had added a dozen, he got his leg in front of a straight one from S. M. Crosfield, who had relieved Smith, and half the wickets were down for 77. Bell super- seded J. J. Crosfield at this total, and Smith, who did not seem at home with the new deliveries, after adding four,was bowled by Bell for a capital2s. Lowndes was bowled first ball, and Bell narrowly missed doing the hat trick,as Major was beaten by the first ball he received. With the total at 89, Smith resumed at his old end, and the finish soon came, for,with only another run on,Major was bowled for a cipher,whilst Lloyd after adding 8 was sent to the right about,and the innings closed at 99. With such a moderate total to face, the chances were certainly in favour of the home team. Messrs. S. M. Crosfield,and J. J. Crosfield opposed Smith and Holden, the former's first over yielding nine runs, all to J.J. However, 13 runs had only been signalled when Holden got past J. J. Crosfield's defence. With Lee joining his captain, runs came at a steady pace, so at 39 Pickworth relieved Smith, who changed ends. Lee scored freely.from the new bowler, but Smith, who was bowliag a capital length, with the score at 71, got 8. M. Crosfield caught in the slips, his 31 being made by sound cricket. Another stand was made by the next pair, Smith scoring but slowly. The total had reached 89 when Smith bowled the professional for a capital 40, made without a chance, the board reading 85-3-40. div.head: EPPING FOREST TRAGEDY.
div.p: THE EPPING FOREST TRAGEDY.

The inquest on the bodies of two children who were found suffocated in a brook, at Epping Forest, was held on Saturday. The woman Heathcote had told a con- stable before being charged that she placed the children in the stream and intended to drown herself by lying on the top of them, but that there was not enough water to drown her and the children. In a letter to her husband she stated that the children would never get better of influenza, and that she could not bear it longer, as everybody seemed cold to her. She requested to be buried by the side of her darlings. The jury returned a verdict of wilful murder, but added a rider that they considered her of unsound mind at the time.
