div.head: lißc SNAPE AND THE HEYWOOD DIVISION.
div.p: lißc SNAPE AND THE HEYWOOD DIVISION.

Mr. Thomas Snape C.C., of Widnes and Liverpool, the selected Liberal candidate for the Heywood Division, I addressed a well-attended meeting of electors at Bags- late, one of the country districts in the ' division near Haywood, on Monday evening. Mr. T. F. Machison, J.P., presided. sMr.Snape said they were not far distant from the general election, and though he was a man of peace, his spirit rose within him at the thought, for he loved a political fight. (Applause.) The Liberals would he returned to power, and amongst matters they would have to deal with would be the reform of, the system of registration of voters. (Hear, hear.) The qualify- ing period should be reduced from twelve to three months, and the voter should be in suc- cession, no matter what constituency the voter had previously resided in. (Applause.) One man one vote should also accompany that reform, for he was told on high authority that the Tory majority at Bassetlaw was gained by " faggot " votes. There should also be shorter Parliaments, and the legal and returning officer's expenses should be borne by the, public. When Charles Fenwick, the working-man member, was re- turned to the House, his election cost him £465, of which £250 was for the returning officer's expenses. The Government had offered the Free Education Bill as a bribe to the country, but it had failed, as the Irish Local Government Bill would fail, in that respect. The tran- quility that had been restored to Ireland was due to the fact that the people:believed that the English people were prepared to deal justly by them. (Cheers.) After speaking in favour of the reform of the land laws, the dis- establishment of the Church in Wales and Scotland, Eng- land to follow afterwards,Mr. Snape dealt at length with the question of retrenchment in the expenditure on the two great services of the State. Since 1801 to 1890 they had paid for war or war debts £4,892,468,000, against £1,241,390 for the civil service ; and still the services were crying out for more expenditure. They wanted members who would protest against that wasteful and increasing expenditure—(cheers)—and they wanted a second thing, which he would support, and that was a disqualification of the officers in those services from sitt- ing in the Houses of Parliament. (Cheers.) In their local authorities no man was allowed to sit who had a contract with that authority, and be would apply the same principle to parliamentary life. In conclusion, Mr. Snape pointed out that the Liberal policy was the policy of progress, as in direct opposition to the Con- servative policy, which was either reactionary or stationary. (Cheers.) A resolution expressing con- fidence in Mr. Snape as the candidate was carried with enthusiasm.

div.head: EXECUTION AT LINCOLN.
div.p: EXECUTION AT LINCOLN.

Arthur Spencer, aged 22, a. butcher, was executed at Lincoln, on Tuesday, for the murder of Mary Ann Gard- ner, a widow with whom he had lodged, and whom he wished to marry. Berry was the executioner, and al- lowed a drop of five feet. The execution was conducted privately, and the only information which was given to the Press was that it was most expeditiously carried out, without any incident whatever. The prisoner, who had been attentive to the ministrations of the prison chap- lain and of the Bishop of Lincoln, had gained two stone in weight since his committal for trial. The murder for which Spencer was executed was committed at Lincoln on March 31. The prisoner went to his victim's home and discharged four shots from a revolver at her, two of which entered the breazt, and death enaued in an hour. Spencer then attempted suicide. He shot himself in the mouth, a bullet lodging in the base of the skull, which the surgeons were not able to extract.

Ketter6 to the etittor:
AN EXPLANATION.

Sir,—Reference was made in your issue of Saturday last to the absence of four ministers from the meeting of ministers held in Bethsada Lecture Hall. Permit me to say that the three Wesleyan ministers were away at Conference, and that the Rev. P. Williams had unfortun- ately everloeked the hour of meeting, otherwise they would have been present. I have received no authority to speak on behalf of the ministers of Runcorn and neighbourhood, but I am in a position to say that all of them deplore the prevalence of drunkenness, and that they are willing to unite for the purpose of trying to remove or at least lessen the evil.—l am, yours truly, CHARLES FINCH.

div.head: L. k N.-W. RAILWAY CO.
div.p: L. k N.-W. RAILWAY CO.

Sir,—l suppose the public has no remedy against the above company for the abominable bad time the Earles- town and St. Helens trains keep. Only last night I had occasion to travel to the former place (five miles) ; my train (7.8) was thirty-four minutes late ;I arrived there in about an hour from leaving home, and I can walk it in an hour and a quarter. My return train (8.40) was twenty minutes late. Now, I ask you, Mr. Editor, if this islnt enough to make an angel swear, especially when you have business engagements waiting for you. spent about an hour of valuable time on the two plat- forms, waiting to travel five miles. I may just say it is no uncommon occurrence for the train due in at 9.35 p.m. to come crawling intothe station at ten o'clock, and often enough after that.—Yours, &c., T. R. FORD. 22, Froghall-lane, Warrington.

div.head: PAID PREACHERS.
div.p: PAID PREACHERS.

Sir,—According to the census returns recently pre- sented to Parliament the number of persons living in England and Wales on the sth of April, 1891, was 29,001,018. Being curious to know what provision is made for the spiritual needs of this large and important section of the human family, I took the trouble to com- pile some statistics on the subject, and the following figures are what I arrived at. Of course I only present these figures as approximately true, owing to the impos- sibility of obtaining complete returns of the ministry in the various denominations.
As far as I can make out there are in England and
Wales :
24,000 Episcopalian 2,600 Roman Catholic 350 Presbyterian 2,800 Congregational 1,900 Baptist 1,000 Calvinistic Methodist 3,000 Methodist 350 Unitarian 326 Society of Friends
Ministers

Roughly'speakinz' theii,we have an army ofconsiderably more than 36,000 paid preachers who are supposed to devote the whole of their time and energies to caring for the souls of our 29,000,000 of people, to saying nothing of the minor army of local preachers, missionaries, scripture readers, bible women, &c., who receive wages for acting as a kind of recruiting sergeants to their superior officers. Dividing the number, after making due allowance for infants and children of tender years, I arrive at the con- clusion that there is.a paid minister of some kind or other for every 500 of the population capable of receiv- ing religious instruction. And pursuing my inquiries a little further, I find that this army and their appliances cost about ten millions per annum, the Episcopalian con- tingent alone absorbing six millions. Now to reSults : Well, we have a large number of churches and chapels scattered all over the country: small crowds of fashinnably-dressed people are to be seen in these places once or twice on Stmdays and we hear a good deal aboutprayer meetings and other spiritual exercises, and a great deal more about ways and means for multiplying ecclesiastics and ecclesiastical buildings. But the close observer of every day life amongst the re- gions classes finds it rather difficult to believe that we have got any real Chrictians at all. There are,no doubt, scattered here and there through all the sects, some God- fearing men and women who live above the world and its ways, but they are so overwhelmed with the sur- rounding formalism as to be almost invisible. Then the great balk of the working-classes will have nothing to do with the priests and their synagogues. 'Rightly or wrongly they have got it into their heads that the preaching business is taken up for a good living and easy life, end that if there were no salaries there would be no reverend pastors, or at least very few of them. Besides, do they not know from better ezperiencethat their greatest,oppres- sors are the rich men who occupy the places of honour in the synagogues; and they cannot brook the idea of being styled as brethren on Sunday, and treated on Mon- day as hands, souless beings whose main function is to toil in order that others aiaay live in idleness and lu:Tury. And so it has come to pass that there is a wide field and an open door for that astute religions adventurer called -"General Booth," who, with banners and bands of music parades the streets, and boasts loudly of " converting " his thousands and tens of thousands of our labouring classes! Surely he would be a bold man who would venture to say that these are satisfactory results for the expenditure of so many reverend men and so much money for religious purposes. Most thinking people outside the charmed eircle of the churches and chapels will be disposed to regard the paid ministry as a miserable failure. The cause of this failure is net a deficiency: in the supply of ecclesiastics ; it is not due to any special hardness of heart in the working classes who form the great bulk of our population; isor lb it owing ç zany change in the Gospel of Jesus 9f
THE CITERDLEY LAMP-THROWING CASE.. ,

At the Liverpool Assizes, on Wednesday, Theresa Taylor (34), no occupation, was charged with hav- ing, at Cuerdley, on the 14th June, unlawtully, maliciously, and feloniously thrown at Matthew Taylor, a labourer, a lighted paraffin oil lamp, with the intention of setting him on fire.—Mr. Coiling- wood Hope, who prosecuted, said that; the prosecu- tor and prisoner had cohabited as man and wife for eleven years. On the night in question the man had some drink, and when he got home he and his wife had words about money. In the room at the time was their daughter, ten 'years of age. . During the quarrel the prisoner picked up a piece of iron and struck the•prosecutor. After this he got on to the bed to rest, and when he was asleep the prisoner picked up the lamp and threw it at him. His clothes were set on fire, and he was badly burned about the left arm and body. After she had thrown the lamp she ran out of the house, calling to the girl, " Let the burn."—The prisoner now stated that her husband had been calling her names and had been aggravating her. She had recently been confined, was very weak, and did not know what she was doing when she threw the lamp.—The jury found the prisoner guilty. his Lordship said that she had been convicted of a dastardly act, and must go to jail for 18 months, with hard labour.
Nazareth. Perhaps the payment may have something to do with the failure. We shall see later ou.—Yours faithfully, lONA.

div.head: MURDER OF A UIRL AT LEEDS.
div.p: THE MURDER OF A UIRL AT LEEDS.

At the Leeds Assizes on Thursday the trial was com- menced of Walter Lewis Turner and his mother, who are charged with the murder of Barbara Waterhouse, aged five years, at Horsforth. It will be remembered that deceased mysteriously disappeared shortly after she had been seen at play, and her body was afterwards found near the Town Hall. Mrs. Turner two days afterwards confessed to the police that she found a bundle in the house, containing the body,and that after asking her son about it they agreed to convey it to Leeds, and they placed it where it was discovered. She knew nothing of the murder, and her son told her that the bundle had been left with him :by "Jack," a quarryman. On being arrested, the male prisoner said, "You will have to prove rt." Evidence was first given against the mother, who was indicted for being an accessory after the fact, the capital charge being held over. The jury, without leaving the box,returned a verdict of "Guilty." Prisoner was sentenced to: penal servitude for life.

div.head: TRIAL OF THE SON YESTERDAY.
div.p: TRIAL OF THE SON YESTERDAY.

At the Leeds Assizes, yesterday, Walter Lewis Turner was charged with the wilful murder of Barbara Water- house, aged five years, at Horsforth. The prisoner pleaded not guilty in a firm voice. Mr. Thomas, address- ing the jury for the prosecution, said the crime was one of fiendish brutality, and he felt that the jury could come to no other conclusion than that the prisoner was the murderer.
The case after lasting the whole day was adjourned until to-day.
APPOINTMENT OF NEW MAGISTRATES FOR WARRINGTON.

The Town Clerk has now been notified of the fact that the County Sealkeeper at Preston, by order of the Duke of Rutland, Chancellor of the Duchy, has placed on the Commission of the Peace for the borough of Warrington the gentlemen named below :—Messrs. James Fairclough, corn miller, Wilson Patten-st. ; John Geddes, tea merchant, Bold-st. ; Edward Greenall, jun., wine and spirit merchant, Hill Top, Latchford; and John Edward Wright, architect, surveyor, and valuer, Wilson Patten-st. There has, as pointed out two or three weeks ago, been an unusually long delay in the final appointment of these gentlemen as magistrates, but that was explained by the fact that the Chancellor of the Duchy has been absent on the continent. The newly appointed justices will pro- bably be formally sworn in and take their seats at the borough court this (Saturday) morning.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.

At this Court on Thursday,before Judge Ffoulkes, there were down for hearing 2 adjourned plaints, 2 default summonses, 160 original plaints, and 100 judgment summonses. The business generally, was of no public interest. CLAIM BY A JEW DEALER.—llarris Sherowitz, draper, 149! Orford-lane, sued Thomas Chrimes, a labourer, for ss. 9d., balance of an account due for a skirt and a pair of sheets. The defendant's wife admitted having kept the sheets, but said she did so because the plaintiff's traveller would not take them away. She bought them unknown to her husband, and had partly paid for them by instal- ments, a balancq of only is. 3d. remaining. She denied having either ordered or received a skirt. As the plaintiff had omitted to enter the skirt in the defendant's book,his Honour said he could give judgment for is. 3d. only.— Peter Brooks, fustian cutter, Lymm, was sued by the same plaintiff for .E 1 165., a balance of an accouut due for a suit of clothes. Defendant's wife declared that no clothes had been brought to the bouse.—A verdict was given for the plaintiff.
PROFESSOR HUXLEY ON HOME RULE.

Mr. Arthur Bennett of Warrington author of "John Bull and His Other Island," a new edition of which, complete in two iolume,. has recently been published, has received the following letter from Professor Huxley : Dear Sir,—l am very much Obliged for your interesting volumes. Years ago,l had occasion to visit many parts of Ireland, and my impressions of the country and people accord extremely well with yours. They are the most charming people in the world to have to do with in busi- ness the transaction of which requires neither punctuality, accuracy nor moral courage, and, with all their surface bonhommie, they have as keen an eye to the main chance as the children of Israel.

The Irish difficulty lies inthe nature of the people, and the physical character of the country, plus the determina- tion of the papacy to make Ireland the base of 'operations for the religious reconquest of Britain. The last is:probably the:key to the present position of affairs. The Bishops want to use Home Rule for their own purposes, and nothing would suit their book less than separation; their price, •I take it, is the endowment of their churcheS and schools, and it would not surprise me if the "Assisted "Education Act just passed through the House of Commons were made a precedent for legislation on that subject before we are much older.—Ever yours very faithfully,
T. H. HtJXLEY.

div.head: EXAMINER, SAT URP -Y, AUGUST 1, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SAT URP -Y, AUGUST 1, 1891.
THE NEW VOTERS' LISIS.

To-day will be published the new lists of persons entitled to vote in Parliamentary and municipal elections in Warrington. The lists may be seen at the doors of any of the churches or chapels in the town,or at' the Liberal Club,and we would urge upon all Liberals who are qualified to vote to see that their names are on the lists and that their addresses and qualifications are correctly described. In case they discover any errors or omissions in these res- pects, they should at once communicate with Mr. Clayton, at the registration offices, Liberal Club. All claims must be served on the overseers not later than the 20th August. It may be pointed out that in all probability the general election will be fought on the present lists, and therefore it is all the more desirable that every properly qualified person should be upon them.

THE RETIREMENT OF SUPERINTENDENT LEIGHTON.—The Superintendent's successor for the Altrincham division will be Superintendent Walker, who will take leave of his division on the Ist of August. UNITED PRAYER MRETING.—The usual monthly united prayer meeting of the various Nonconformist churches took place in the Primitive Methodist Ohapel, Eagle Brow, Lymm, on Wednesday evening. At. the Lymm Police Court, on Wednesday, before Dr. Brabazon, Edwin Gil- berts, of Newfield, was charged with being drunk on the previous day. Prisoner was fined 55., Including costs, and was allowed seven days in which to pay. The Cross, as usual,came in for a good share of attention, and also "the hollow," the church, &c. The day was not satisfactory, for though bright and clear, and other- wise suitable, the wind shook tho trees badly, and the cameras were not over steady.

THE CORPORATION DEEDS.

The borough auditors—Councillor Muir, and Messrs. J. Harrison and J. Bolton—report to the Finance Com- mittee as follows :—" In accordance with instructions, we have examined the Corporation Deeds, including the Charter of Incorporation,conveyances of property bought bonds given by officials, and other miscellaneous dccu- ments, and have compared thew with the Schedules in the Town Clerk's Office. The conveyances of the Bride well and a plot of land in Leglx-st., have been missing for many years. With these exceptions, we have seen all the deeds, and find them in perfect order and to agree with the lists." div.head: LONGFORD WIRE WORKS. A SPECIAL VISIT.
div.p: THE LONGFORD WIRE WORKS. A SPECIAL VISIT.

The other week we quoted, from Mr. 3. Bucknall Smith's new book upon " Wire : its manufacture and uses," the descriptions therein given of the works of Messrs. Rylands Bros. and the Whitecross Co. Since then one of our own representatives has been privileged to look through the works of the Longford Wire Co., another Warrington firm which has now established a great reputation, particularly by its special products in wire. It may be premised that the Longford Company first put its machinery in motion in the April of 1875. Mr. Buck- nail Smith, in his book,mentions the name of Mr. A. Thornton as the original inventor of the process for reducing wire three or four sizes at one operation, but this is an error, as Mr. Edwin Woods, whilst in the employ of Messrs. Rylands Bros., first devised this process, and a patent for it was secured in 1872 in the names of Messrs. George and Edwin Woods. The Longford Company was, in fact, started for the purpose ot working this patent, and the two patentees were then, as they are now, the managers of the Company. At the commencement, Mr. Geo. Woods, the commercial manager, was secretary and 'Mr. Edwin Woods manager of the works. Both have lately been appointed managing directors, and it is mainly owing to the skill and perseverance of these two gentlemen that the Longford Wire Co. owes its success. They have carried the concern through a period of commercial depression under which many older firms have come to grief. The Company is now paying a good diviend, and is largely extending its business operations. It began business at a perilous time indeed for the English wire trade. German competition is keen now but it was keener still in the later seventies, and it is no wonder that the new enterprise did not at first meet with the success which had been anticinated. Unlike, however, many firms which ventured into the same business about that time, and in later years, they held their ground tenaciously. Atten- tion was given to special branches of wire produc- tion, and at length, about 1885, the Company began. to manufacture those

WIRE 3IATTRASSES which are now extensively used not only in the British Isles but also in many other parts of the world. The managing directors devoted them- selves to the development of this new branch ot trade with characteristic energy. The various ex- hibitions which were held five or six years back were largely utilised for the purpose of bringing the merits of "Woods' patent wire-wove mat- trasses " under the notice of the public, and many a visitor to these exhibitions must have had his curiosity aroused upon seeing the twisted coils of slender wire—of which the mattresses are composed —pressed down with heavy weights, generally reaching above a ton, and yet directly upon the weights being removed the mattrass springing back to its original position. Another development in the same, or at least a similar, line within the. last few years at Longford wire works has been the making of

div.head: WIRE-WOVEN SPRING SEATS
div.p: WIRE-WOVEN SPRING SEATS

and cushions for railway carriages. These are made in similarly-woven wire to the mattrasses, and they seem to have grown rapidly into favour, as, we be- lieve, all the railway companies in England, with the exception of four, have now made use of them,. and last year the Great Eastern Railway Company decided to use no other for their third and second class carriages. In addition to this, large orders for these seats have been placed with the Longford Company by the Indian Government for use on Indian railways. While dealing with this subject it is worth mentioning that the Compau fitted up with their wire-woven specialities the carriage which the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany sent to the Paris exhibition and which won a gold medal ; and they did the same for the sleeping saloon the 'treat Western Company provided for the use of the Prince of Wales. The greater part of the apparatus which is used in the production of these wire-woven fabrics is used in no other place than the Longford works, as it has been devised by the inventive genius of Mr. Edwin Woods himself. This of course gives the Company a great advantage as against competitors in this particular branch of their business, and another advantage they have is a monopoly in the use of a superior class of wire which they do not supply to other mattrass makers.

THE 'WORKS OF THE COMPANY are admirably laid out, each department following in regular succession and in a straight line. A sid- ing of the London and Noah-Western Railway runs the whole length of the works, and from this, coal and the raw material of manufacture can be intro- duced at any point where it may be required, while, on the other .hand, the finished article an be run direct into the wagons from any department. In the matter of carriage, in fact, much ingenuity has been expended in saving labour. A tramway runs from one end of the works to the other, and on this small trucks, capable of carrying between one and two tons, are run, while from the varnishing shed to the railway siding an ingenious little "switch- back" has been raised. At one end of this small trucks are raden with the newly varnished coils of wire, and when once set in motion they run without any further effort right through the main building and come to a stop in the railway wagon which is being laden. On

div.head: ENTERING THE WORKS
div.p: ENTERING THE WORKS

•the attention of the visitor is naturally attracted by the engine house with its large cylinder and gigantic fly-wheel, twenty feet in diameter and fif- teen tons in weight. These engines are the chief source of the motive power employed, but not the only one as there are about half-a-dozen smaller engines at different parts of the establishment. Passing on from here one notices numercus work- people engaged in drawing wire to various degrees of thickness—or thinness, for in some cases it is brought down to a very fine state,and it is interest- ing to note that a certain kind of wire, nefore un- dergoing the "drawing" process is first immersed in buttermilk, and another kind is similarly dipped in the dregs of beer, though the reason for this may not seem very obvious to the uninitiated. In another part of the building the men are busy " coppering " wire by dipping it in chemical solu- tions, to all appearances a spcedy and a simple process; and further away still is

div.head: GALVANIZING SHED.
div.p: THE GALVANIZING SHED.

in which many separate strands of wire are con- tinually being drawn through a large iron trough full of molten " spelter," as the galvanizing metal is called. One cannot go through the Longford Company's establishment without being struck by the fact that their business is by no means confined to the making of wire mattrasses and railway seats, for several of the departments seem to be exclusive- ly engaged in turning out finished wire of other kinds.

div.head: OTHER MACHINES
div.p: OTHER MACHINES

which were in "full blast," so to speak, were the crimping and punching machines which were used preparing the iron bars to which the wire-woven carriage seats are fixed by means of a steam rivett- iug machine. All these machines do their work at e. very rapid rate, the punching machine turning out a couple of bars about every minute. The large room in which the weaving of the mattresses and i carriage seats is carried on s filled with valuable machinery all of wbich was in full work and was manipulated for the most part by young women. As we have before mentioned much of the appara- tus used is of Mr. Edwin Words' own devising. It should be added too, that outside the extensive block of buildings there is a considerable extent of land occupied by the Company. Part of this is taken up with two large reservoirs, of about 120 feet in length each, which are used for condensing the water from the engines, while another part is short- ly to be utilised for a considerable extension of the building. _

div.head: CHARGE AGAINST A LYME BAKER.
div.p: CHARGE AGAINST A LYME BAKER.

Thomas Oregson, a young man, baker, of Eagle Brow,Lymm,and conductor of the Lymm Church of England Temperance band,was charged at the War- rington Police Court, on Monday, with assaulting Eleanor Cook, domestic servant, Mill-lane,Heatley, and Alice Power,domestic servant to Mr. Ramsden, grocer and provision dealer, Lymm, on the London and North-Western Railway Co.'s line, between Warrington and Thelwall, on the 28th June last and also with interfering with the comfort of passengers on the same occasion. Mr. H. Lloyd, of Liverpool, solicitor for the Railway Co., appeared for the prosecution and Mr. Brown, of Stockport, for the defence.—Mr. Lloyd said °nth'. 28th June,the complainants' Sunday out,they went to Warrington,and came back by train leaving Bank 'Quay at 8.15 p.m. rhe defendant assaulted his clients in the train, Cook indecently. Cook complained to her master and mistress, and next day to the station master and Railway Detective Atkinson. The prisoner was ap- prehended, and said "I did pull them about, but it was only for a lark. I was fresh in drink. I don't remem- ber committing an indecent assault, but if I did I am very sorry."—Eleanor Cook said Gregson first pulled Power and then herself about. He pulled her on his knee and assaulted her indecently. She asked him to let her alone, but he would not, and she dragged herself away from him. In the struggle her dress got pulled out of the gathers. She got into a second class compartment at Thelwall.—By Mr. Brown: She saw the defendant and others at Arpley Station, but neither she nor Power called to two of them to come in. Power put her head out of the carriage window, and witness was standing behind her. Power said "There is George Simpson; and all the bandmen." They all got in. No complaint was made at Latchford Station. When witness got out at Thelwall she complained to Alice but nobody else. There were four in the next carriage, which they got into, including two females. She did not complain to them. She never told her affairs to strangers. She denied beinc, out all night that week from her mistress's. Wit- ness'had given her notice to leave.—George Winstanley, gardener, at Beechwood. Lymm, said he got into the carriage at Arpley. There were 14 passengers in it. There was a good deal of larking and touching each other between the complainant and defendant and other young men, but the girls made no objection. They were continually jumping from one seat to another. The defendant did nothing wrong.—Mr. Lloyd said after that evidence he would withdraw the charge as far as Cooke was concerned but would proceed with the other charges. —Alderman Harrison: How was it there were so many in one compartment ?—Mr. Browne: The fault of the Railway Company.—Mr. Fairclough : 14 in that and 4 in the next.—ln reply to Mr. Lloyd, Winstanley said he saw one of the girls strike Gregson.—Mr. Browne : A love tap. (Laughter.) Alice Power corroborated Cooke's evidence except that she denied putting her head out of the window at Arpley. They were standing against the window. On Mr. Browne asking her why they were doing so she replied " Because we did. (Laughter.) They were knocked about from one place to anocher. Her employer was a rival baker to the defendant.—Mr. Browne: Has he interested himself in this.—Witness : That has nothing to do with it.—Witness was not larking with the men—The Bench dismissed both charges of assault.—Mr. Lloyd then proceeded with the charge of annoying passengers.—Cooke was recalled and stated that she told the men there was not room for them and was very much annoyed at their coming in. She and Power could not get out at Latchford because of the men. She screamed when she was assaulted.—A porter who travelled from Arpley in the next compartment de- posed that he heard sounds of laughinc, and larking but no scream. She jumped out at Roebuck siding, and fell, but made no complaint, only said, "I will make him remember it." The defendant was not sober when he alighted.—The Bench dismissed this case also.—Mr. Browne said it was very desirable that the Company should be told if they allowed 14 people to travel in a compartment, they must not come there and prose- cute.

div.head: ST. JAMES' CHURCEI, LATCHFORD.
div.p: ST. JAMES' CHURCEI, LATCHFORD.

The dedication festival was held in the above church, on Sunday. The day's proceedings com- menced with the celebration of the Holy Commu- nion at eight o'clock. At the morning service the preacher was the Vicar (the Rev. F. Slater) and at the evening service the Rector of Warrington (the Rev. F. W. Willis). In the afternoon a children's flower service was held. The offertories were devoted to the church expenses. On the following evening the anniversary supper was held in the schools, the Vicar (the Rev. F. Slater) in the chair. Among the ladies arid gentlemen present were the Rector of Warrington ; Mrs. Slater. Mrs. Carleton, the Rev. H. Ashe, Mr. Charles White, the Misses White, Mr. and Mrs. John White, Mr. and Mrs. Lister Ilaye, Mr. and Mrs. McGregor, Mrs. Gibson Smith, Miss Smith, Mrs. Hall, Miss Bolton, Mr. C. S. Burgess (vicar's warden), Mr. J. W. Tauranac (people's warden), Captain Hutchinson, Mr. and Mrs. H. N. Houghton, Mr. and Mrs. Hollowell, Mrs. Fairhurst, Mr. and Mr. G. Venn, and Mr. Frank Booth (organist of the church). A band, organised by Mr. Whitfield, was in attendance, and played an interesting selection of music during the evening. The supper was supplied by Mr. T. 0. Speakman, of Wildersp.ool. The toast of "The Queen" was pro- posed by the Chairman, and "The Bishop and Clergy of the Diocese" by Mr. H. N. Houghton. The CHAIRMAN responded, and in the course of his remarks referred to the schools, and said that when they looked forward they were not quite sure of their posi- tion—whether they would be able to maintain it or not. He did not intend to say much about the probable work- ing of the Education Act; their correspondent and their good churchwardens would be able to explain what was likely to take place, but everyone was quite alive to the necessity of doingsomething. The Bishop of the diocese, who was, unfortunately, in bed owing to an attack of influenza, had been doing his best to organise some kind of union among the various schools of the diocese,so that their po:i itio n should be strengthened instead of weakened. There seemed to be a feeling that the Free Education Act was a step—built by friendly hands—but nevertheless a step towards what seemed looming in the distance, namely, the extinction of voluntary schools. It seemed extremely likely that the position of the voluntary schools, like their own, where religion and the Church's teaching was taught, would become extremely difficult, almost impossible in fact. He did not mean to say at once, but in the future. What did it mean? It meant that where schools were not voluntary,but were supported by Government, or by the rates, that it would become impossible to teach religion, as they now taught its Their children would grow up without any definite idea. about religion. They would not know their Bibles, still less their Prayer Book and their catechism would be altogether unknown. They would have a kind of general notion that they ought to be good, and nothing more. He 'wondered whether all parents quite saw that. He maintained that it was not half an education if the most important thing of all was forgotten, and if the children could not give a sensible reason for the faith that was in them. (Applause.)—The Vicar con- cluded by proposing " The Festival preacher."— The RECTOR responded, and congratulated the congre- gation of St. James' upon the excellent service which was held on the previous night. They had need to be thankful and to take courage. He (Mr. Willis) had had no ambition to be Rector of Warrington, but he was consumed with a desire to promote the faith of the Catholic Church and everything connected with it. a•nd he longed to see the clergy more united to help each other. He believed they were coming more and more together. (Applause.)—Mr. C. WHITE proposed "Our friends," and Mr. JOHN WHITE responded.—Mr. JOHN WHITE proposed "The Church and parish of St. James," and congratulated them upon the position of Church matters in the town, and expressed a hope that they might not lose their worthy Rector by his being taken away and made a Bishop, as a former Rector was. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He was glad to hear Mr. Willis say that he had no ambition, and that might serve as a safeguard against his removal; and for their own sake, and for that of the parish, he also hoped Mr. Slater would not be taken from them. (Hear, hear.)— Mr. C. S. BURGESS responded, and referred at length to the work of the parish, and remarked that the reports relating to the schools were exceedingly good. The teaching was both conscientious and thorough, and the discipline and tone everything one could desire. Deno- minational schools appeared to be on their trial, and if their friends who were wealthy did not do more than they had done, the results in most cases would be disas- trous, unless the Church schools combined and decided upon some new action, whereby the poorer schools might be assisted by the richer ones. If that was not done they would have to have recourse to a school board, and there was no one who would regret that more than himself. (Applause.)---Mr.TAIIRANAC proposed the

div.head: SMALL DEPUTATION.
div.p: A SMALL DEPUTATION.

The Sanitary Committee have resclved that Councillor Henry Roberts and the Medical Officer, of Health be appointed to attend the International Congress of Hygiene and Demography to be held in London in August.

div.head: COIYNCILIOR HEATON RESIGNS
div.p: COIYNCILIOR HEATON RESIGNS
The Cemetery Committee reports that Councillor Hea- ton has resigned his place as deputy-chairman of the Committee, and that Councillor Jenkins has been ap- pointed in his stead.

div.head: TEMPORARY LINE IN .THE MERSEY.
div.p: THE TEMPORARY LINE IN .THE MERSEY.

The Rivers Committee reports the following corres- pondence relating to the Vyrnwy Aqueduct :—Warring- ton, June 29th, 1891. Dear, Sir,—l am instructed by the Rivers Committee to say that on the 15th inst. the joints of the temporary pipe line were above the level of the bed of the channel. Yours truly, Thos. Longdin. G. F. Deacon, Esq., C.E.—Westminster, S.W., 3rd July, 1891. Dear Sir,—Mersey Temporary Crossing. lam obtaining a report upon the subject of your letter; but I think it will be found that although some of the flanges at the joints might be bare, they were below the level of the bed on either side of tbe pipe. In such.cases the sand is almost invariably scoured away to a larger ex- tent at the flanges thin elsewhere. Yours truly, George F. Deacon. T. Longdin, Esq.

div.head: FIRE BRIGADE.
div.p: THE FIRE BRIGADE.
The Fire Engine Committee recommendlhat Thomas Ratcliffe be appointed engineer to the brigade.
TFIE WARRINGTON GYMNASIUM.

The Town Clerk has laid before the General Purposes Committee a copy of the Scheme of the Charity Com- missioners, and the Rules and Regulations for the man- agement of "The Warrington Gymnasium and Reading Room," by which it is provided that the Town Council of Warrington may appoint three members of the Com- mittee of Management, and the Committee has resolved that Alderman Wright and Councillors Pierpoint and Henry Roberts be appointed members of the Committee accordingly.

div.head: TELEGRAPH LINE,
div.p: A TELEGRAPH LINE,

The Post Office Telegraph Department having applied for permission to lay a line of telegraph from Winmar- leigh-st. along the south side of Wilson Patten-st. to the Wigan Coal & Iron Co.'s yard, Arpley, the General Pur- poses Committee has resolved that the Corporation con- sent to the' laying of the wires on the undertaking of the Postmaster General to make good any damage which may be done in the execution and maintenance of the work.

div.head: COUNTY COUNCIL AREAS.
div.p: THE COUNTY COUNCIL AREAS.

The Local Government Board has issued an order with regard to the alterations of the County Council i electoral areas of Warrington and Winwick n conse- quence of the recent extension of the borough. The following contains the list of the order :—The boundaries of the number one, number two, and number three elec- toral divisions of the borough of Warrington shall be altered so that those electoral divisions shall respectively consist of the areas described hereunder; namely,— The number one electoral division shall comprise the Town Hall, Whitecross, and Bewsey Wards of the borough; the number two electoral division shall comprise the Orford, St. John's, and Fairfield Wards of the borough; the number three electoral division shall comprise the Howley, Saint Austin's, and Latchford Wards of the borough. The Winwick electoral division of the County of Lancaster shall be altered by the exclu- sion therefrom of so much of the township of Warrington as was added to the borough of Warrington by the Warrington Extension and Water Act, 1890.

div.head: GAS METER RENTS.
div.p: GAS METER RENTS.

There are two motions standing in the name of Coun- cillor Hill. The first reads as follows :—" That when a deposit is charged to any persons about to consume gas it be inserted on the deposit form the amount of deposit paid the Gas Committee, the rate of interest of such deposit, and the date such interest is due." The follow- ing is the second -motion : "That the Gas Committee be requested as soon as possible to abolish all meter rents; and all meters in the possession of the gas consumer and their property be purchased by the Gas Committee."

div.head: VIGOROUS PERENNIAL.
div.p: A VIGOROUS PERENNIAL.

I motion which has appeared on several agenda papers in the name of Councillor Dixon is again on that for next Council meeting. The motion is in the following terms: —That the members of the Sanitary Committee be re- quired to resign forthwith in consequence of their mismanagement of Longford and the Intercepting Depots."
Lord Dartmouth was weaker yesterday morning. Mr. Wroughton, . member for North Berks, will not seek re-election.

The Prince of Naples and staff left London yesterday, for Plymouth, where the royal visitor will be the guest of the Duke of Edinburgh. Captain O'Shea telegraphs to the " National Press " that any suggestion that he was under pecuniary obligation to Mr. Parnell is false.

div.head: LIBEL ON A WARRINGTON SOLICITOR.
div.p: LIBEL ON A WARRINGTON SOLICITOR.
THE CASE AT THE ASSIZES.

On Thursday, John Warburton, a well-known farmer, living at Lovely-lane, Warrington, was in- dicted at the Liverpool Assizes, before Mr. Justice Smith, with having published defamatory libels with regard to Mr. W. IL J. 'Jenkins, solicitor, of Warrington, and a member of the Warrington Town Council, in the shape' of a post card and a letter on the 6th and 26th May. Mr. McConnell, instructed by Mr. Unsworth, of Warrington, prosecuted, and Mr. Slice, instructed by Mr. Arthur Browne, of Warrington, defended. The defendant pleaded guilty. Mr. McConnell said, on behalf of the prosecutor, that those proceedings would not have been taken had it not been that the defendant had issued a series of libels which had been going on for some time.and of which the present was only a part. Pro- ceedings for libels of a similar nature had been taken against the prosecutor in the civil court. The Judge : Is that the verdict for £2O damage? Mr. McConnell: Yes. There have been previous ver- dicts against the prisoner but he did not wish to go into that as it had reference to proceedings in which Mr. Jenkins acted as solicitor for defendant's wife. The pri- soner had now pleaded guilty. and he wished to say that Mr. Jenkins had not taken those proceedings as a matter of criminal punishment, and on behalf of the prisoner's family he would recommend him to his lordship's favour- able .consideration. All Mr. Jenkins wanted was to have an end put to that system of pestering him at his house and his business and as a member of the Corpora- tion of_Warrington.

The Judge: What is your suggestion ? Mr. McConnell said he should suggest that In con- sideration of the defendant paying part of the costs, he should be bound over to come up for judgment in case those libels were renewed.

Mr. She said the prosecution were inclined to mercy, and he thought his learned friend had been very fair in that matter, and he thanked him for the course he had taken. He might be allowed to say one or two words in respect to the prisoner. He was a man passed middle life, and was the father of ten children, one of whom he understood, was over 21 years of age and the others younger. All his misconduct in reference to the libels had arisen out of the relationship existing between the prisoner and his wife. Mr. Jenkins having acted pro- fessionally for the wife. He believed that the prisoner had noanimosity againsb Mr.:Jenkins on any other ground than that. Prisolier's wife had died since his commit- ment; and he had been broken down with grief, and did not now entertain any ill-feeling towards anybody. He was quite willing that byegones should be really bye- gones,and he had resolved never again to repeat the libels. Prisoner had some time ago been in a lunatic asylum. He (Mr. Shee) was glad that no real harm had been done to Mr. Jenkins, who was far too well-known in Warring- ton for the libels to have any effect, and he asked that the prisoner might, under the circumstances, be allowed to go out on his own recognisances. The Judge (to Mr. Jenkins who had entered the witness box) : What about the costs? Mr. Jenkins said the costs were upwards of £5O, but he was willing to take only £35 from the prisoner. The Judge: What position r is he in with regard to money? Mr. Jenkins replied that prisoner was very well off, being worth £5,000 or £6,000. The Judge (to prisoner) : You have pleaded guilty to libelling the prosecutor, and you have libelled him more than once,simply because he acted as yourwife's solicitor. He has acted very generously, and has asked me not to send you to prison. I will not do so, but I will tell you this: I will put a stop to this libelling. I will bind you over to come up for judgment when called upon, and if you go on libelling Mr. Jenkins, the judge who comes after me will pass my sentence and will send you to prison for six months. If you do not libel Mr. Jenkins, you will hear no more about the matter. You must pay the costs, £35. The prisoner was then bound over in the sum of £lOO to come, when called upon, before any court of assize in the county to receive judgment for the misdemeanour to which he had pleaded guilty.

At the County Sessions PoliCe Court, Liverpool, on Saturday, a young girl named Alice Stapleton, an in- mate of the Lancashire Roman Cdtholic Reformatory School, at Old Swan, was sentenced to a month's hard labour for attempting to stab Lucy Ennis, one of the teachers.
DIOCESAN ANNIVERSARY 11-I,ETING AT WARRINGTON.

The anniversary in connection with the united dioceses/of Ch3ster and Liverpool and the arch- deaconries of Manchester and Blackburn clergy institutions was held at Warrington on Wednesday at the Training College. The annual meeting of subscribers was the first part of the proceedings. At this Mr. Clement Royds, of Rochdale, presided. The report of the chaplain (the Rev. F. W. Willis) and of the Committee of Management were read. Canon Penrhyn was appointed secretary in place of Canon Greenall, resigned and Mr. H. Greenall, his son in place of Mr. E. Greenall as treasurer —The anniversary sermon was afterwards preached in the Parish Church, by Bishop Cramer Roberts, before a large congregation. —ln the afternoon dinner was partaken of at the institution. A number of toasts having been proposed, Mr. W. P. Fullagher proposed "The town and trade of Warrinz- ton." He remarked that Warrington, in the future, was going to be a more important town than in the past, when the dirty ditch,' as the Mayor of Liverpool so un- courteously termed the Ship Canal, was completed.—Mr. J. R. Buckton responded. He said the town of Warring- ton was in a most flourishing condition. Further works were contemplated, and land would be taken up for them before long, without waiting for the completion of the canal.—The proceedings then concluded.

div.head: CRICKET.
div.p: CRICKET.
Gloster beat Notts by-one-i;:iings and 122 runs ; Kent beat Somerset by four wickets; Yorkshire 97 for five. SERIOUS REGIMENTAL FIRE.

The officers' mess of the Ist Battalion Royal Irish Regi- ment, at Colchester, was destroyed by fire yesterday morning, with the colours of the battalion and the relics of battles fromßlenheim to the Soudan. THE EARLDOM OF BERKELEY.

The House of Lords yesterday, gave judgment in the Berkeley Peerage case. They found there was no evid- ence of marriage between the fifth Earl and Mary Cole, in 1675, and that their issue was, consequently, illegiti- mate. The claim of Baron Fitzhardinge therefore fell to the ground,and Mr. Randall Mowbray Thomas Berkeley's claim to the title of Earl of Berkeley was sustained. THE FRENCH RAILWAY CATASTROPHE. MESSAGE FROM THE QUEEN. The Queen sent the following telegram to Lord Salis- bury on hearing of the railway disaster near Paris : "Pray express to M. Waddington my concern at the terrible railwaydisaster near Paris, and my sympathy with the bereaved relatives, and hopes that the injured are doing well. V.R." Her Majesty's message was duly communicated to the French Government. MR. SPURGEON'S ILLNESS. Mr. Spurgeon's condition was unchanged on Thurs- day, except that he has taken less nourishment. Yesterday, Drs. Miller and Kidd issued the following bulletin 9.30 a.m. Rev. C. H. Spurgeon had a good sleep last night. His strength is maintained." MR. DWYER GRAY REPUDIATES MR. PARNELL'S

div.head: LEADERSHIP.
div.p: LEADERSHIP.

Mr. E. Dwyer Gray writes to the " Freeman's Jour- nal" that he entirely agrees with Mr. Dillon's speech, yesterday, repudiating the leadership of Mr. Parnell. His marriage is no marriage according to the Catholic Church, and he has a letter respecting Mr. Campbell which removes all doubt as to certain circumstances. As the owner of nearly half the property of the "Freeman," he might be held responsible, and he feels bound to make this statement.

TUB LIVERPOOL MURDER. At the Liverpool Assizes, yesterday, John Conway, 60, was indicted for the murder of the boy Nicholas Martin, on the 16th of May. Prisoner pleaded not guilty in a firm voice, and listened attentively to the opening of the case. Mr. Hopwood narrated the facts from the dis- covery of the bc4dy in a sailor's bag floatingin the docks. The prisoner was proved to have purchased the bag, and the deceased was last seen in company With the pri- soner. Blood was found at the prisoner's office as :secre- tary of the Firemen's Union. Counsel concluded the opening address by saying thathe could assign no motive for the crime. Evidence for the prosecution was then called. The case was heard at great length, and it was not expected to end yesterday.
COLLISION OFF DOVER

div.head: LIVERPOOL BARQUE RUN DOWN. EIGHT MEN DROWNED. •
div.p: LIVERPOOL BARQUE RUN DOWN. EIGHT MEN DROWNED. •

A shocking collision occurred off Dover yesterday morning, only one survivor of a crew of nine hands being saved. The barque Forma, which was hound from Liver- pool with a cargo of salt to Copenhagen, was about five miles off Dover when she was run into by the London steamer Godrnunding, at d sank immediately. The only survivor, the carpenter (Jensen) on being interviewed tit the Sailors' Home, and who appeared almost dazed at the fate which had befallen the rest of the crew, states that he was picked up by the fishing smack Gem. He heard loud cries on deck And a crash. He ran up from his cabin and on reaching the deck found the vessel sinking bowsfirst. The crew were near the head of: the ship trying to get on the steamer, but the vessel sank im- mediately, and they disappeared with her. He ran to the stern, which rose in the high water. The barque then capsized, floating bottom upwards. He had a most miraculous escape, and cannot account for being saved at all, but he clung to some wreckage and managed to get on to the bottom of the ship, from which position he was rescued by the fishing smack and brought to Dover. Nothing was seen of the rest of the crew, some of them being, it is supposed, drowned in their bunks. Another telegram says the steamer proceeded on her voyage leaving the poor fellows to their fate.
TERRIBLE DISASTER AT SEA. 260 PERSONS DROWNED.

SAN FRANCISCO, FRlDAY.—Advices from Yokohama state that the Tamae Maru of Hakodate, while returning from Suto on the 12th inst., with 320 labourers on board, collided w ith the steamer Vigoshi Maru off Shira- game. The Tamae Maru sank, and 260 persons were drowned or are still missing. The captain, the first officer, and sixty labourers were saved. • YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at quarter-past four. Earl Delawar gave notice for next session to call attention to railway charges for the carriage of British timber. The rates and charges bills of various Railway Companies were read a third time. The Redemption of Rent Ireland Bill was read a second time and the House adjourned at 5.25.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.

The Speaker took the chair at five minutes past three. THE INDIAN CouNcirs.—Mr. SAMUEL SMITH gave notice that on the Indian Budget he would move—" That this House is of opinion that some measure to amend the Indian Councils Act, embodying the elective principle, is highly desirable, and should be passed into law as soon as possible." SMALL HOLDINGS.—Mr. GOSCHEN, replying to Mr Jesse Colling, said the Government had no intention to de- part from their pledges in regard tosmall holdings. The President of the Board of Agriculture would introduce a bill next session dealing with the question.

UNCONSTITUTIONAL CONDUCT.—kr. GOSCHEN, replying to Sir W. Harcourt in reference to the Lords' amend- ment to the Free Education Bill which the Speaker had pronounced to be unconstitutional, said the Govern- ment would introduce a similar amendment witheut in- volving a breach af principle. Sir W. HARCOURT con- tended that the business of the House of Commons was to reject the Lords' amendment, and allow that House to introduce another_ if it choose. (Opposition cheers.) _ _ _
SUPPLY.—The House went into C6nimittee of supply and the Lord advocate introduced the Scotch Educa- tion Vote.—Considerable discussion followed.

div.head: FARM FIRE NEAR WARRINGTON.
div.p: FARM FIRE NEAR WARRINGTON.

Late on the afternoon of Thursday a teamsman in one of the adjoining fields observed smoke issuing from the straw shed in the farm yard of Hill Foot Farm, Stockton Heath, occupied by Mr. Thomas Percival. An alarm was raised, and the Wilderspool fire brigade were on the spot in about ten minutes. The straw shed adjoins a large shippon of which about thirty head of cattle had just been taken ont to grass. A valuable horse, which was in the loose box close at hand was rescued from the flames and smoke with much difficulty. The fire continued burning till late in the night, and the straw shed was destroyed, only the bare walls remaining. The damage done is estimated at .£l5O which is covered by insurance.

WARRINGTON UNION. —RELIEVING OFFICER WANTED.—The Guardians require the services of a Relieving Officer for the No. 2 District of the Union. The person to be appointed must be active and intelligent, com- petent to keep accounts and to comply with the duties as they are required to be fulfilled by the Law and by the Consolidated Orders. His whole time will be due, by law, to the duties. He will be required to appropriate such time to office attend- ance, visitation of the poor. payment of relief, Bcc., according to regulations of the Guardians. He will also be required to resideat such part oh is District as they may approve. Salary £lOO per annum, payable quarterly.—Candidates must apply, in their own handwriting, by letter, (with not more than three recent testimonials) endorsed "Re- lieving Officer" and to be sent to roe on or before Tues- day, August 11th. Selected candidates will be at liberty to attend before the Guardians at their Board meeting on Wed- nesday, August 26th. The person appointed will be required to enter into a bond for £lOO with an approved guarantee society. Canvassing the Goardians is strictly prohibited, and will be deemed a disqualification. By order, JAMES C. SUTTON, Union Clerk. Bewsey Chambers, Warrington..

The winning hit was sent up by Clarke after seventy-five minutes' play. With the total at 111. Madden was tried in place of Smith, and after being knocked to the tune of 23 runs in three overs, had the satisfaction of taking both batsmen in successive balls. Voisey, who was fielding as substitute, dismissing Clarke, Captain Manson was run out on attempting a third run; but Bell was not dismissed until he had added 16. The liveliest cricket of the afternoon was shown when Voisey and Yonge were together. Both are reputed big hitters, and on Saturday they were seen at their best. Smith brought off a fine catch on the boundary,which dismissed Voisey, but Yonge and Podmore played out time, the former hitting out brillantly to the close. The total had reached 246 at seven o'clock when stumps were drawn. Yonge being credited with 36, whilst Podmore had a dozen. Warrington fielded well throughout, whilst Clarke kept wickets in first-class style. Birkenhead naturally tired in their long outing, but taken on the whole they performed creditably, and the catches which dismissed Smith, Voisey, and S. M. Crosfield were indeed smart. A VOLUNTEEER KILLED. While a squad of hien belonging to the Chorley Rifle Volunteers were practising on Saturday evening, a shot fired by Private Kay was not signalled. A man was sent 0 ascertain the reason, and he found Sergeant Hodgkin- son, the marker, lying dead under the mantlet with a bullet wound through his breast. THE COLCHESTER TRAGEDY. Thomas Sadler was found guilty at Chelmsford Assizes on Wednesday of the murder of William Wass at Colchester. The convict had taken Mrs. Wass away from her home, and he had the audacity to ask Wass to allow the children to visit their mother. Wass refused, and the prisoner stabbed him fatally. He expressed no remorse. He was sentenced to death. SIX MEN KILLED AT GATESHEAD. A fatal accident occurred on Sunday Aight at Friars' Goose Chemical , Works, Gateshead-on-Tyne. Six con- densers were used for the production of hydrochloric acid, and one of them fell, the debris falling upon a man named Elesslop. Six men went to his assistance, and three adjacent condensers, each 90ft. high and 6ft. square, fell upon them. Of the men thus crushed six were killed, and one, who was jammed in a small open space, escaped. The body of Mcßuskin, one of the victims of the Gateshead disaster, was recovered on Thursday morn- ing. All the bodies have been found except Heslop's.

AN ELECTIONEERING ROMANCE. The recent cettest at Carlow has been followed by an event quite idyllic in its character. Mr. John Deasy, M.P., one of the anti-Parneltite Whips, took part in the struggle; but politics did not blind his eyes to the charms of a young lady whom he met. He came, he saw, he compered ; and next week he will be married to Miss Tynan, the daughter of a large hotel keeper at Carlow. SENTENCE OF DEATH. At the Central Criminal Court, London, on Thursday, Robert Bradshaw (54), labourer, was sentenced to death for the murder of his wife at Bermondsey. The prisoner and his wife had lived unhappily, and the woman had taken out a summons against him for threatening her. As she refused to withdraw the summons the prisoner cut her throat, nearly severing the head from the body. The defence was that the prisoner was not accountable for his actions 'at the time. • RAID ON BETTING MEN IN LIVERPOOL. The Liverpool police on Thursday made a raid upon the Opera House Hotel, Williamson-square, and Arrested a large number of persons,alleged to have been found en- gaged in betting transactions. A raid was also made on the premises at the corner of Scotland-lane and Old Post Office-place, and a beerhouse at 199, Wavertree- road, and in all eighty persons were taken to the Detective Office. All were liberated on giving their naraes and addresses, with the exception of eight. Seven of the persons arrested by the Liverpool police on 1 hursday, in raids on public-houses and beerhouses, were yesterday remanded and admitted to bail.
